scored.name: UK land promotion / grey-belt freehold (hunt 9)
scored.one_line: Buy or option edge-of-settlement farmland, win outline consent, sell to housebuilders or build.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: Hope value priced in; LandTech scores grey belt; promoter keeps 5-25%.
scored.frame: The rung is strategic land promotion: option or buy a field and win outline consent, without building anything. This rung is discrete and sellable, and housebuilders are capitalised buyers. But "discovery" (picking the right site) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is the proving step itself: a contested planning, legal and political process of local-plan representations, technical reports, committee and appeal. That step is hard and is not abstracted away.
scored.step_up: Bare farmland is about £10k/acre. With detailed consent it reaches about £500k/acre, and up to £1m/acre in the south of England (£600k/acre in the north), per Farmers Weekly. A York benchmark paper (June 2025) cites a Leeds residential site at £523k/ha. That is a raw ~50-100x, but edge-of-settlement and grey-belt land already trades or options at hope value (often £25-100k/acre, or a 75-90% share of proceeds to the landowner). Under a promotion agreement the promoter keeps about 10-15% (one promoter says 10-15%; a law-firm case study says about 15% of net proceeds). Realistic return on promotion capital is a few-x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs roughly £100k to £1m+ of planning, technical-report and appeal costs, and takes 3-7 years. Sources: law-firm guidance (planning costs run to tens of thousands of pounds or more; the promoter is not reimbursed if consent fails) and an appeal case study (often several years). Base rate: a 2018 CPRE briefing found 54% of promoter-led appeals allowed, against about 28% for housing appeals generally. That puts the base rate inside the relaxed 30-70% band. ML's lift on picking sites is plausibly 1.2-1.5x, because outcomes depend on politics, the 5-year housing land supply position and the planning inspector, which data predicts only partly.
scored.data: The data is public and semi-illegible: planning portals, appeal decisions, SHLAA/HELAA assessments, local-plan evidence bases, Green Belt reviews and committee minutes, scattered across more than 300 local authorities as PDFs. But LandTech, Searchland and Nimbus already extract it and score grey-belt sites. The key outcome signals (HELAA suitability ratings, plan allocations, 5YHLS status) are written into legible fields, which is the regulator-writes-the-answer problem.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. Options and promotion agreements are negotiated with farmers. But landowners are usually advised by land agents who know about hope value and grey belt, so the purchase discount relative to proven value is limited.
scored.buyer: Volume housebuilders such as Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey and Vistry, plus regional builders and registered providers. They are deep-pocketed and buy consented land routinely.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: promotion, then land servicing and infrastructure, then housebuilding (the UK volume builders are £3-6B companies), then build-to-rent and other operated assets. A path to a large company is real, though it is a UK-only prize.
scored.fatal_flaw: It is an informed, competitive market. Hope value is already priced in by agents and established promoters (Gladman, Catesby, Richborough), and grey-belt scoring is already sold by LandTech and Searchland. The proving step is a political and legal process, not a hidden-data discovery. So ML adds only a marginal hit-rate edge and does not create a spread that informed buyers miss.
scored.one_line_reason: Real capitalised buyers and a large ladder, but site discovery is a minority of the work, hope value is already priced, data incumbents already score grey belt, and ML's lift on consent odds is about 1.2-1.5x at best.

scored.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
scored.one_line: Buy patents from Chapter 7/11 estates, ABC sales, dead startups (fabless, LiDAR, photonics, quantum, microLED) and lapse-bound owners for $2-50k; ML maps claims against FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, SEM cross-sections, datasheets, driver code and papers to build evidence-of-use charts; sell charted patents to NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools and funders.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion whose value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation (about $2-5M per case to trial, with roughly 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidating all challenged claims). So buyers pay roughly 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4x, and the market is thin. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy an orphan patent and turn it into a charted, assertable patent'. Inside that rung, finding the infringing product and mapping claims to it (from FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, datasheets, driver code) is about 80-90% of the work. The physical step, buying a teardown or SEM cross-section, costs a few thousand dollars and is easy. But the rung's output is a contestable opinion, not proof. Real proof (a license, settlement or verdict) sits in the next rung, litigation, and there the work is mostly legal spend and fights over validity, not discovery. Buyers exist (NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools like RPX and Unified Patents, litigation funders), but the market is thin and opaque.
scored.step_up: Unproven: orphan patents from estates, ABC sales and lapse-bound owners go for about $2-50k each (the candidate's figure, consistent with bulk estate sales). Large estate portfolios cleared at about $0.5M per patent (Kodak about $525M for about 1,100; Nortel $4.5B for 6,000+), but those were premium, already-licensed SEP-heavy pools. Proven: a well-charted patent on a high-volume product typically sells for about $100k-$1M to an NPE or funder. Asserting it ourselves, NPE campaigns settle at $0.5-10M+ per defendant (outlier: Samsung's $191M NPE verdict). That is roughly a 10-30x step on the sale route. Asserting ourselves can reach far more, but at about $2-5M per case to trial.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Producing the chart is cheap, about $5-30k per patent with ML plus a teardown, so on that measure proving fails the C3 'expensive' test. The real proving step is litigation or licensing: about $2-5M and 2-4 years per case to trial, with about 98% of district-court cases settling. Rough base rate: maybe 20-40% of assertions give a positive return. About 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidate all challenged claims. ML can plausibly lift the share of bought patents with a real, high-revenue infringer by 1.5-2x, because it filters before purchase. It does little for validity risk, which is the main way cases fail. Net, about 1.2-1.5x on cost per monetised patent. Sources: patent-litigation cost surveys (AIPLA, my estimate from memory), Unified Patents slide (98% settle), PTAB statistics.
scored.data: The signal is public but hard to read: FCC equipment-authorization internal photos and test reports, third-party teardowns, die shots, datasheets, open-source driver code, academic papers. These are scattered, image-heavy and unstructured, and no legible field records 'this patent reads on product X'. That does not hold for validity. Prior art and PTAB outcomes are legible and widely mined. Incumbents (RPX, Unified Patents, aggregators, claim-chart vendors) increasingly run their own AI charting tools, so the edge is real but eroding.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought, not claimed first-come. Sellers are Chapter 7/11 trustees, ABC assignees, dead startups' investors and owners about to let maintenance fees lapse. They usually cannot chart against products and sell cheaply, often in bulk at section 363 auctions. Lapse dates are legible from USPTO maintenance data, so the cheapest orphans are visible to anyone. The discount comes from the charting work, not from data access.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: NPEs (for example IP Bridge-type entities), aggregators (Acacia, Dominion Harbor), defensive pools (RPX, Allied Security Trust, Unified Patents) and litigation funders (Burford, Fortress). Under round 6 the company can also operate as its own funded NPE. The market is thin, prices are negotiated privately, and buyers discount heavily for validity risk.
scored.ladder: orphan patent purchase -> ML evidence-of-use chart -> sale to NPE or funder, or own licensing campaign -> funded assertion vehicle / patent fund -> maybe a defensive-pool or licensing platform. It tops out at a few-$B NPE, fund or aggregator: global patent assertion and licensing revenue is roughly $10-20B a year, and political and legal headwinds against NPEs and litigation funding keep growing. There is no physical-industry chain to integrate into, so no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proof is never actually established. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion, and value comes only after years of litigation or licensing (about $2-5M per case, with about 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions killing all challenged claims). ML improves the infringement side but not validity, which is the main way cases fail. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a vertically integrated chain.
scored.one_line_reason: Under the round-6 rubric, operating as our own NPE lifts C2 to a real 2-5x on capital, but charting is cheap, real proof (litigation) is a validity coin-flip ML barely helps with, and the ladder caps at a niche few-$B assertion business.

scored.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
scored.one_line: Option farmland next to substations ML predicts have load headroom; prove with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter; sell powered land to data-center developers. Rescore of powered brownfields with a real purchase discount.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: Proving here is not a cheap discovery event that the landowner then owns. Utility capacity is allocated to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the data first. The study result is non-binding and decays as others queue. Rising tariffs specifically target speculative flippers. And well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen the same public grid data. So the 10^3x step-up needs heavy capital commitment and network upgrades, not an ML-fou
scored.frame: The rung is a farmland option plus a utility large-load study or will-serve letter, sold as 'powered land'. Picking the site from public grid data is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is site control, rezoning, study deposits, and above all committed capacity. Committed capacity needs a signed ESA, collateral and network upgrades, and it goes to whoever commits capital, not to whoever reads the data first. Altus (80 transactions, 2026) finds that committed utility load, not a study result, is the strongest predictor of price. The physical and capital step is not trivial. A capitalised buyer does exist: hyperscalers and developers like QTS, Amazon and Tract.
scored.step_up: Farmland runs about $9.5k-23k/acre (PA average $9,560; NE Wisconsin $23k). Data-center land runs a $28k/acre median in markets with limited committed load, $60k/acre offered for 261 PA acres, about $330k/acre paid by QTS in Salem Twp PA (35x farm value), and a $2.8M/acre median in N. Virginia. Sites within half a mile of a high-voltage substation trade at about 2x sites 2-5 miles away. So the realistic step-up is 3-35x and only arrives with committed capacity; a study alone earns far less. Sources: Altus Group, Fortune, farm press.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $75k-600k plus 6-24 months. Examples: AEP Ohio charges a load study fee of up to $100k per 100 MW plus a deposit and an 8-year minimum term. Xcel Colorado has a $120k study deposit, about $600k upfront in total. EKPC charges $75k plus $1k per MW. Option payments come on top. Proving is expensive, so it passes the relaxed C3. I estimate the base rate that a chosen substation shows usable headroom on a reasonable timeline at about 30-50%. ML over hosting-capacity maps, FERC 715 data and IRPs plausibly lifts that 1.2-1.5x. Earlier work found lookup tables and queue data match ML on grid siting, so 1.5x+ is doubtful.
scored.data: The signal is semi-legible. Utility hosting-capacity maps, FERC Form 715 data, IRPs, queue data and large-load tariff dockets are public and partly structured. Well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen them. Some illegible pieces exist, such as scanned IRP appendices and substation one-lines, but the outcome (available MW) is increasingly published in hosting-capacity fields.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the option is bought from farmers. But owners near substations are now informed and pricing up: a PA farmer rejected $15M at $60k/acre, NE Wisconsin farmland doubled in 3 years, and the 'powered land' rebrand is widespread. The purchase discount is shrinking quickly and is being arbitraged by many players.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Google), colocation and data-center developers (QTS, Vantage, Aligned), and land platforms (Tract). They are heavily capitalised and paying $60k-330k+/acre for sites with committed capacity.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: powered land, then entitled and energized land with committed capacity, then powered shell or build-to-suit, then data-center development and operation, then owned on-site generation or PPAs. Tract shows that the land-to-campus path supports a multi-$B company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proof is not a cheap discovery event the landholder then owns. Value comes from committed utility capacity, which goes to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral (large-load tariffs at 36+ utilities now require study fees, deposits, minimum bills and exit fees designed to screen out speculators). The grid signal is semi-legible and already screened by well-funded incumbents. Farmers near substations are already pricing in the premium, so the ML read does not create the spread.
scored.one_line_reason: There is a real buyer and a big ladder, and relaxed C3 lets an expensive study count. But the step-up requires capital-committed capacity rather than ML discovery, grid data is semi-legible to incumbents, and the farmland purchase discount is eroding fast. Total 14/25.

scored.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Options agricultural parcels in counties whose planning records imply data center approval, obtains rezoning or special exception, and sells entitled parcels to data center developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The proving step mostly succeeds already (an estimated ~60-80% of rezonings and special-use permits are approved), so ML can raise the hit rate by at most ~1.5x, not 10x. The value step-up is driven mainly by power availability, which planning records cannot prove, rather than by zoning. Incumbents such as Tract and brokers already run this playbook on land owners who know the premium exists.
scored.frame: The rung is "entitled land": a parcel under option, rezoned or granted a special exception, then sold to a data center developer. Choosing the parcel and predicting approval from planning minutes, comprehensive plans and hearing records is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is not discovery. It is political and legal work (hearings, organising against opponents, lawsuits) and, above all, proving power through utility will-serve letters and interconnection, which planning records cannot show. The rung does have capitalised buyers (hyperscalers and developers such as Tract, QTS and Vantage). But the physical/legal proving step is not trivial, and power, not zoning, is the main thing that makes a site valuable.
scored.step_up: Unproven: farmland at about $6k/acre in Kentucky and $10.5-23k/acre in northeast Wisconsin. Developer offers on likely data center sites: $35k/acre in Mason County KY (2025), about $60k/acre in Lancaster PA (2026), and $26M for a Kentucky farm, about 10x farm value. So the step-up is about 5-10x (10^0.7-10^1), not 10^4. Most of that premium is already offered to owners before rezoning, and it depends on power being available. Sources: Fortune Feb 2026, TweakTown, Dairy News Today.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not sourced: each rezoning or special-exception attempt costs roughly $100k-$500k (legal, engineering, traffic and noise studies, option fees) and takes 6-18 months, so the proving step is expensive enough to qualify. Base approval rate was an estimated ~60-80% for rezonings and special-use permits, but it is falling. Data Center Watch counts about $64B of projects blocked or delayed in the two years to March 2025, $98B in Q2 2025 alone, and at least $152-156B (48+ projects) in 2025. Hundreds of opposition groups were active in 42 states. Saline Township MI denied a 575-acre rezoning. If approval falls toward ~50%, ML that reads meeting minutes and opposition signals plausibly gives about 1.3-1.6x on cost per entitled parcel. That is close to full strength under the relaxed C3, but it is capped because power is the real gate.
scored.data: Planning commission minutes, hearing videos and transcripts, comprehensive plans, overlay districts and public comment records are public, illegible and scattered across about 3,000 counties. That is genuinely hard data that incumbents extract only by hand or through brokers. The outcome is not pre-written in a status field before the vote. Legibility is falling, though: Data Center Watch and others already track opposition with LLMs, and the power signal (utility IRPs, interconnection queues) is the main driver and is already semi-legible.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought: options are taken on private farmland, not claimed first-come. But sellers can now read the opportunity. Nationwide press coverage of $35k-60k/acre offers means farmers ask for data center premiums before any rezoning, and land trusts compete (Lancaster Farmland Trust bought development rights). The cheap-buy spread is mostly gone in hot counties and survives only in counties nobody is watching yet, where power is often missing.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) and developers or REITs (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, Tract, CyrusOne) have large budgets for sites. They pay most for land that is both powered and entitled.
scored.ladder: Option, then entitled parcel, then powered land (substation and interconnection), then powered shell, then a built and leased data center campus, then operator or REIT, possibly with self-generated power. The ladder runs to a very large company: Tract-like land banking leads to QTS-scale operators. Each rung above entitlement needs large capital and power access, which the ML edge does not supply.
scored.fatal_flaw: What makes the land valuable is power availability, not zoning. Planning records cannot prove power, and the zoning premium is already widely known: farmers are offered $35k-60k/acre before rezoning, and Tract and brokers run this playbook. So the ML-led proof of approval leaves little spread between the purchase price and the proven price.
scored.one_line_reason: The ladder is real and well funded, and ML on illegible minutes can lift approval odds about 1.3-1.5x on an expensive step. But power, not zoning, drives the 5-10x premium, and sellers already know it, so there is little cheap-buy spread to capture.

scored.name: Orphaned defense spare-part production lines, re-qualified as the DLA source
scored.one_line: Buy tooling, drawings and inventory of discontinued defense spare-part lines from shuttered small manufacturers and estates at liquidation prices. ML over DLA solicitation and award history picks part families with persistent unfilled demand and high single-source prices. Pay for first-article testing and source approval, then run the line as the qualified source and capture sole-source margins.
scored.unproven_right: Assets of a closed or exiting supplier (tooling, legacy technical data, part numbers, inventory), bought for ~$100k-2M in liquidation by sellers who cannot judge which NSNs still carry demand.
scored.proving_step: Source Approval Request plus First Article Test or qualification per part family: ~$50-500k each, 6-24 months, SAR approval perhaps 40-60%. ML over solicitation text, past award prices and rejection reasons plausibly lifts approved-and-profitable families 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: DLA, Army, Navy and Air Force sustainment commands and defense primes buying under multi-year IDIQs at sole-source prices; or a defense aftermarket roll-up (TransDigm-style, 15-20x EBITDA).
scored.public_data: DLA DIBBS solicitations and award history, SAM.gov and FPDS awards, DLA tech data packages and AMSC/AMC codes, GAO/DoD IG DMSMS reports, PACER and UCC liquidation records, largely scanned or unstructured attachments.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$1-4M per line against $5-20M value as a sole-source line, roughly 3-5x. Multi-$B prize (DoD spares sustainment $40B+/yr). Ladder: aftermarket roll-up, then subsystem OEM. Related to the killed FAA PMA parts idea; rescore honestly.
scored.frame: The rung is "qualified source for a defense part family". Picking NSNs with persistent unfilled demand is maybe 25-35% of the work. Most of the rest is physical and ongoing: restarting tooling, AS9100 and quality systems, first articles that come back rejected, and then actually producing parts at scale for years. Unlike a drill hit, the manufacturing step is neither trivial nor abstracted. A buyer with capital exists (DLA, the services, and roll-ups like TransDigm), but what they buy is a running, cash-flowing production line, not a proven right sitting there to be picked up.
scored.step_up: The candidate's claim is $1-4M all-in per line against $5-20M value as a sole-source line, about 3-5x. TransDigm shows sole-source spare parts carry huge margins. A DoD IG report found $16.1M of excess profit on 46 of 47 parts sold for $26.2M (2015-17), with profit of 17% to 4,451%. A 2021 follow-up found at least $20.8M of excess profit on 105 parts, and 94 of 107 TransDigm parts studied were sole-source. Three things cut against this. Most orphaned NSNs have small annual demand, so a single line is often worth under $5M. DLA Competition Advocates exist to break sole-source pricing: a SAR is by definition a request to become an additional source, and a 2014 DLA slide (possibly no longer current) says a new source can get 40% of an award even when it is not the lowest bidder. And IG and congressional scrutiny caps prices on parts below the TINA threshold. A realistic return is about 2-4x on capital. The prize is multi-$B only as a roll-up of hundreds of lines.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Per DLA SAR guidance and briefings, a SAR plus first article costs roughly $50-500k per part family. Full approval typically takes 12-18 months (DLA 2016 slide on the related RPPOB program). DLA publishes no current approval rate, so 40-60% is the candidate's own assumption. Proving is therefore expensive, which meets the relaxed C3 bar. But the ML edge in choosing families is moderate. Award history, prices and AMSC/AMC codes are already legible in DIBBS and FPDS, and incumbents and brokers already mine them. The more likely ML lift is ~1.2-1.5x, not 2x, and would come mainly from reading rejection reasons and scanned tech data packages.
scored.data: The signal is partly illegible: scanned TDPs, SAR rejection narratives, PACER and UCC liquidation records. But the outcome is largely written into legible fields. DIBBS award history, unit prices, AMSC codes (which flag sole-source or restricted status) and the approved-source CAGE lists already show which NSNs are sole-source and how often they are bought. That is the regulator-writes-the-answer problem the rubric warns about. On the right: assets of shuttered shops do sell cheaply at auction and from estates. But the buyer often does not get an ownable right. A build-to-print shop's drawings usually belong to the OEM or the government, approved-source status is tied to the CAGE code and facility and may not survive an asset sale, and the government can compete the NSN anyway. The right is weak and not exclusive.
scored.right_bought: Tooling, inventory, legacy drawings and part-number history of a closed or exiting small defense supplier, bought in liquidation for ~$100k-2M. Legal title to the technical data and transfer of approved-source status are uncertain.
scored.buyer: DLA Land and Maritime, Aviation and Troop Support; the services' sustainment commands; primes buying under IDIQs. Exit buyer: aftermarket roll-ups at 15-20x EBITDA (TransDigm, and private-equity defense aftermarket platforms).
scored.ladder: There is a strong ladder: single part lines, then a roll-up of hundreds of proprietary or sole-source NSNs (the TransDigm playbook, worth ~$70B+ in market value), then subsystem OEM and design authority, then platform sustainment prime. This is the strongest criterion.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is captured by manufacturing, not by discovery. Requalifying and then running a defense production line (first articles, AS9100, years of making parts) dominates cost and risk, so no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. The sole-source status the margin depends on is legible in DIBBS, AMSC codes and award fields, and DLA's competition program exists to erode it. This is the same flaw that killed FAA PMA parts.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough to pass the relaxed C3, and the roll-up ladder is real. But manufacturing dominates the work, the sole-source signal sits in legible DIBBS and AMSC fields, and the bought right often carries no transferable technical data or source status. So it fails C1 and C4, much as FAA PMA did.

scored.name: Entitlement arbitrage on exurban residential land (ML over planning records)
scored.one_line: Option raw agricultural or exurban parcels at farm value on the Sun Belt growth fringe. ML over scanned planning-commission and council minutes, meeting video transcripts, staff reports, comp plans, sewer and water master plans, CIPs and past rezoning votes predicts which parcels will get utility service, annexation and rezoning. Push entitlements through and sell entitled acreage or finished lots to national homebuilders, who pay the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options or contingent contracts on 50-500 acre farm parcels at ag or unentitled value ($5-30k/acre), from farm families, estates and local brokers who do not read utility master plans or council voting patterns.
scored.proving_step: Annexation, rezoning, PUD or preliminary plat approval with utility will-serve letters: engineering, traffic, drainage and environmental studies plus hearings. About $150k-$2M and 1-4 years per project, base approval roughly 40-65%. ML trained on thousands of hearing outcomes and staff-report language plausibly lifts hit rate 1.5-2x and drops doomed options before deposits go hard.
scored.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, NVR, Toll) running land-light strategies through land bankers (Millrose, Varde), paying cash for entitled land and finished lots.
scored.public_data: Scanned and PDF city and county planning-commission and council agendas, minutes and staff reports (Granicus/Legistar archives, YouTube video), municipal Capital Improvement Plans, sewer and water master-plan PDFs, annexation agreements, comprehensive and future land-use plans, past rezoning case files and votes, county GIS parcel, zoning, assessor and deed records. Approval odds are in no legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: Raw land at $10-30k/acre becomes $80-300k/acre entitled (3-10x on land); about 3-8x on cash at risk with an option structure. Multi-$B prize (US homebuilders buy $50B+ of land a year). Ladder: horizontal development, build-for-rent or vertical homebuilding, master-planned community operator.
scored.frame: The rung is clear and sellable: an entitled parcel or finished lots, sold to a homebuilder or land banker. But discovery is not 80%+ of the work. Finding a parcel in the path of sewer and water is maybe 25-40% of the work. The rest is the entitlement campaign itself: engineering, traffic, drainage and environmental studies, negotiating with staff, managing neighbors, hearings and offsite utility commitments. That is a 1-4 year political and engineering job, the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: doing the proving step is harder than picking the site.
scored.step_up: Entitled land sells for about 2-4x equivalent raw land (acres.com), or about 2x (allieddev). The candidate's 3-10x figure is optimistic for the US Sun Belt; the 22x UK green-belt figure comes from a much more restrictive planning system. Realtor.com/MortgagePoint: raw-land price per acre fell 2.4% YoY into 2026 against 1.1% for build-ready land, so the spread is real but modest. With an option structure the return on cash at risk might be 3-5x on winners, but entitlement spend of $150k-$2M per project plus carry, spread across the failures, pulls the blended return on total capital toward about 2-3x. The prize is multi-$B: builders buy tens of $B of land a year, and Millrose alone took 24,000 homesites from Rausch Coleman for about $900M.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about $150k-$2M and takes 1-4 years, so the expensive-proving leg is met. The base rate is moderate: projects that reach a hearing are usually approved, because staff negotiate them first, while early-stage parcel picks fail more often (the candidate's own 40-65%, no hard source found). Staff recommendations and the comp plan's future land-use map already predict outcomes well. The only ML precedent I found is a Frederick County MD logit study, which found rezonings largely follow the ordinance and staff. So ML's realistic gain on cost per entitled parcel is about 1.2-1.5x from dropping doomed options early, not 2x+.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned minutes, meeting video, CIP and master-plan PDFs. But many cities now publish searchable Legistar/Granicus records, and staff reports carry a legible approve/deny recommendation that summarises much of the outcome. Comp-plan future land-use maps and sewer service-area boundaries are often already GIS layers. ReZone AI (now part of Shovels) already extracts rezoning decisions from US council and planning minutes, so the extraction edge is being commoditised.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought via options or contingent contracts, as Dhruv's rubric requires. But Sun Belt fringe farmland is an informed market. Builder land-acquisition teams, land brokers, land bankers and local entitlement developers all read the utility master plans. Fringe sellers routinely ask hope-value prices well above ag value; WSJ/Land.com: Sun Belt vacant land per acre more than doubled in two years through Q2 2022. Sellers who truly cannot read the plans exist, but at the margin, not at scale.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and active: public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, NVR, Toll) and land bankers such as Millrose, which earned $185M of option fees in Q1 2026 and went from 11 to 18 third-party partners. Millrose describes its assets as having 'limited entitlement and development risk', which confirms that buyers pay up for entitled land and avoid raw-land risk.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is strong: entitlement, then horizontal development and finished lots, then build-for-rent or vertical homebuilding, then master-planned community operator (Howard Hughes, Forestar-style). The chain is very large, but every rung is crowded with well-capitalised incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Entitlement is a political and engineering campaign of 1-4 years and $150k-$2M per project. It runs in an informed, competitive land market: builder land teams, brokers and land bankers already read the master plans, and fringe sellers price in hope value. The approval signal is also largely legible already, in staff recommendations and future land-use maps. So ML neither makes discovery 80% of the rung nor buys the land at a deep discount to its proven value.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer, ladder and prize are real, but the rung is an execution-heavy entitlement campaign in a market of informed bidders, so ML-led discovery gives only a modest ~1.2-1.5x edge, not a Terranox-style frame.

scored.name: Local-permit-first utility solar and BESS projects in moratorium-risk counties
scored.one_line: Lease-option farmland near substations and secure county conditional-use or special-use permits for solar or storage. ML reads scanned county minutes, hearing transcripts, public comment, petitions, moratorium ordinances and local news to predict which counties and townships will approve before a moratorium hits. Sell permitted, NTP-ready projects to IPPs or own and operate them. Not queue arbitrage: queue position is taken as given and still needs interconnection.
scored.unproven_right: Land lease options at roughly $5-200/acre/yr during the option period, signed before competitors know which counties will approve; landowners and most small developers cannot read county politics.
scored.proving_step: County CUP or siting-board approval plus environmental and cultural surveys, decommissioning plans and hearings. About $200k-$2M and 1-3 years. Local denial and moratorium rates run 30-50% in many Midwest counties; ML avoiding hostile boards plausibly gives 1.5-2x on cost per permitted MW.
scored.proven_buyer: IPPs, utilities and infrastructure funds (NextEra, AES, Brookfield, Invenergy), paying $0.05-0.15/W for permitted NTP-ready projects versus near zero for raw site control.
scored.public_data: County board and zoning-board agendas, minutes and video across about 3,000 counties, ordinance and moratorium text, public comment letters and petitions, local news archives, state siting-board dockets (Ohio OPSB, Illinois county filings), LBNL and Columbia Sabin Center opposition databases, USFWS/SHPO review letters (scanned). Approval is not in a legible field until the vote.
scored.rough_step_up: About $1-3M development spend becomes $10-30M for a 200MW project (roughly 5-20x per success, 3-5x across a portfolio). Multi-$B prize. Ladder: own and operate generation, merchant storage platform, utility-scale IPP. Partly overlaps the killed interconnection idea.
scored.frame: The rung is greenfield development: site control plus permitting, sold as a development-stage asset. Buyers for this rung exist (IPPs, utilities and infrastructure funds buy late-stage pipelines). But discovery (picking which county will approve) is only about 15-30% of the work in that rung. The rest is negotiating land with many landowners, environmental and cultural surveys, decommissioning plans, community engagement, hearings, and above all interconnection studies and deposits. Permitting is a procedural and political grind, not a trivial physical step. The bigger problem is that a project is not NTP-ready without an interconnection agreement. The candidate treats queue position as a given, so 'permitted but no IA' is not a clean rung that sells at the NTP price.
scored.step_up: I found no US market price for permitted versus raw-site projects. The candidate's own figure is $0.05-0.15/W for NTP-ready versus near zero for raw site control. The closest real benchmark is an independent valuation of a Zenith Energy pipeline in Italy (March 2026): EUR 0.30/Wp at the permitting stage (after land), EUR 0.50/Wp at ready-to-build, and EUR 1.30/Wp operational. That puts the permit-to-RTB step at about 1.7x. Raw land to RTB is much larger, but most of it requires interconnection, not just the permit. On a portfolio basis, $1-3M of development spend becoming $10-30M per successful 200MW project looks like 3-5x after failures, which is a normal developer margin and not an ML-created spread. Owning and operating earns infrastructure returns of about 8-12% IRR. The prize is multi-$B, but the market is competitive.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $200k-2M and 1-3 years per project for the CUP or siting approval, surveys and hearings, plus interconnection study deposits. That meets the cost requirement. On base rates, the Sabin Center sixth edition (data through 2025) counts 865 local restrictions and 567 contested projects, with 22 projects (about 9.8 GW) cancelled in 2025 alone. Local denial is real but is a minority of attrition. LBNL queue data show roughly 70-80% of queued capacity withdraws, mostly for interconnection cost or timing reasons. If ML avoids hostile boards, it may lift the permit success rate by about 1.3-1.5x, but the gain in cost per NTP-ready MW is diluted by interconnection attrition. Experienced developers also already screen counties using local land agents and Sabin/LBNL lists. So the lever is about 1.2-1.5x, not 2x.
scored.data: Signal: county agendas, minutes, video, public comments, petitions, local news and state siting dockets. These are public and illegible (about 3,000 counties, scanned or video, scattered), so there is a real extraction moat. However, the outcome is partly summarised already. Moratoria and restrictive ordinances are posted text, and Sabin, LBNL and RE-Site style trackers compile them. Sophisticated developers also attend hearings and track sentiment. Right: land options are bought cheaply ($5-200/acre/yr), and the landowners cannot read county politics. But the parties the edge is meant to beat are competing developers, who are sophisticated. Land near substations with capacity is contested, so options are not cheap relative to proven value because of hidden information. The moat comes from the developers who lack the data, not from the sellers.
scored.right_bought: Lease or purchase options on farmland near substations, signed with individual landowners at $5-200/acre/yr during the option period. The rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Value rises once the county issues a CUP and, critically, once interconnection is secured.
scored.buyer: IPPs, utilities and infrastructure funds (NextEra, AES, Brookfield, Invenergy, and others) that buy late-stage or NTP-ready pipelines. They are well capitalised and buy development assets regularly, but they price in interconnection status and pay much less for projects that have a permit but no IA.
scored.ladder: Development, then own and operate solar and BESS, then a merchant storage platform, then a utility-scale IPP and possibly retail or utility services. The ladder is real and large (multi-$10B IPPs exist), but the upper rungs are commoditized, cost-of-capital-driven businesses dominated by incumbents with cheaper capital.
scored.fatal_flaw: Interconnection, not local permitting, is the binding constraint and the main source of attrition. A county-permitted project without an interconnection agreement is not NTP-ready and does not sell at the NTP price. So the ML edge on county politics addresses a minority of the risk, inside a crowded market of sophisticated developers who already screen counties for opposition. The result is a normal developer margin, not an ML-created spread.
scored.one_line_reason: Expensive proving step, real buyers and a big ladder, but discovery is a small share of development work. Interconnection dominates value and attrition, and county-opposition signals are partly legible and already tracked, so the ML lift is about 1.2-1.5x on a commodity developer margin.

scored.name: Reviving zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats)
scored.one_line: Buy or option distressed parcels in stalled or antiquated pre-recession subdivisions where vested plat rights have lapsed or are uncertain and REO desks price them as raw land, re-entitle or confirm vested rights and secure will-serve letters, and sell finished-entitled lots to national homebuilders.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The jump from paper lot to finished lot comes mostly from horizontal development: physical construction at $40-100k+ per lot, which is hard, bespoke and capital-heavy. Entitlement or vested-rights proving on its own gives only about a 2-5x step-up, and land brokers and builders already price entitlement status reasonably well. So discovery is not 80%+ of the value creation in any rung a builder pays a jackpot for.
scored.frame: The rung is the entitled paper lot: confirmed or re-won vested plat rights plus will-serve letters, sold to builders or land developers. Inside that rung, finding which plats still hold legally defensible rights is perhaps 30-40% of the work. The rest is political and legal: hearings, utility negotiations, impact fees, re-platting to current code, and often re-engineering. A buyer exists (Forestar, Lennar and others buy paper lots), but builders mostly pay for FINISHED lots. Getting from paper to finished means horizontal construction at about $40-65k per lot. That step is physical, bespoke and costs as much as or more than the land.
scored.step_up: Distressed raw or stalled plat land trades at about 15-25% of finished-lot value. Entitled paper lots fetch more, but still well below finished value. That comes from one forum source, a Southern California land dealer on BiggerPockets, so treat it as anecdotal. The 2025 US median finished-lot value is about $59k (NAHB), and Forestar's average lot price is about $106.6k. Entitlement alone is roughly a 2-5x step-up, not 10^3-10^4. Going to finished lots adds about $40-65k per lot of horizontal cost.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt is expensive. Re-entitlement or vested-rights litigation plus engineering and utility studies costs about $50k-$500k+ per subdivision and takes 1-3 years, so the expense test passes. This is an estimate; no single source gives it. The base success rate for reviving rights is moderate, maybe 30-60%. ML that reads scanned plats, development agreements, council minutes and utility capacity filings could lift it by about 1.2-1.5x, by spotting where vesting survives and where water or sewer capacity is real. It is unlikely to reach 2x, because the outcome turns on local politics rather than hidden facts.
scored.data: The data is public but partly illegible: scanned plats, recorded development agreements, extension ordinances, council minutes and utility will-serve history. Vesting status is a real legal ambiguity that incumbents don't parse systematically, and Lincoln Institute work documents how widespread zombie subdivisions are. But the plat itself is a legible recorded instrument. County planners, land brokers and the REO desks at banks and servicers routinely know whether a plat is recorded, expired or in a moratorium. The rights can be bought rather than claimed free, which passes that part of the test. The sellers, though, are banks, funds and HOAs or lot-owner groups with advisors. They are moderately sophisticated, and fractured ownership of scattered paper lots makes assembly costly.
scored.right_bought: Fee title or purchase options on stalled plats, distressed REO tracts, or assembled lots inside antiquated subdivisions. These are bought from banks and servicers, tax-deed sales and scattered individual owners. Assembling fragmented antiquated lots means many small transactions and holdouts.
scored.buyer: National and regional homebuilders and their lot-banking arms: DR Horton/Forestar, Lennar, land bankers such as Millrose and Varde. They are well capitalised, and 64% of builders rated developed-lot supply low or very low in 2025. But they pay mainly for finished lots on takedown schedules, not for proven rights. Under the round-6 rubric the company could instead develop the lots itself, which makes it a Forestar-style lot developer.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs: revived entitlement, then horizontal lot development, then lot banking, then homebuilding, then build-to-rent or master-planned communities. These rungs are real and large. DR Horton and Lennar are each worth tens of billions of dollars. So the path to a big company exists, but every rung above the first is capital-heavy construction where discovery is not the edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: Most of the value comes from horizontal construction and local politics, not discovery. Entitlement-only proof gives about a 2-5x step-up that land brokers and REO desks already roughly price. Operating the lots yourself turns the company into a Forestar-style developer with about 20% gross margins. On that path, ML-led discovery is a minor input rather than 80%+ of the work, so the round-6 C2 (returns from operating) does not rescue it.
scored.one_line_reason: Rescored under round 6, little changes. Proving is expensive, so C3 earns a moderate score, and the ladder is large. But discovery is a minority of the work in every sellable rung, and plat status is fairly legible to sophisticated sellers. Self-development returns look like ordinary lot-developer margins of about 20% gross, under 2-3x on capital, not a 5x+ ML-created spread.

scored.name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
scored.one_line: Take abandoned-in-place pipelines and easements from operators carrying decommissioning liabilities; ML over easement instruments proves broad 'any substance' assignable scope and continuity; sell to CO2/H2 trunkline and fiber developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The proving step is not where the value or the difficulty is. Corridors that look cheap are often legally void (the easement lapsed on abandonment, or its scope has to be litigated per parcel), every parcel in the chain must pass (one gap kills the corridor), and turning a proven corridor into value still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or hydrogen buyer that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, and owners who can read their own easements alre
scored.frame: The rung is buying an abandoned-in-place line and proving that its easement chain is continuous and broad in scope ('any substance', assignable). Title proving is maybe 40-50% of the work in this rung. The rest is physical and bespoke: in-line inspection, hydrotest, dehydration and crack-propagation analysis (the CO2 repurposing studies flag these), compression, and jurisdictional changes such as Trailblazer's FERC abandonment. Buyers are CO2 and H2 trunkline developers and long-haul fiber. CO2 trunklines are largely stalled (Navigator cancelled, Summit delayed), so the capitalised buyer is thin. This is not an 80%+ discovery frame.
scored.step_up: No clean unproven vs proven price exists. Abandoned lines are liabilities that operators sell at roughly zero or negative value. A requalified corridor's value comes from avoided new-build cost. Repurposing estimates range from about 25% cheaper over the life cycle (PipeChina/CUP study) to about 80% cheaper on pipe cost (Indonesian IPA case study). New-build CO2 pipe costs roughly $1-4M per mile, so a proven corridor is worth perhaps $0.3-3M per mile of avoided cost. But that value is only realised after requalification capex, and only if a CO2 or H2 shipper exists. Trailblazer (392 miles, more than 10 Mtpa) was converted by its own operator, Tallgrass, so the spread went to the incumbent.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, with no sourced figure: proving one corridor means title work on roughly 1,000-3,000 parcels (about $0.5-2k each), so roughly $1-5M plus legal opinions. Proving is expensive, which satisfies C3. My guessed base rate is 30-60% of corridors that come out clean or curable, because one parcel gap or one narrow-scope instrument breaks continuity. ML over scanned instruments could plausibly triage corridors about 1.3-1.6x better. But the decisive outcomes, whether an easement lapsed on abandonment or what its scope covers, are settled by state law and litigation per parcel (e.g. the Georgia Plantation Pipe Line case found no telecom rights in the easement). That caps the lever.
scored.data: The easement instruments are scanned, unstructured and scattered across county recorders, so the data is genuinely illegible and public. But the outcome (scope and lapse) is a legal question that is often already litigated, not a hidden physical fact. The sellers are pipeline operators with right-of-way and land departments who hold their own ROW files. They are not owners who cannot read the data, and Tallgrass converted Trailblazer itself.
scored.right_bought: Yes, in principle. Operators carrying decommissioning liability would transfer abandoned-in-place segments cheaply, possibly with liability attached. But the purchase discount reflects a liability the seller understands, not an information gap. Where a corridor has real reuse value, the operator keeps it.
scored.buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Tallgrass, Summit; the demand is stalled), hydrogen hub pipelines (early, with DOE hub funding uncertain), and long-haul and dark-fiber builders (real but small value per mile). The capital is thin and policy-dependent, mainly 45Q.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: corridor title, then a requalified line, then an operated CO2 or H2 transport utility, then sequestration hubs or storage, then a full midstream energy-transition network. The top of the ladder is a large midstream company. The weak point is the bottom rung, not the ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: The spread is captured by the incumbent operator, not by the ML reader. Operators have land departments that can read their own easements, and they convert valuable lines themselves (Tallgrass and Trailblazer). What sellers will hand over cheaply are mostly the segments that are legally void or too narrow in scope. Even a proven corridor still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or H2 shipper that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode: the hard part is the build and the demand, not the discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the hit-rate score modestly, because title proving is expensive and ML can triage corridors. But the sellers can read their own easements, the outcome is set by law rather than hidden in data, and value depends on bespoke requalification and stalled CO2/H2 demand. It stays weak.

scored.name: Senior surface water right change-of-use decrees (Colorado and Western prior appropriation)
scored.one_line: Buy senior agricultural surface-water rights and ditch shares at ag prices, use ML over scanned diversion records, ditch-company ledgers, past decrees and Landsat ET to predict which rights keep the most transferable consumptive-use yield, win a water-court change-of-use decree, then sell or lease the firm municipal yield. Front Range and Utah cities (and data-center or fab developers) pay the step-up. Surface rights only, no groundwater or drilling.
scored.unproven_right: Senior direct-flow rights and mutual ditch company shares (South Platte, Arkansas and Colorado River basins), bought at about $5-15k per acre-foot of raw entitlement from farmers and estates who cannot reconstruct their own 50-year diversion history or know their transferable yield
scored.proving_step: A change-of-use case in Colorado water court (or state-engineer transfer in NM/UT): historic consumptive-use engineering, return-flow modelling, opposer settlements and dry-up covenants. Costs $150k-$3M and takes 2-7 years. Yield haircuts of 20-70% are common. ML predicting decreed yield per share plausibly gives 1.5-2x more decreed acre-feet per dollar.
scored.proven_buyer: Municipal water providers (Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Parker, Denver Water, St. George area and Utah districts), homebuilders needing water for new development, data-center and semiconductor developers, and water investment funds, paying about $30-80k+ per acre-foot of firm decreed municipal yield
scored.public_data: Colorado CDSS/HydroBase diversion records (decades of handwritten and scanned ditch-rider logs and water commissioner field books), historical water court decrees, resumes and case files with prior change-case engineering reports, ditch company bylaws, minutes and share ledgers, Landsat ET history 1984+ and historic aerial irrigation imagery, NRCS soils. Transferable consumptive use is never a legible field and has to be reconstructed case by case.
scored.rough_step_up: Ag $5-15k/AF becomes decreed municipal yield at $30-80k+/AF, about 3-6x on total capital after the yield haircut and legal costs. A single 2,000 AF portfolio is worth about $100M; the prize is multi-$B across western states. Ladder: storage (gravel-pit reservoirs), augmentation plans and conveyance, then a wholesale water utility.
scored.frame: The rung is owning ag ditch shares and getting a water-court change-of-use decree. Rebuilding historic consumptive use (HCU) from records is maybe 40-50% of that work. The rest is the physical and legal step, which is not trivial: opposer litigation and settlements, return-flow replacement and augmentation, dry-up covenants and revegetation. Under the anti-speculation doctrine, extended to change cases in High Plains A&M v. Southeastern (Colo. 2005, 120 P.3d 710), you also need a named end user before the court will decree. So the buyer often has to be locked in before you can prove the asset. A capitalised buyer exists (Front Range cities, homebuilders, funds), but discovery is well under 80% of the rung.
scored.step_up: Proven (decreed municipal) side: Colorado-Big Thompson (C-BT) water, the most liquid Front Range benchmark, traded at about $85k/AF in 2025, down from $101k/AF in 2022 (WestWater, reported by the Colorado Sun in 2026). A 2024 Northern Water auction averaged about $74.6k/AF. Unproven (raw ag) side: the candidate's own figure is $5-15k/AF of raw entitlement. A Box Elder Ditch valuation put HCU credit at about $4.8-5.2k/AF in the 2000s. In 2003 Greeley offered $6k/AF, about twice the going ag rate, and still found no sellers. After a 20-70% yield haircut, $150k-$3M in legal and engineering costs, and 2-7 years of carry, the realistic return is about 2-3x on capital. That is a step-up of a few times, not 10^3. The gap is mostly the known cost and risk of the change case, and informed buyers already price that in.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost: $150k-$3M and 2-7 years per change case, using the candidate's figures; I could not find a sourced total, but this range matches practitioner experience. Base rate: most change cases do end in a decree, but with yield haircuts. The 'hit' is decreed acre-feet per dollar, not decree versus no decree. ML that ranks shares by likely decreed HCU before purchase could plausibly give 1.2-1.5x. It could reach 1.5x where ditches have had no prior change case. However, experienced buyers' engineers already run HCU screens on HydroBase before buying, so the claimed 1.5-2x is optimistic.
scored.data: This partly fails the rule that the outcome must not already be summarised in a legible field. CDSS/HydroBase diversion records are largely digitised as structured daily and annual series. For any ditch that has already had a change case, the per-share HCU is written into the decree; a 2009 Colorado Springs Chilcott Ditch filing, for example, quantified 24.61 AF/share. The market prices ditch shares off those numbers. The illegible edge (scanned ditch-rider logs, ledgers, historic aerial imagery and Landsat ET) is real only for ditches that have never been through a change case. Those are also the ones with the most opposer risk.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought, not free: ditch shares and direct-flow rights are bought from farmers and estates. But sellers are not blind. Front Range ag water is a brokered market with active municipal, broker (WestWater) and fund buyers. Farmers know what their shares sell for, as shown by Greeley's below-market offer finding no sellers. Investor buy-and-dry purchases are also politically targeted: SB20-048 set up a work group on water speculation. The cheap entry exists mostly in remote basins (lower Arkansas, the West Slope), where conveyance to buyers is the binding constraint.
scored.buyer: Municipal water providers: Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Parker, Denver Water, Greeley, and Utah districts such as Washington County. Also homebuilders that must show water before building, and data-center or fab developers. All are well capitalised and already pay about $50-100k/AF for firm yield.
scored.ladder: Above the decree: gravel-pit storage, augmentation plans, conveyance, and then a wholesale or retail water utility. Pure Cycle (Rangeview) is the precedent, at a market cap of a few hundred million dollars. Municipal monopoly, the politics of buy-and-dry, and physical limits on conveyance cap the ladder. It is a sizable regional company, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Front Range ag water is already priced by an informed market, and in practice the outcome is already legible. Per-share consumptive-use yields are quantified in prior change decrees and digitised HydroBase records, and municipal buyers, brokers and funds price ditch shares off those numbers. The gap between ag and municipal prices is mostly the known cost, time and haircut of the change case, so ML leaves only a thin spread. On top of that, the anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains A&M) requires a committed end user before a decree, so you cannot cheaply prove the asset on spec.
scored.one_line_reason: The value chain is real and the buyers are well capitalised. But the spread is a 2-3x transaction-cost spread in an already informed, brokered market. Prior decrees and HydroBase have largely made the answer legible. Proving is legal and physical work, not discovery, and it cannot be done on spec.

scored.name: Orphaned university materials patents, proven at pilot scale
scored.one_line: Option exclusive licences to unlicensed university patents on catalysts, battery and electrolyte materials and membranes for about $10-50k each. ML scores which claims will reproduce and scale. Pay for independent replication and pilot-scale validation, then make the material or sell the de-risked licence package to a chemical or battery strategic.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive option or licence on one of the many university patents tech transfer offices never licensed, for small upfronts plus royalties; owners cannot rank which will reproduce.
scored.proving_step: Third-party replication plus kg-scale synthesis and application testing (cell cycling, catalyst lifetime, membrane flux). About $150k-$1M and 6-18 months per asset; base hit rate about 20-40%.
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty chemical and battery-materials companies (BASF, Umicore, Albemarle, Solvay, cell makers) and corporate VC, paying $5-50M for validated, scale-proven exclusive IP with data packages.
scored.public_data: USPTO bulk full-text XML linked to papers and supplementary data (often scanned figures), theses, NSF/DOE grant final reports (OSTI scanned PDFs), citation and failure-to-replicate signals, TTO availability listings. Reproducibility at scale is in no legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: $50k option plus $0.5M proof leads to a $5-50M sale or royalty-bearing sublicence, about 5-20x on winners and maybe 3-6x across a portfolio. Ladder: toll manufacturing, own production, components.
scored.frame: The rung is: take an option on a university patent, pay for a third-party replication and a kg-scale pilot, then sell or sublicense the de-risked package. Inside that rung, picking which patent to option is maybe 30-40% of the work. The other 60-70% is the physical proving: synthesis at kg scale, impurity and process control, and application testing such as cell cycling or catalyst lifetime. That step is neither trivial nor fully abstracted. In materials, whether something scales is a question of process know-how, not something read off a page. Buyers exist (BASF, Umicore and other strategics, plus corporate VC). But they mostly buy teams and companies with process data, not bare university IP packages. The frame only partly holds.
scored.step_up: Unproven: university TTO options and licences on never-licensed patents typically cost tens of thousands of dollars upfront plus royalties. The candidate's figure is $10-50k; my searches found no public price schedule, so this is an estimate. Proven: the candidate claims $5-50M for a scale-proven exclusive package. I found no public deal comps for pure IP sales at that size. Disclosed university battery deals are licences to startups (AquaLith from UMD) or small raises (Pure Battery Technologies, A$1.7M for a pilot plant). Realistic outcomes for validated IP without a team look more like $0.5-5M upfront plus 1-5% royalties paid many years later. Expected step-up is about 3-10x on winners and roughly 1-3x across a portfolio after a 20-40% hit rate. A Wharton/Mack study also found universities realise only about 16% of the value of comparable corporate patents.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $150k-$1M and 6-18 months, which clears the 'expensive' bar (estimate; scale-up facilities are scarce enough that UCSB got $28M from the California Energy Commission to build one). The base hit rate is the candidate's own 20-40% guess. No meta-analysis of coin-cell-to-pouch or lab-to-kg failure rates turned up, and the literature points to manual-assembly variability and cell-format effects as the main confounds. ML can flag exotic precursors, single-lab results, missing controls, unrealistic test conditions and cost red flags. A plausible lift is 1.2-1.6x, on a weakly labelled training set.
scored.data: The data is genuinely public and illegible. USPTO full text, supplementary information with scanned figures, OSTI scanned grant final reports, theses, and replication and citation signals are huge and scattered. Whether a result reproduces at scale is in no legible field, which passes the 'outcome not written in a status field' test. The weaknesses are the training labels and noise. Labels for 'scaled successfully' are sparse and mostly private (industry evaluations are not published). Most of the signal that matters, such as process cost, impurity tolerance and manufacturability, is not in the documents.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Estimates put 60-83% of university patents never licensed (a USPTO slide citing AUTM data says 1 in 6 inventions ever gets licensed; another study says about 60%). TTOs routinely grant cheap options. However, the TTO's low price reflects that most of these patents are genuinely worthless, not an inability to read them. University claims are often narrow or easy to design around, and they are frequently near expiry by the time scale-up finishes. Exclusive licences also carry diligence milestones and royalty stacks that eat the spread.
scored.buyer: Specialty chemical and battery-materials strategics (BASF, Umicore, Solvay, Albemarle, cell makers) and their venture arms. They are capitalised, but they buy validated IP mostly as part of a company or team, rarely as an orphan patent package. Their in-house R&D also discounts data from outside labs, so the buyer pool for the claimed $5-50M bare-IP sale is thin.
scored.ladder: In principle there is a ladder: toll manufacturing, then own production of the material, then components such as electrodes, membranes or catalyst modules, then cells or systems. In practice each rung is brutally capital-intensive. Chinese incumbents compete on cost, and the value sits in process know-how rather than the patent. Climbing means becoming a materials manufacturer, which has a poor track record for venture-backed firms.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step is not trivial. In materials, the value is created in scale-up and process know-how, not in finding the patent. Kg-scale synthesis, impurity control, cost-down and application qualification are the hard part. Strategics rarely pay multi-million sums for bare university IP without a team and commercial-scale data. So realising the $5-50M forces the company to do the bespoke, capital-heavy physical work itself. This is the same trap as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: proving is harder than discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The rights are cheap and the data is illegible, but proving the material at pilot scale is the hard, expensive part rather than a trivial step, and the claimed $5-50M exit for bare IP has no comps, so portfolio returns look like 1-3x.

scored.name: Closed-loop pumped storage sites via FERC preliminary permits (federal, state trust and optioned private land)
scored.one_line: Use ML over decades of surrendered FERC preliminary permits (whose scanned filings say why earlier permittees gave up: geology, water, money), old USBR/USACE reconnaissance scans, LiDAR head and state geology/borehole files to rank off-river reservoir pairs with large head near HV substations. File FERC preliminary permits (first-to-file, essentially free, 4-year exclusive priority, transferable with FERC approval), plus BLM/USFS ROW or state trust land use at schedule rent, or land options on private parcels. Pay for geotech borings (dam and tunnel foundations, not mineral exploration), water-supply, interconnection screening and an NOI/PAD, then sell the de-risked project to a storage developer, utility or infrastructure fund that pays the step-up because a feasible, permitted site saves it years. Must sell at the permit-plus-geotech rung, since the build is enormous.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The unproven right cannot be bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit that is statutorily non-transferable (16 U.S.C. 798(d)) and open to competing filers, and NREL's public atlas already maps the legible candidate sites. And most of the value step-up is paid only through milestone-contingent deals at licence or offtake, years and tens of millions of dollars after the permit-plus-geotech rung, not immediately on the proving result.
scored.frame: The rung is a permit plus geotech, water and interconnection screening, delivered as an NOI/PAD-ready site. Site discovery is maybe 30-50% of the work in that rung. The rest is regulatory and commercial: interconnection queue position, water rights, environmental studies, and finding an offtaker or utility RFP. None of those steps is trivial, and many permittees give up for money or market reasons rather than geology. Capitalised buyers exist (CIP, utilities, infrastructure funds), but there are few deals and they come at the licence stage or later. Example: CIP bought Swan Lake after its 2019 FERC licence, and Goldendale after its 2020 licence application, not at the permit stage.
scored.step_up: No reported sale prices exist for permit-stage pumped storage rights. CIP's 2020 purchase of 1.6 GW (Swan Lake and Goldendale) from Rye/National Grid was undisclosed and came at or after licensing. The input is almost free: FERC preliminary permits cost only filing and study effort. My estimate of the realistic premium for a licensed, shovel-ready GW-scale project is roughly $50-150/kW, or $50-150M per GW. That comes after about $20-50M and 5-8 years of licensing. At the permit-plus-geotech stage the step-up is small and paid through milestone-contingent deals.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My rough estimate is that a geotech, water and feasibility campaign costs $1-5M+ and takes 1-3 years per site, so the proving step is expensive. Of hundreds of preliminary permits issued, only a small share reach a licence, and fewer still get built. Example: Swan Lake was licensed in 2019 and is still not built. Base success at the permit-to-licence step is far below 30%, and much of the failure is non-geological (offtake, financing, interconnection). Better geology and water screening plausibly gives about 1.3-1.6x on cost per licensable site. That is a real but partial lever, because ML does not touch the main failure modes.
scored.data: Partly illegible. Decades of surrendered-permit filings in FERC eLibrary (scanned, unstructured, with reasons for surrender) and old USBR/USACE reconnaissance scans are genuinely hard to extract. LiDAR head and substation proximity are legible, and NREL's closed-loop pumped storage atlas already maps them. The outcome (surrender, issued, licensed) is written into FERC docket status fields, which weakens the ML edge.
scored.right_bought: No. The key right is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit that is open to competing applications. Contrary to the candidate's claim, I believe permits are not freely transferable: the old fatal flaw cites 16 U.S.C. 798. I did not verify this new. Land (BLM/USFS ROW, state trust land at schedule rent) is priced administratively, not bought from an owner who cannot read the data. Private land options are the only case where the right is bought, and rural landowners already price reservoir land at agricultural or option rates. That spread is modest compared with total project value.
scored.buyer: Infrastructure funds (CIP), utilities and storage IPPs (Rye, Daybreak, etc.) buy late-stage, licensed or near-licensed projects through bespoke, milestone-contingent deals. Few transactions happen, and none are disclosed.
scored.ladder: Strong in principle: permit, then licence, then EPC and construction ($3-5B per GW project, e.g. the $4.9B Halverson Canyon), then owning and operating a long-duration storage fleet and trading capacity and energy. Under round 6, operating is allowed. But each step up needs billions and 8-12 year timelines. Swan Lake was licensed in 2019 and is still unbuilt.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right is a free, competitive, first-to-file FERC permit (and I believe non-transferable). It is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data, so ML-led proof creates no purchase spread. Value is realised only at licence, or by building $3-5B plants over a decade or more. The physical build, not discovery, dominates, as in the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, since proving is expensive and ML can screen geology and water. The round-6 C2 allows self-development, but that means a multi-billion-dollar bespoke build where discovery is a small share of the work. The free, competitive permit gives no bought-cheap spread, so the score barely moves.

scored.name: Discontinued-ANDA revival for shortage-prone generics
scored.one_line: Buy approved-but-discontinued generic drug ANDAs at token prices from holders who stopped making them. ML on FDA review packages, DMF status and shortage filings picks revivals with a sourceable API, simple CMC and a lasting shortage premium. Pay for tech transfer and a prior approval supplement. Make and sell the drug on owned or CMO lines, or sell the relaunched product plus supply to a generic company.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of a discontinued ANDA and its DMF references (Orange Book discontinued section, 10k+ entries), bought for ~$50-500k from small or acquired generics firms that treat them as dead paper and cannot judge transferability or shortage durability.
scored.proving_step: API source qualification, tech transfer, exhibit batches, stability and a Prior Approval Supplement to FDA approval. ~$0.5-3M and 12-24 months; base success maybe 40-60% (fails on API sourcing, BE or CMC). ML over CRLs, DMF status, shortage history and competitor ANDA count plausibly picks winners at 1.5-2x. Already-approved products, so the proof is manufacturing, not clinical.
scored.proven_buyer: Own sales into GPOs, wholesalers (McKesson, Cardinal, Cencora) and hospitals at shortage prices, or a sale to mid-size generics and injectables specialists (Hikma, Amneal, Fresenius Kabi, Eugia, Civica) at $5-30M per relaunched, supply-secured product.
scored.public_data: Orange Book discontinued section, Drugs@FDA approval letters and scanned review packages (CMC and BE sections, image PDFs), FDA and ASHP drug shortage databases, the DMF list, Form 483s and warning letters for referenced API and incumbent sites, CMS Part B/D, Medicaid SDUD and NADAC pricing. None of the revivability judgement sits in a legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$1-4M per molecule against $3-30M of product value or $3-10M/yr of margin, roughly 3-15x. A portfolio of 50-hundreds approaches multi-$B. Ladder: owned sterile or oral plant (pairs with the plant-remediation idea), vertical API, 505(b)(2) reformulations, integrated generic company.
scored.frame: The rung is clear and sellable: own a discontinued ANDA, revive it, then sell or market the relaunched product. Capitalised buyers exist (ANI, Hikma, Amneal, Aurobindo, Civica, plus wholesalers and GPOs). But choosing the molecule is only about 25-35% of the work. Most of the work and the failure risk is physical: qualifying an API source, tech transfer to a CMO with free capacity, exhibit batches, BE, stability and the PAS inspection. This is the geothermal-plant failure mode on a smaller scale: making the drug is harder than picking it.
scored.step_up: Unproven: ANI paid $2.6M plus a royalty for 23 previously marketed ANDAs from IDT Australia in 2018, about $110k each. Perrigo paid $16-53M for single approved, marketable ANDAs. So a proven, relaunchable product is worth roughly $3-30M against a dead ANDA at about $0.1M. Most of that gap is bought with the $0.5-3M CMC spend and the 12-24 months, not with information. Realistic return on capital is about 2-4x per success. Shortage pricing fades as other holders re-enter, and generic prices keep falling.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $0.5-3M and takes 12-24 months per molecule. The PAS fee was removed under GDUFA II, and a PAS review is 6-10 months when a pre-approval inspection is needed. The base success rate of roughly 40-60% is the candidate's own estimate and I could not verify it. The main ways it fails are API supply, CMO capacity and BE or CMC problems, which ML on review packages only partly predicts. The proving step is expensive enough to qualify. A realistic ML gain over an experienced BD and regulatory team is about 1.2-1.5x, not 2x.
scored.data: The data is mixed. The scanned CMC and BE sections of review packages, the 483s and the warning letters are illegible and rarely mined, which is a real edge. But the main selection signals are already legible fields: the Orange Book discontinued section, the DMF list with its activity and completeness status, the FDA and ASHP shortage lists, competitor ANDA counts and NADAC or SDUD prices. Rights are bought, not claimed, and they are cheap. But the seller side is already worked by informed specialist buyers: ANI (23 ANDAs from IDT, flecainide from Teva, vancomycin from Shire), IGI/Teligent (18 retired products from AstraZeneca), Aurobindo (45 non-marketed ANDAs) and Civica (asks for donations). Owners who cannot judge value are partly cut out by these buyers.
scored.right_bought: Ownership of a discontinued ANDA plus its DMF references and regulatory records, bought from small, acquired or retiring generics firms or big pharma. Typical price is about $50-500k, or about $110k each in the ANI/IDT basket.
scored.buyer: The company's own sales into GPOs, the big three wholesalers and hospitals. Or a sale or licence of the relaunched, supply-secured product to ANI, Hikma, Amneal, Fresenius Kabi, Eugia, Civica or similar firms for about $3-30M.
scored.ladder: The ladder goes from owned CMO or sterile capacity, to vertical API, to 505(b)(2) reformulations, to an integrated specialty generics or injectables company. The ladder is real, but the end state is low-margin, deflationary generics. ANI, which ran this revival playbook, is roughly a $1-2B company, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proof is manufacturing, not discovery. Most of the cost and failure risk sits in API sourcing, tech transfer, CMO capacity and BE/CMC work. The selection signals mostly sit in legible FDA fields that specialist acquirers like ANI, Aurobindo and IGI already work, and they already buy discontinued ANDAs at about $100k each. ML adds only a modest edge on an already-competed spread, and shortage premiums fade once other makers re-enter.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is real and capitalised, and proving is expensive enough to count, but discovery is a minority of the work, the key data is mostly legible, and informed buyers already exist, so ML's edge and the value it captures are both modest.

scored.name: Post-Sackett wetland reclassification land
scored.one_line: Buy parcels priced as unbuildable because they appear on National Wetlands Inventory or older Corps maps. ML over scanned Corps jurisdictional determinations, NRCS soil surveys, historic aerials and permit files finds parcels that are no longer federal waters after Sackett v. EPA (2023) and the 2023 conforming rule. Get a written non-jurisdictional determination and sell the newly buildable land to developers.
scored.unproven_right: Fee simple or options on wetland-flagged tracts at roughly $1-5k/acre; sellers and lenders assume the land cannot be built on.
scored.proving_step: Professional wetland delineation plus a Corps Approved Jurisdictional Determination and state-law check. About $30-150k and 6-18 months per tract; with ML pre-screening success plausibly 40-60% in states with no state wetland program (TX, inland FL, Southeast).
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, industrial and logistics developers, and data-center site selectors paying buildable-land prices.
scored.public_data: USACE ORM2 and Regulatory Request System JD archive (scanned PDFs with rationale forms), NWI polygons, NRCS SSURGO hydric soils, USGS historical aerials, county permit files, Section 404 public notices.
scored.rough_step_up: $3k/acre to $30-100k/acre buildable (about 10x on land); roughly 3-6x on capital after delineation costs and failures. Federal rule could swing back.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy or option a wetland-flagged tract, then get a written Corps non-jurisdictional AJD and sell it as federally unencumbered. Inside that rung, discovery and legal proof are about 70-80% of the work. The physical step is a field delineation plus paperwork, so it is cheap and abstracted. The weak point is that a legal 'non-jurisdictional' ruling is not the same as 'buildable'. Land that is still physically wet needs fill, drainage, stormwater, floodplain and zoning work, plus state and local wetland checks. That remaining work is often the real reason the land is cheap. Developers will buy it, but they price in that physical work, so the rung is less clean than it looks.
scored.step_up:
The candidate claims about $3k/acre unproven and $30-100k/acre buildable. I found no data on the post-Sackett price effect for non-jurisdictional parcels. The empirical wetland discounts I found are modest:
- North Dakota: permanent wetlands cut farmland prices by about $161/acre.
- South Dakota: easement-encumbered sales were about 6.6% lower.
- Palm Beach County: appraisers cut wetland values by about 40% in one case, and landowners contest it.
These suggest wetland-flagged land trades at a discount to upland land in the same market, not at 1/10-1/30 of it. The 10-30x gap the candidate implies compares remote wet land with entitled, serviced land near a market, and most of that gap is location and physical development cost, not federal jurisdiction. A realistic legal-reclassification uplift is maybe 1.5-3x on the affected acres.
