scored.hit_rate_capex: For a typical tract, a delineation costs about $5-30k. It rises to the candidate's $30-150k only for large tracts. The Corps issues AJDs at no fee, but they are slow (months to more than a year), and some districts have suspended AJD processing since Sackett (Kimley-Horn). That means the cash cost per attempt is often below the ~$50k threshold, but the time cost is long. A 40-60% base hit rate is plausible. However, the post-Sackett guidance (direct abutment, no linking through ditches) is a simple geometric test that consultants already run as cheap desktop screens over NWI, LiDAR and hydrography layers. ML would add maybe 1.2-1.4x over that, not 1.5-3x.
scored.data:
Some of the data is legible and some is not:
- Legible GIS layers: NWI polygons, SSURGO hydric soils, NHD/3DHP hydrography and LiDAR. Anyone can screen these.
- Illegible sources: scanned JD rationale forms, older paper JDs and permit files.
- Outcomes already published: where a parcel has been determined, Corps districts post approved JDs online with the jurisdictional or non-jurisdictional result stated (e.g. the Vicksburg AJD list). That is the same 'regulator writes the answer down' failure seen in earlier hunts.
For parcels never determined, the abutment test is mostly computable from legible layers, so incumbents can replicate the edge cheaply.
Buying the right: the land can be bought, often from rural owners who cannot read the data. But Sackett is universally known among brokers, developers and wetland consultants, and the September 2026 supplemental proposal (a perennial-flow test) is widely covered, so the market is re-rating broadly. Florida runs its own statewide wetland permitting (the Environmental Resource Permit program), so 'inland FL' is a poor target. The rule is likely to be litigated and could swing back.
scored.right_bought: Fee simple or options on wetland-flagged rural or exurban tracts at about $1-5k/acre, from farmers, timber owners and estates. The right is genuinely bought, not free to claim. However, sellers' brokers and every developer's consultant also know about Sackett.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders, industrial and logistics developers, and data-center site selectors. All are capitalised, but each runs its own wetland due diligence and prices in fill, stormwater and floodplain costs plus litigation risk on the rule.
scored.ladder: The chain runs from land banking to entitlement, then horizontal development, then vertical construction or build-to-rent and industrial parks. It is a real ladder with large markets. But land development is fragmented and commoditised, and the rungs above have no data moat, so climbing them is ordinary real-estate execution.
scored.fatal_flaw: The spread is not information-created. Most of the discount on NWI-flagged land comes from the land being physically wet and remote: fill, drainage and floodplain costs, local and state rules, and location. The federal-jurisdiction label is only part of it. Meanwhile Sackett and the 2025-26 narrowing proposals are universally known, and the abutment test can be computed from legible GIS layers, so an ML-read legal reclassification creates little spread that informed developers do not already price.
scored.one_line_reason: The idea is not excluded and the land can be bought, but the edge is thin. The proof is a cheap, slow consultant exercise, and the outcome is largely computable from legible GIS layers or already posted on Corps AJD lists. The real cost of building is physical, not legal, and Sackett is common knowledge, so ML-driven arbitrage would likely return around 1.5-2x, not 5x.

scored.name: Heirs' property and clouded-title clearing via quiet title
scored.one_line: Buy fractional heirs' property interests, tax-deed parcels and land with chain-of-title gaps or unprobated estates at 10-30% of clear-title value. ML over scanned deeds, probate dockets, obituaries and tax rolls predicts which defects can be cured, at what cost, and which parcels sit in growth paths. File quiet-title or partition actions and sell clear, insurable land at full value.
scored.unproven_right: Fractional heir interests, quitclaimed interests and tax deeds bought for cents on the dollar because title insurers will not insure them and most buyers cannot judge how hard they are to cure.
scored.proving_step: Title curative work, a quiet-title or partition action with notice and service, and a title-insurance commitment. About $15-100k per parcel and 1-3 years, base success about 50-70%; ML triage plausibly gives 1.5-2x on cost per cleared acre. Requires fair dealing with heirs under the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act and avoiding displacement of occupant heirs.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, infill developers, adjoining landowners, timber REITs (Weyerhaeuser, Rayonier) and utility-scale solar developers assembling land, paying full value once title is insurable.
scored.public_data: Scanned county deed books, mortgages and liens going back decades, probate dockets, tax-delinquency and tax-sale records, obituary archives, plat books and court e-filing records across about 3,000 counties. Curability is in no legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: Buy at 10-30% of value, sell at 100%: 3-8x per parcel, about 2.5-5x on capital after legal costs, plus a premium when aggregated into contiguous tracts. Roughly $1B per region; low single-digit $B unless rolled up across the Southeast.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a clouded interest and turning it into clear, insurable title. ML-led discovery (which parcels can be cured, where the heirs are, whether the land sits in a growth path) is maybe 30-40% of the work. Most of it is the 'physical' step: finding and serving dozens of heirs, curative work, litigating a quiet-title or partition action, appraisal, and dealing with occupants. That step is slow, done by hand, contested and specific to each county. It is not trivial or abstracted, so this looks more like the geothermal counter-example than like Terranox. The capitalised buyers are real (homebuilders, timber REITs, solar land assemblers).
scored.step_up: Unproven fractional or clouded interests trade at about 10-30% of clear value; the claim, not verified. Proven means clear, insurable title at 100%. That is a 3-8x step on the purchase price but well under 2-3x on total capital. Average heirs' parcel value is about $82k (SRDC / Alcorn State: 579,000 parcels, 6.8M acres, $47.3B across 14 southern states). So a parcel bought for about $16k plus $15-100k of curative and litigation costs gets sold for about $82k, before court-ordered fees (Alabama practice is about 10% of sale price). Also, under UPHPA (enacted in roughly 20+ states) the other heirs can buy out the investor's share at its appraised fractional value. The investor then gets only fair value for the fraction and none of the clear-title uplift on the whole.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $15-100k and 1-3 years per parcel (candidate's estimate; I found no published quiet-title cost data), with a base success of about 50-70%. That passes the 'expensive' test. ML triage over deeds, probate and obituaries could plausibly lift the cured-per-dollar rate by about 1.3-1.6x. But the result is decided by heir behaviour, UPHPA buyout elections and the court, not by a hidden physical fact ML can read. And the cost per attempt is close to the parcel value, so a better hit rate saves little absolute value.
scored.data: The signal sits in scanned county deed books, probate dockets, obituaries and tax rolls across about 3,000 counties. That data is genuinely public, illegible and scattered, and curability is in no legible field (good). Rights are bought from owners who cannot read the data (good). However, title abstractors and tax-deed investors already read these records parcel by parcel. The UPHPA's notice, independent appraisal and co-tenant buyout rules are designed to stop exactly this 'buy a fraction cheap, force a sale' play, so the cheap-purchase spread is legally pushed back toward fair value.
scored.right_bought: Fractional heir interests, quitclaims and tax deeds bought for cents on the dollar from dispersed heirs. Under UPHPA, the remaining co-tenants can buy out the investor at appraised fractional value, and a court controls any sale. So the right does not reliably turn into control of the whole clear parcel.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders, infill developers, adjoining owners, timber REITs (Weyerhaeuser, Rayonier) and utility-scale solar developers pay full value for insurable, contiguous land. These buyers are real and capitalised, but most heirs' parcels are small rural tracts worth about $80k with limited development pull.
scored.ladder: Clear title, then assembling contiguous tracts, then entitlement and development (residential, solar, timber), then homebuilding or long-term land holding. Each step up is a mature, competitive real-estate business, not a new technical frontier. The path to a very large company is weak: this is a regional land-banking or roll-up company, low single-digit $B at best.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is slow, contested legal work that costs about as much as the parcel is worth (about $15-100k against an average $82k heirs' parcel). On top of that, UPHPA buyout rights and court-supervised sales legally move the cheap-fraction spread back to the heirs at appraised value. The structure is the well-documented mechanism of Black land loss in the South, which brings heavy legal, regulatory and reputational blowback. So the ML edge in discovery does not create a capturable spread.
scored.one_line_reason: The data really is illegible and the buyers are real, but the bulk of the work is the legal cure, not discovery. Parcel economics are thin (about $82k average value against $15-100k cure cost), and UPHPA buyout rights are designed to erase the discount, so returns are well under 2-5x on capital in a low-$B, reputationally toxic market.

scored.name: Legal-unit-count and grandfathered density arbitrage (NYC and older cities)
scored.one_line: Buy small multifamily or mixed-use buildings whose legal unit count or floor area under historic certificates of occupancy, I-cards and pre-1961 zoning exceeds current use or listing. ML over scanned DOB CO archives, I-cards, tax photos and BSA variances finds them. Prove the vested right with a zoning determination and sell or redevelop at the higher density.
scored.unproven_right: The building, bought at a price based on its current rent roll and visible unit count from small landlords and estates that have not pulled the historic records.
scored.proving_step: Architect's zoning analysis, DOB reconsideration or determination, and CO amendment or alteration filing. About $50-200k and 12-24 months, about 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Small and mid-sized NYC developers and condo converters paying per buildable square foot.
scored.public_data: NYC DOB BIS/DOB NOW scanned CO archive, HPD I-cards, 1940 and 1980s tax photos, BSA calendar archive, historic zoning maps; equivalent scanned CO archives in Boston, Chicago and SF.
scored.rough_step_up: 1.5-3x on the asset, about 1.5-2.5x on capital. Smaller, city-by-city prize.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a small NYC building, get a zoning determination or CO amendment confirming the vested unit count or floor area, then sell it with that entitlement. Inside that rung, finding the record is perhaps 40-50% of the work. The rest is legal and architect work (DOB reconsideration, BSA, objections) and, for most of the value, real construction: gut renovation, adding units, egress, sprinklers and HPD compliance. Two things cap the uplift. Grandfathered non-complying floor area is lost if you demolish, so you have to keep the building. And adding units in buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974 can pull them into rent stabilisation. A buyer exists (small developers and condo converters paying per buildable square foot), but the physical step is not trivial. That looks more like the geothermal counter-example than Terranox.
scored.step_up: The candidate's own estimate is 1.5-3x on the asset and 1.5-2.5x on capital. That is roughly 10^0.3, against Terranox's 10^4. NYC multifamily sells at roughly $300-700 per buildable square foot, so an extra legal unit or two on a $1.5-3M building adds perhaps $200-600k. Transaction costs, holding costs, the $50-200k proving cost and 40-60% odds take much of that. No source found a documented market discount for buildings whose legal count exceeds their current use. Round 6 drops the step-up requirement, but the spread is still thin.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $50-200k and 12-24 months per attempt (architect zoning analysis, DOB determination or reconsideration, CO amendment). The candidate puts base success at 40-60%. The search confirmed that the controlling record really is hard to read: a DOB official called CO records largely paper 'unintelligent PDFs' that have to be opened one by one, and it is sometimes a legal debate which final CO controls. ML that ranks candidates before purchase could plausibly lift success 1.3-1.6x. Much of the failure, though, is legal judgment and DOB discretion, which ML does not predict well. Score: a middle 3.
scored.data: The DOB BIS scanned CO archive, HPD I-cards, 1940 and 1980s tax photos and BSA decisions are public and illegible at scale, so that part of the test is met. But for any single building the outcome sits in a document that every competent buyer, broker and lender's attorney pulls in standard diligence: the CO, which lists units by floor on page one, or the I-card for pre-1938 buildings with no CO. HPD registration also shows legal class A units in a legible field. ML gives a screening edge across the whole city, not an edge on the deal itself, because the counterparty and rival bidders read the same CO before closing. Rights are bought rather than claimed first-come, which passes, but they are priced in competitive sales against developer bidders.
scored.right_bought: You buy fee title to the building from small landlords or estates, at a price based on the current rent roll. The buildings are mostly marketed by brokers who pull the CO, so a discount exists only in off-market estate or distressed sales. The 'owners who cannot read the data' assumption is weak, because one $100-500 expeditor records pull reads it.
scored.buyer: Small and mid-sized NYC developers, condo converters and multifamily investors paying per buildable square foot or per legal unit. They are well capitalised but price-disciplined, and they do their own CO diligence. The company could also hold and operate the building.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: develop the building, own and operate multifamily, then move to larger assemblages and to other cities' CO archives (Boston, Chicago, SF). That leads to a real estate developer or REIT. The path is large in total dollars, but it is a commoditised, capital-heavy business with no proprietary advantage beyond sourcing. City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (adopted December 2024) raised as-of-right density broadly, which shrinks the premium on grandfathered density. Each new city needs its own legal regime.
scored.fatal_flaw: The hidden right is not really hidden at the deal level. The legal unit count is printed on the CO or I-card, which every buyer, broker and lender's counsel pulls in routine diligence. So there is little purchase discount for ML to unlock. Turning the right into value then needs real construction plus rent-regulation and non-complying-bulk constraints, all for a 1.5-2.5x, city-by-city prize.
scored.one_line_reason: The scanned CO archive really is illegible at scale, but the answer for each building is printed on a document every buyer reads. Realising the value needs construction rather than a trivial step, and the return is about 2x on capital with a small, city-by-city prize.

scored.name: Old Master 'sleeper' attribution upgrades
scored.one_line: Buy paintings at regional auctions catalogued as 'circle of', 'workshop of' or 'after'. ML over digitized historical auction catalogues, provenance indices, photo archives and stylistic image models picks works whose provenance leads to a master. Pay for technical analysis and expert review, then resell at the upgraded attribution to collectors and major dealers.
scored.unproven_right: Title to the physical work, bought at about $2-50k at regional houses lacking specialist research capacity.
scored.proving_step: Technical study (IRR, dendrochronology, pigment analysis), conservation, provenance research and expert or catalogue-raisonne opinion. About $50-200k and 1-3 years per work; ML provenance linking plausibly lifts hit rate 2-3x.
scored.proven_buyer: Top-tier collectors, museums and major dealers via Sotheby's or Christie's evening sales, where upgraded works sell for $0.5-20M+.
scored.public_data: Getty Provenance Index, digitized sale catalogues (Frick, Lugt, Gallica, HathiTrust), RKD and Witt photo archives, museum open-access images.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-100x on purchase for hits, maybe 3-6x on portfolio capital, but sub-$1B prize and weak ladder (dealer only).
scored.frame: Rung: buy a miscatalogued work, then prove an upgraded attribution and sell it. Inside that rung, discovery and proving (provenance linking, connoisseurship, expert consensus) are about 80-90% of the work. The physical steps (IRR, dendrochronology, pigment analysis, cleaning) are cheap and done by contractors. The weakness is the proof itself. It is not physical like a drill core. It is a social consensus held by a few catalogue-raisonne authors and the specialists at Sotheby's and Christie's, who can veto or simply never answer. A capitalised buyer does exist: evening-sale collectors, museums and major dealers.
scored.step_up: Recorded cases show the jump happens mostly before proof, because informed bidders already price the sleeper. Jan de Bray portrait: estimate EUR 600, sold EUR 13,500 at a regional house, then EUR 169,000 at Artcurial once attributed. That is about 12.5x from the regional price, not from the estimate. Fede Galizia: estimate EUR 1,100, but the provincial house sold it for EUR 148,000. After cleaning and Cottino's authentication, Sotheby's estimate was GBP 400-600k, about 3-4x the purchase. New Jersey 'Rembrandt': estimate $500-800, sold $870,000 without being confirmed. Salvator Mundi (about $1,175 to about $450M) is the outlier. Realistic step-up on the actual hammer price is about 3-15x per hit and roughly 1.5-4x on portfolio capital after misses and costs.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $50-200k (technical study plus conservation plus provenance research) and takes 1-3 years per work. That clears the expensive-proving bar. No published base rate exists for 'circle of' works being upgraded to autograph, so this is an estimate. Among works a skilled hunter bids on, perhaps 10-30% achieve a full upgrade. ML provenance linking (Getty Provenance Index, Lugt sale records, RKD images) could plausibly lift that 1.3-2x, but the lever is unproven. Style-image models compete with human connoisseurs, who are already good at this. The candidate's '2-3x lift' is an assumption, not sourced.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: scanned 18th-19th century sale catalogues (Lugt, Frick, Gallica, HathiTrust), the Getty Provenance Index, RKD and Witt photo archives. The outcome (true authorship) is not sitting in a legible field, so a real ML edge is possible. The catch is the right. Regional lots are now listed on Invaluable, LiveAuctioneers and Drouot Digital and watched by a global pool of specialist sleeper hunters and dealers. Prices are bid up 20-130x over estimate before any proof, as the de Bray and Galizia cases show. So the asset is not reliably bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data, because other bidders can.
scored.right_bought: Title to the physical painting, bought by competitive public bidding at regional auction houses. It is not a first-come right and there is no option structure. Because bidding is open, the spread is shared with rival hunters, and the seller-side cataloguing error often gets corrected by the room.
scored.buyer: Top-tier collectors, museums and major dealers (Old Master evening and day sales at Sotheby's and Christie's, TEFAF). The pool is capitalised but thin and shrinking. Global Old Master auction sales fell 25% to $803M in 2024, a 15-year low, with only four lots above $10M (Art Basel/UBS 2025).
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are: dealer/gallery, then private sales and art-backed lending, then perhaps an auction house. Each is a small, relationship-driven, reputation-bound business. The whole Old Master category is under $1B a year in auction turnover, with no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Tiny, contested prize. The whole Old Master auction market is about $803M a year (2024). Regional lots are already broadcast online to a global pool of sleeper hunters, who bid them up 20-100x before any proof. On top of that, a few gatekeeper experts control whether the 'proof' is accepted. The ML-created spread is thin, the prize is under $1B, and there is no ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery-heavy, with illegible public data and an expensive proving step, but rival hunters capture the spread at purchase, proof depends on gatekeeper opinion rather than physical evidence, and the market is under $1B a year with no ladder.

scored.name: Large-load powered site on state trust land (data centre)
scored.one_line: Company applies for commercial or option leases on school-trust parcels next to transmission substations, in states that lease by application at appraised or schedule rents (MT DNRC, ND, SD, WY OSLI, OK CLO). It funds a utility large-load study to get a will-serve letter for 100-500 MW, then assigns the powered lease to a hyperscaler or data-centre developer.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: State trust boards lease commercial land by competitive RFP or auction at fair market value for the proposed use, and must approve and can reprice any assignment. The publicly noticed RFP also reveals the site. The step-up therefore goes to the trust, not to the applicant who read the substation data. A second problem: utilities will not issue a firm will-serve to a speculator with no named load.
scored.frame: The rung is "powered site": a land right plus a utility commitment to serve 100-500 MW. The discovery part is picking substations with headroom and the parcels next to them. I put that at roughly 40-60% of the work. The rest is not trivial. It covers the utility large-load study, network upgrades the load customer often has to pay for, a named-load requirement before a firm will-serve, and trust-board approval of the lease and of any assignment. Capitalised buyers exist (hyperscalers and data-centre developers), so the frame is real, but the physical and regulatory step is not abstracted.
scored.step_up: The powered-land premium is real. In Texas (Claros, via Bisnow), power-ready sites go for about $800k/acre against about $2.5k-10k/acre for sites with no power study, a 100-300x step. In Northern Virginia (Avison Young), powered land is about $6M/acre against about $4M for entitled land without power. Altus Group's analysis of 80 deals found committed utility load was the strongest predictor of land price. On trust land, though, the applicant does not keep the spread. Montana law (77-1-904 MCA) requires an RFP to lease trust land for any commercial purpose, at fair market value for the proposed use. Assignments need board approval and can be repriced. Wyoming's Board of Land Commissioners judges every long-term lease on what best serves the beneficiaries.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Per proving attempt, a large-load or system-impact study plus engineering and legal work probably costs about $50k-$500k and takes 6-24 months. These are my estimates, not sourced. I would guess 30-50% of requests at well-chosen substations clear without prohibitive upgrades, also unsourced. ML over transmission topology and load-flow data could plausibly lift the hit rate about 1.2-1.5x. The limit is that the key inputs (FERC 715 base cases, which are CEII-restricted, and private utility large-load queues) are not public, so the model would work from partial data. Proving is expensive enough to count under the relaxed C3, but the lift is moderate.
scored.data: Transmission headroom data is partly public: OASIS postings, interconnection queues, and utility IRPs. The binding data, though, is either restricted (CEII power-flow cases) or private (utility large-load queues). It is also mostly legible to developers, who already screen substations with commercial tools. Trust parcel maps are fully public and legible. Prior hunts found a lookup-table approach matched ML on interconnection queues, and the same likely applies here.
scored.right_bought: No. Trust land is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. The trust leases commercial land through a publicly noticed competitive RFP or auction, at fair market value for the stated use, and that notice reveals the site to competitors. Assignment needs board consent and can be repriced. Note that "lease by application at schedule rent" covers grazing and agricultural leases, not commercial ones.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft is building a roughly 3,500-acre campus at Cheyenne on private land) and data-centre developers. They are well capitalised and pay heavily for committed power. Some trust boards now market their own sites to these buyers directly.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: powered land, then entitled shell, then a built data centre (colocation or build-to-suit), then on-site or behind-the-meter generation and a power-plus-compute platform. That is a multi-$B chain if the first rung could be won.
scored.fatal_flaw: The trust, not the applicant, captures the powered-land spread. Commercial trust leases go by public competitive RFP at fair market value for the proposed use, which also reveals the site. Assignments need board approval and can be repriced. Utilities will not issue a firm will-serve to a speculator with no named load. Developing or operating the site yourself under round 6 does not fix this: the lease is still bought at fair market value for data-centre use, and the physical build (about $10M+/MW) dwarfs the discovery work.
scored.one_line_reason: The powered-land premium is real (about $2.5k-10k/acre to about $800k/acre in Texas), and a large-load study is expensive enough to qualify under the relaxed C3. But the right is not bought cheaply: trust land goes by public fair-market-value RFP with repricing on assignment. The key grid data is restricted or already legible, and power proving needs a named load. The old fatal flaw stands, and the round-6 change to C2 does not rescue it.

scored.name: Air-permitted behind-the-meter power pad for DC campuses
scored.one_line: Option industrial or ag parcels on interstate gas laterals, prove a PSD/Title V or minor-source air permit for 100-500MW of onsite turbines or engines plus a gas tap agreement, and sell the permitted, fuel-secured pad to off-grid AI campus developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The binding constraint is not the permit. Gas turbines have ~5-year backlogs (GE Vernova sold into 2030, Mitsubishi sold out through 2028, 260-week lead times), and firm pipeline capacity is also scarce. Air permits are written for specific equipment and are fast to get in Texas (60-90 days expedited). A permitted pad with no turbine slot or firm gas is not where the scarce value sits. Buyers like Amazon, Crusoe and Williams permit for themselves around the turbines they have secured, so the ste
scored.frame: The rung would be a permitted pad with a gas tap, sold to developers of AI campuses that run off-grid. A market for this exists: powered land is a real asset class, and about $6B of data-center land was bought in H1 2026. Inside this rung, though, discovery (finding a parcel near a lateral that has spare capacity, in an attainment area, with willing sellers) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is permit engineering, dispersion modelling, negotiating the tap and interconnect, and above all securing turbines and firm gas. None of that is discovery, and none of it is trivial. The physical step is not abstracted away: without turbines the pad is not usable.
scored.step_up: Powered land carries a real premium. In Northern Virginia, entitled land with no power sells for about $4M/acre and powered land for at least $6M/acre (Andril, via Data Center Knowledge/TechTarget), a 1.5x uplift. Rural powered listings ask about $50k/acre (Denver, 100 acres for $5M). Against ag land at about $3-10k/acre, that is a 5-15x jump on the dirt. But the dirt is a tiny share of value, and buyers knock a lot off the price of a pad that has no turbine slot or firm gas.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not from a source: a PSD/Title V permit runs roughly $0.5-2M and 12-24 months, while a Texas minor-source or expedited permit takes 60-90 days and costs much less. A gas tap or interconnect study is about $50-250k. On parcels that are screened sensibly, I put the base rate of getting a permit and a tap at a usable site at maybe 50-70%. ML site screening (lateral capacity, nonattainment status, setbacks) might lift cost per proven pad by about 1.2-1.4x. The inputs are mostly legible GIS layers that conventional screening already uses.
scored.data: The signal mostly sits in legible or semi-legible data: EIA and pipeline-operator maps, FERC Form 2 and capacity postings, EPA nonattainment maps, county parcel data and state air-permit databases. PHMSA NPMS is restricted but structured. The outcome (spare capacity, permittability) is close to the surface in posted capacity and attainment fields, so an ML edge over a competent site-selection broker is thin. Ag landowners can be optioned cheaply. But powered-land brokers, pipeline companies (Williams, Energy Transfer) and hyperscalers already work this exact screen, and pipeline operators control the taps.
scored.right_bought: Purchase or option agreements on ag/industrial parcels from farmers. These are cheap to buy and must be bought (not free first-come), which is fine. The scarce complementary rights are firm transport capacity and turbine reservation slots. Those cannot be bought cheaply from naive owners: they belong to pipelines and OEMs who price them fully.
scored.buyer: Developers of off-grid AI campuses and hyperscalers: Crusoe, Amazon (8,000-acre Pecos TX gas site), Terravolt, Alpha Compute, Williams' Socrates-style projects. They are well capitalised, but they mostly assemble and permit sites themselves around the turbines they have already secured.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong. Permitted pad, then owning and operating the onsite power plant (IPP selling under a PPA to the campus), then the powered shell or data-center campus itself, then multi-GW energy parks. The path is credible and the prize is multi-$B.
scored.fatal_flaw: Unchanged by the relaxed C3: the air permit is not the binding constraint. Gas turbines have about 5-year backlogs (GE Vernova sold into 2030, Mitsubishi through 2028), firm pipeline capacity is scarce, and air permits are tied to specific equipment and fast in Texas. So a permitted pad with no turbine slot or firm gas holds little of the scarce value. Capitalised buyers permit for themselves around the turbines they have secured. Operating the plant yourself (round-6 C2) would mean winning the turbine queue and funding IPP-level capex. That returns about 1.5-2.5x, a utility-like return, and the edge comes from equipment access, not from ML discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Powered land carries a real premium, but the scarcity sits in turbines and firm gas, not in finding or permitting the pad. The data is mostly legible GIS, so ML adds little, and C1 and C4 stay weak even with the relaxed C3 and the operate-it-yourself C2.

scored.name: Floodway Narrowing for Urban Infill Parcels
scored.one_line: Buy urban and suburban parcels made near-worthless by sitting in the regulatory floodway, where no-rise rules ban building. Use ML to find floodways drawn from coarse old models or pre-channelisation topography, fund a corrected floodway model and LOMR, and sell now-buildable infill land to multifamily developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: A floodway is not a property of one parcel. It is a reach-wide allocation under a surcharge cap. To narrow it, the community must find no practicable alternative, notify affected owners and jurisdictions, accept higher flood elevations on others, and formally adopt the change. Even after a win, the land stays in the 100-year fringe with elevation and no-net-fill burdens. So the proving step is political and regulatory, not a discovery hit, and the step-up is capped well below 10^3.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a floodway-encumbered parcel and getting a LOMR that narrows the floodway. Discovery (finding floodways drawn from coarse HEC-2-era models or pre-channelisation topography) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is hydraulic remodelling of the whole reach, a CLOMR/LOMR through FEMA, and the community's formal adoption. That adoption means notifying owners, finding no practicable alternative, and reallocating the surcharge onto other owners. The physical step is cheap, but the proving step is political and regulatory, not abstracted. The buyer (a multifamily developer) is well capitalised.
scored.step_up: Unproven floodway land is discounted heavily. In one Kittitas County, WA appeal an appraiser put a partly floodway lot at about 83% below full-use value (a fully usable lot would sell for about $3/sf). A Louisville, CO appraisal priced the floodway/floodplain component separately and much lower. If narrowing works, the realistic uplift is about 3-6x. The land stays in the 100-year fringe with elevation, no-net-fill and insurance burdens, so the gain is far below 10^3. Under round 6, C2 rates return on capital, not step-up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: One Cass County, ND memo puts a simple floodway LOMA/LOMR at about $2k-8k. A real floodway re-delineation needs a new reach-wide hydraulic model, survey, CLOMR, FEMA review and local adoption. My estimate is $50k-250k and 1-3 years; I found no published figure. That clears the >=$50k bar. My guess at the base success rate is 30-50%, mostly set by local politics and no-rise analysis on neighbours, not by hydraulics. ML can rank reaches by how stale the model and terrain are, against LiDAR, plausibly 1.5x+ on finding hydraulically valid candidates. It cannot move the adoption odds, so the gain in cost per proven asset is about 1.2-1.5x.
scored.data: Effective FIS reports, old HEC-2/WSPRO models, historic channel-improvement records and LiDAR are public and partly illegible (scanned FIS profiles, archived model decks). The outcome, whether the floodway is mis-drawn, is not written into any legible field. The NFHL only shows current lines. That is a real ML edge.
scored.right_bought: Parcels can be bought from owners or assessors who treat floodway land as near-worthless (one appraiser applied an 83% discount). But the right that matters, the floodway line, is not owned or bought. It is a community-adopted, reach-wide allocation, and neighbours and the floodplain administrator can block it. Buying single parcels does not secure the reallocation.
scored.buyer: Multifamily and infill developers, homebuilders and land bankers, who are well capitalised and pay full price for entitled infill land.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from parcel to entitlement to vertical multifamily development to ownership and operation. That is a normal real-estate development ladder. It is large in aggregate but fragmented and local, with no proprietary chain beyond it, so it is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: A floodway is not a property of one parcel. It is a reach-wide allocation under a surcharge cap that the community must formally adopt after notifying the owners it pushes flood elevations onto. The proving step is political and regulatory, not a discovery hit, so ML cannot lift the binding odds. Even after a win, the land stays in the 100-year fringe with elevation and no-net-fill burdens, which caps the uplift at a few x.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, since proving is expensive and ML can rank stale floodways. But the proof depends on community politics, and the capped fringe-land uplift gives only a modest, fragmented return.

scored.name: Retired fossil plant sites with reusable interconnection (surplus/replacement rights)
scored.one_line: Buy or option retired or retiring peaker and coal plant sites from co-ops, munis and IPP estates who see only a decommissioning liability, prove FERC/RTO replacement or surplus interconnection rights for co-located generation, storage or large load before they lapse, and sell the energised brownfield to hyperscalers or power-plus-DC developers. Adjacent to the killed powered-brownfields idea; the edge is ML on which sites keep deliverable MW, and remediation must be screened.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry. Retired-plant interconnection is now the most-shopped asset in US power: the retirement lists and ISA MW values are legible fields, and the owners and their advisors already price the right at data-centre value. Meanwhile, the remediation and build steps, not discovery, decide whether a deal works.
scored.frame: The rung is: control a retired or retiring fossil plant site and secure its replacement or surplus interconnection right (a FERC/RTO filing plus a study), then sell or develop the energised brownfield. Discovery, meaning knowing which sites keep deliverable MW, is perhaps 20-35% of the work inside that rung. Most of the work is the regulatory filing and study, negotiating with the owner, remediation and demolition (Kansas City: $20M cleanup against a $13.6M site value), and building new generation or load inside the replacement deadline. That physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. A capitalised buyer does exist (hyperscalers, and power-plus-DC developers such as TeraWulf and Homer City).
scored.step_up: There is no clean public $/MW benchmark, and most deals are undisclosed. Cheswick, PA: 47 acres sold for $14.3M, which supports 180MW of IT load, or about $80k/MW for land plus the interconnection position (my arithmetic). Didcot A, UK: RWE got EUR225M from a hyperscaler. Kansas City: about $160k/acre less demolition and cleanup, with $20M remediation against a $13.6M site value. Owners already capture data-centre pricing, so the gap between unproven and proven is perhaps 1.5-3x, mostly paid for by remediation and filing work, not 10^3. Sources: DCD on Cheswick, DCK on RWE/Amazon, DCD on PowerTransitions.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. Each attempt needs an RTO surplus or replacement study and FERC filing (roughly $100k-$1M+ and 1-3 years), plus site control and environmental diligence. The base rate at which an identified retired site keeps usable deliverable MW is probably 40-60%. The answer mostly sits in legible fields (EIA-860 retirement dates, ISA MW, RTO deliverability studies), so ML lifts it perhaps 1.1-1.3x, not 1.5x. Estimate from PNNL coal-to-DC report context, no direct source for hit rates.
scored.data: The signal is legible: EIA-860 lists retirements, RTO queues and ISA MW values are structured, and PNNL and brokers already publish screens of coal-to-DC sites. The answer (MW at the point of interconnection, retirement date) is written into status fields, which is the failure mode prior hunts found. Some illegible signal remains in scanned ISAs, deliverability studies and remediation records, but it moves price only at the margin.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought rather than claimed first-come: you buy or option the site from the owner, and replacement interconnection rights travel with it. But the sellers (co-ops, munis, IPPs such as RWE and Talen) are sophisticated and advised, and they run auctions at data-centre value. Small co-op peakers may be mispriced, but they carry few MW.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Amazon bought Didcot), power-plus-DC developers (TeraWulf at Morgantown, Homer City at 4.5GW, PowerTransitions), and IPPs. All are heavily capitalised and actively buying.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: site plus interconnection, then new gas, storage or solar generation, then powered shell or data-centre campus development, then owning and operating an IPP or utility-scale campus. That is a multi-$B to $10B+ path, and Homer City's 4.5GW campus shows the scale.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry. Retired-plant interconnection is the most-shopped asset in US power: retirement lists and ISA MW values are legible fields, and owners and their advisors already price the right at data-centre value. Remediation and the time-limited build, not discovery, decide whether a deal works. Dropping the step-up requirement and relaxing C3 do not fix this, because ML adds little to a lookup of public fields.
scored.one_line_reason: The prize and ladder are real and the buyers are well capitalised, but the asset is already priced at data-centre value from legible public fields, and remediation and build dominate the work. So ML gives at most about 1.2x and creates no real spread. Score: 11 of 25.

scored.name: Non-powered and unpowered dam hydropower licensing
scored.one_line: Acquire unpowered or retired private mill dams cheaply, or secure FERC preliminary permits plus owner leases on some of the roughly 80,000-90,000 US non-powered dams. ML over scanned dam inspection reports, historic flow records and FERC lapsed-permit filings picks the dams with licensable head, flow, fish-passage and grid access. Carry each through FERC licence or 10MW exemption, then sell the licensed project to hydro IPPs or own and operate it as firm clean baseload for data centers and utilities.
scored.unproven_right: Fee ownership of an existing small dam and its flowage and riparian rights (often a liability to its owner, sold for $1-$250k in New England, Mid-Atlantic and Upper Midwest), or a FERC preliminary permit (4-year exclusive priority, filing cost only) plus a lease or easement negotiated cheaply with an irrigation district, county or USACE/BOR partner that cannot value the hydro potential
scored.proving_step: Feasibility, interconnection study and a FERC licence or 10MW exemption with state 401 water-quality certification and fish-passage studies. Costs $0.3-3M and 2-5 years, with a base success rate of perhaps 40-60%. Most historic permits lapsed because developers picked dams blindly; ML that avoids structural, fish-passage and ownership blockers buried in inspection PDFs plausibly lifts licence rate 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Hydro IPPs and aggregators (Brookfield Renewable, Eagle Creek, Rye Development, Enel), utilities with renewable mandates, and data-center PPA offtakers paying a premium for firm, ITC-eligible clean power
scored.public_data: USACE National Inventory of Dams, state dam-safety and USACE periodic inspection reports (scanned), historic mill and water-power surveys (e.g. 1880 Census water-power reports), USGS NWIS gage records, FERC eLibrary lapsed and surrendered permit filings (which explain why projects died), ORNL NPD/HydroSource assessments, EIA substation and line maps. Site licensability is not a legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: Dam or permit plus early work at about $0.1M/MW becomes a licensed, shovel-ready site worth $0.3-0.6M/MW, or a built 1-5MW asset worth $3-15M (about 2-8x on capital if built and operated). Small per site, low multi-$B aggregated (about 10 GW of potential). Ladder: own and operate the fleet, pair with storage, become a firm-clean-power provider to data centers.
scored.frame: The rung is a FERC licence (or 10MW exemption) on a non-powered dam. Discovery and proving are maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung: siting, 401 certification, fish passage and interconnection. Most of the cost sits in negotiation and environmental study, and ML does not help with that. The rung also sells poorly. Rye Development, the best-known NPD developer, licensed its Pittsburgh lock-and-dam projects and then moved to sell the unbuilt licences to a turbine maker's affiliate (Snowmass/Mavel). So licensed-but-unbuilt NPD sites change hands at modest prices, and there is no deep pool of buyers paying a large premium. Real value only appears after the bespoke civil and electromechanical build. That build is the hard part, the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a permit costs only the filing, and a small private dam goes for $1-250k (candidate's figure). Licensed but unbuilt: no public price, and Rye's licence sales do not suggest a big premium; the candidate's $0.3-0.6M/MW is unverified. Built: comparable operating hydro sold for about $2.2M/MW (Brookfield bought 351 MW from NextEra for about $760M in 2012). Building costs $2,200-34,000/kW, mostly under $12,000/kW before development costs (ORNL 2020 NPD cost analysis), so at about $5-12M/MW build cost against about $2-3M/MW value the spread is thin or negative. It turns positive only with the ITC plus a data-center premium PPA (Rye-Iron Mountain 150 MW deal). Realistic return is under 2x to about 2x on total capital.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. FERC licensing takes 5+ years; a small utility put its own relicensing at $750k-1.5M (Okanogan PUD), and the full process can reach tens of millions. Base licence success is maybe 40-60% (candidate's estimate; no lapse-rate statistic found). Most permits lapse because of economics (capex against power price), financing or agency conditions, not blind site picking. ML over inspection PDFs might lift the hit rate about 1.2-1.5x by flagging structural and fish-passage blockers. It cannot fix the binding constraint, which is construction capex per kW. ORNL already publishes NPD screening and a 2024 reduced-form cost model for pre-feasibility.
scored.data: Partly legible already. The NID lists every dam with owner, height and purpose; ORNL NPD/HydroSource already estimates head, flow and potential MW for about 54,000 NPDs; USGS gage data is structured. The illegible part (scanned state inspection reports, FERC eLibrary narratives on why permits died, 1880 water-power surveys) adds some signal on licensability, so the ML edge is real but marginal. On the right: the best sites (USACE/BOR locks and dams) are not bought. They come by first-come FERC permit plus federal coordination, which is free but contested; Rye and Free Flow Power swept the USACE locks years ago. Small private mill dams can be bought cheaply from owners who see them as liabilities, but those dams are tiny (under 1 MW), often need expensive dam-safety repair, and often face removal pressure from fish agencies.
scored.right_bought: Mixed. A FERC preliminary permit is first-come and costs only the filing, not a purchase from an owner who cannot read the data. A private small dam is bought cheaply ($1-250k) but comes with dam-safety liability and removal pressure. Federal dams need a lease or agreement with USACE/BOR, which do not sell the right cheaply in the Terranox sense.
scored.buyer: Hydro IPPs (Brookfield, Eagle Creek, Enel), Snowmass/Mavel-type turbine affiliates, utilities and data-center offtakers. These buyers want operating assets or near-build projects. Demand for unbuilt licences is thin, as Rye's licence sales show.
scored.ladder: Moderate. The rungs go licence, then build, then own and operate the fleet, then pair with storage and pumped hydro, then sell firm clean power to data centers. The theoretical prize is about 10-12 GW of NPD potential, low multi-$B. Every rung above licensing is capex-heavy bespoke civil construction with weak per-MW economics, so the climb dilutes the discovery edge rather than compounding it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step is not trivial. Each powerhouse retrofit is bespoke civil and electromechanical construction at $5-12k/kW (ORNL), and a built asset is worth about $2-3M/MW. Value is made or lost in construction, not discovery, the same failure as geothermal in coal mines. ML siting cannot fix the capex economics that killed most past NPD permits, and the licensed-but-unbuilt rung has no capitalised buyer paying a large premium.
scored.one_line_reason: Licensing is expensive and ML adds a modest hit-rate lift, but build capex at about $5-12k/kW against about $2-3M/MW asset value leaves under about 2x on total capital. Discovery is not the dominant share of work in any rung that sells.

scored.name: Certificate-of-Need bed licence relocation (skilled nursing and behavioural health)
scored.one_line: In CON states, buy dormant or under-used nursing-home and behavioural-health bed licences from distressed or closing operators. ML over scanned CON applications, need-methodology reports, hearing decisions and competitor-opposition patterns predicts which relocation or transfer applications will be approved. Win approval to move the beds to high-demand counties, then build and operate or sell to post-acute chains and REITs, who pay the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: CON-protected bed licences embedded in failing rural or underperforming facilities, bought at about $5-30k per bed of embedded value because relocation approval is uncertain.
scored.proving_step: State CON relocation, transfer or modernisation approval with need studies, legal work and contested hearings: about $100-500k and 1-3 years, approval about 40-70%. ML on past contested-case outcomes plausibly lifts approval odds about 1.5x and steers purchases to licences that can move.
scored.proven_buyer: Post-acute and behavioural operators and REITs (Ensign, PACS, Omega, Sabra, Welltower), health systems and PE-backed operators, paying licence-scarcity premiums of $30-150k per bed in high-demand counties.
scored.public_data: State CON program dockets and decisions (NC, GA, NY, VA, KY, TN; largely scanned), staff analyses and hearing transcripts, state health plan bed-need tables, CMS cost reports and ownership files, inspection reports. Outcomes depend on narrative board reasoning, not a field.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-5x per bed (up to 5-20x in the best relocations); 2-4x on capital net. Prize about $1B+ in CON states, dependent on CON rules. Ladder: developer, operator, regional post-acute platform.
scored.frame: The rung is a CON-approved relocated bed right. Inside that rung, predicting approval is maybe 30-40% of the work; the rest is need studies, lawyers and contested hearings. The approval is worth almost nothing until you build a new facility at about $230k+ per bed and then staff and run it. Measured by capital, the licence is under 10% of a working bed, so discovery is a small share and the physical step dominates. This matches the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, not Terranox.
scored.step_up: An unproven bed licence trades at about $2k per bed in weak regions and $25-30k in strong ones (Bed License Exchange co-founder quoted by Skilled Nursing News). A finished, operating SNF bed traded at an average of $83,800 in 2024, down from $97,700 in 2023 (Irving Levin via Skilled Nursing News). Outliers like Las Vegas hit $325k per bed, but Nevada has no CON. The licence-only step-up after a relocation approval is maybe 2-5x, about $10-30k a bed. Realising that value as an operator means spending about $230k+ per bed on construction (an Illinois 68-bed project cost $233.8k per bed), and that is more than the average operating bed sells for.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about $100-500k and takes 1-3 years, which is expensive, so it passes the cost test. I found no published approval rate. North Carolina competitive-review cases show some applicants approved and others rejected, then contested. Uncontested relocations within a county are approved often, so the base rate is probably 50-80%. ML gives perhaps a 1.2-1.5x lift, because experienced CON counsel already predict outcomes well and the agency findings spell out conforming and nonconforming criteria. Sources: NC case law (Johnston Health Care v. NC DHR, AH NC Owner), Florida AHCA cases.
scored.data: The dockets and hearing records are public, often scanned, and scattered across states, so they are illegible to some degree. But each decision is written up as approved or denied, with criterion-by-criterion findings, so the outcome is already summarised. The state bed-need tables are published as legible numbers. Bed licences are also a brokered, known market (Bed License Exchange, Senwell), so sellers know roughly what their beds are worth. The discount comes from distress, not from sellers being unable to read the data.
scored.right_bought: Yes, bed licences can be bought from closing or distressed operators in CON states such as MO, NC, KY and WA, where retained bed rights after closure are allowed. But they are priced by brokers, so there is little information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: There are capitalised buyers: Ensign, PACS, Omega, Sabra, Welltower, PE-backed operators and health systems. They mostly buy operating facilities, not bare relocated licences, and SNF prices per bed are falling, Medicaid-heavy and thin-margin.
scored.ladder: The rungs are licence, then development, then operator, then regional post-acute platform, then REIT. The ladder is real, but every rung above the licence is capital-heavy, low-margin, labour-limited operating work, and CON repeal (a trend in several states) can erase the scarcity value that the bottom rung depends on.
scored.fatal_flaw: The licence is the cheap, small part of the value. A relocated bed has to be built at about $230k+ per bed and then operated, and that is more than an average operating SNF bed sells for ($83.8k in 2024). So the physical step dwarfs discovery, just as in the geothermal counter-example. On top of that, CON outcomes are written into legible decisions, licences are already brokered, and CON repeal can wipe out the scarcity premium.
scored.one_line_reason: Predicting CON approval is cheap compared with building and running the relocated beds. The licence step-up of about $10-30k a bed is small against $230k+ of construction, it is brokered, and repeal can erase it.

scored.name: 9% LIHTC allocation winning (affordable housing tax-credit awards)
scored.one_line: Option sites and use ML over historical QAP scoring sheets, award lists and scanned application packets to pick the sites and configurations that win competitive 9% housing tax-credit allocations, then own and develop the projects with a syndicator's equity.
scored.unproven_right: Site control options on parcels near qualifying amenities, at market land value
scored.proving_step: Competitive 9% LIHTC application: $75k-$250k per application (market study, architecture, environmental) and 6-18 months. Win rates 20-50%; ML scoring-point optimisation gives roughly 1.5-2x lift.
scored.proven_buyer: Tax-credit syndicators and banks (CRA buyers) paying about $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar, i.e. $10-20M of equity per award
scored.public_data: State HFA QAPs, scoring sheets and award lists, scanned application binders via public-records requests, HUD QCT/DDA maps, opportunity-area data
scored.rough_step_up: $150k at-risk application spend becomes a $15M equity award, plus a $1.5-2.5M developer fee and long-term ownership. Ladder: owned portfolio.
scored.frame: The rung would be "win a 9% allocation on an optioned site." Inside that rung, site selection and application tuning are maybe 50-60% of the effort. The rest is the market study, architecture, environmental work, financing commitments and local approvals. The bigger problem is that the award is not a cleanly sellable output. HFAs restrict transfers, and syndicators only fund equity as a real $20-40M building gets built and placed in service. The physical step (construction, lease-up, the 15-year compliance period) is the bulk of the work, so this looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the asset is harder to deliver than to find. Discovery is well under 80% of any frame a capitalised buyer actually pays for.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a site option at market land value plus about $75-250k of application spend. Proven: an award worth about $10-20M of syndicator equity at $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar, but that equity funds construction and is not profit. The developer captures a fee of about $1.5-2.5M, often partly deferred, plus a residual ownership interest of modest value. The real spread is roughly $0.5-1M of sunk spend per win (4-5 applications per award) against a $1.5-2.5M fee with guarantee and construction risk. That is roughly 2-4x on at-risk capital, not 10^2+. These figures are from the candidate and industry norms, not verified per state.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $75-250k and 6-18 months per application. Base hit rate is about 20-25%. Oversubscription is about 4:1 in California's North/East Bay region (July 2015 round) and about 4-5:1 in North Carolina (2019-2020). Sources: TCAC workshop materials and NC Housing Coalition. The ML lever is weak, because TCAC says most 9% applications get a perfect score and awards are decided by published, formulaic tiebreakers (public-funds leverage, cost efficiency). Those can be computed directly from the QAP without ML, and experienced developers and consultants already optimise them. Realistic ML lift over a competent consultant is about 1.1-1.3x, mostly from better site screening against opportunity-area and amenity maps.
scored.data: The data fails the legibility test. QAPs are published deterministic scoring rubrics, HFAs publish scores and award lists, and QCT/DDA and opportunity maps are clean GIS layers. The outcome is written straight into legible fields, which is exactly the failure mode from prior hunts. Scanned application binders exist, but the winning logic is the published rubric, not hidden signal. On the right: land options are bought at market value from owners and brokers who know the affordable-housing market. Amenity-proximity points are obvious from public maps, so there is no informational discount on the land.
scored.right_bought: Site-control options or purchase agreements on parcels, at market price. They are bought rather than free, but there is no discount driven by illegibility.
scored.buyer: Tax-credit syndicators and CRA-motivated banks buy the credits at about $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar. They are well capitalised, but they buy credits from a delivered building, not a paper award.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but moderate: 9% wins, then 4% bond deals, an owned affordable portfolio, in-house construction and property management, then syndication or a fund. 9% supply is capped by state per-capita allocations, so the top rung is a large affordable-housing owner-operator (multi-$B portfolio), not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is scored by a published, deterministic rubric. Most competitive applications already hit maximum points and are separated by formulaic tiebreakers anyone can compute from the QAP. There is no illegible signal for ML to extract, and no information discount on the land. On top of that, value is only realised after building and operating a $20-40M project, so the physical step dominates.
scored.one_line_reason: Expensive applications and 20-25% win rates satisfy the relaxed C3 cost test. But the scoring is public and legible, perfect scores are the norm, tiebreakers are formula-driven, and land is bought at market price. The real work and capital go into construction, so the spread is a 2-4x developer fee with little ML edge.

scored.name: Continuation Forge: live patent families with pending continuations
scored.one_line: Buy patent families with a still-pending continuation from small inventors, robotics or materials startups and bankruptcy estates for $5-100k; ML finds written-description support in the spec for claims reading on products shipping today; prosecute to allowance with an EoU chart and sell.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: This is already the standard NPE playbook. IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, IV and Acacia, plus brokers who screen for live continuations, already buy families with pending continuations and draft claims to read on shipping products. Pending status is a legible field, and LLM claim-charting tools are commoditising the matching. The proven value is not realised on allowance: it depends on years of litigation exposed to IPR and Alice. That caps the immediate step-up at about 10-50x rather than 10^3-10^4
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy a live family and get a product-reading continuation claim allowed'. Inside it, discovery (finding written-description support for claims that read on today's products) is perhaps 60-70% of the work. Prosecution through allowance (~$20-60k, 1-3 years, examiner fights over 112 and 103) is a real step but it is mostly abstracted to patent counsel. The problem is that an allowed claim is not a finished, sellable product. Its value appears only through licensing or litigation, and that is the hard, bespoke 'plant-building' step (often $2-5M per campaign, plus IPR and Alice risk). The buyers of the rung's output are a thin brokered market (~$300-350M/yr per ROL) and NPEs.
scored.step_up: The unproven family costs $5-100k. Brokered median asking prices have historically been ~$83k-250k per US asset (ROL 2016-2018), and realised sale prices run below asking. A continuation with an EoU chart against a shipping product might sell for $250k-$2M. That is roughly 5-50x on the asset, not 10^3. Holding and litigating can reach $5-50M settlements in rare cases, but only after $2-5M of litigation spend and years of IPR exposure.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving to allowance costs ~$20-60k plus 1-3 years per attempt (attorney fees and USPTO fees; my estimate, not sourced), so it only borderline-meets the expensive threshold. Continuation allowance rates are high (~60-80%), so allowance itself is not the bottleneck. The real hit rate is 'allowed claim that reads on a product AND survives IPR and 101'. That is plausibly 20-40%, and ML-led selection of specs and targets could lift it ~1.3-1.6x. The truly expensive proving step is litigation, and there ML adds little.
scored.data: Specs and file wrappers are public, full text and searchable (USPTO and Google Patents). They are big but legible, not scanned or illegible. Pending-continuation status is a legible PAIR/Patent Center field that brokers already filter on. The illegible half is product teardowns, docs and firmware, where LLM claim-charting tools (and incumbents using them) are commoditising the matching. Rights are genuinely bought, not taken first-come, and small inventors and bankruptcy estates do underprice them. That part of the right is real, but sellers increasingly go through brokers who screen for exactly this.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patent families are bought outright by assignment from inventors, startups and bankruptcy trustees, usually for $5-100k for small families, often through brokers or auctions.
scored.buyer: NPEs and aggregators (IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, Acacia, IV, RPX defensively), litigation funders, and operating companies buying defensively. They are capitalised but price-disciplined, and the brokered market is only ~$300-350M per year.
scored.ladder: Weak. Above the rung sit licensing campaigns and litigation (the funded NPE model), then a litigation-finance fund. None of these leads to owning a physical value chain or a trillion-dollar path. Acacia itself has pivoted to buying operating businesses because the model gets little credit in its valuation.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value is not realised at allowance. It depends on years of $2-5M-per-campaign litigation exposed to IPR and Alice, the realisation step that dominates the work. Meanwhile the discovery signal (pending continuations, full-text specs) is legible and already worked by NPEs, brokers and LLM claim-charting tools. That leaves a small (~$300M/yr) contested market rather than an ML-created spread with a multi-$B prize.
scored.one_line_reason: Under round 6, holding and litigating the asset is allowed, but that makes the hard step litigation, not discovery. The data is legible and contested, the prize is small and the ladder is short, so the relaxed C3 lifts it only modestly (about 10/25).

scored.name: Australian rural-to-urban rezoning (NSW, SEQ and Victorian growth corridors)
scored.one_line: Option broadacre rural land near the growth fronts of Western Sydney, the Hunter, South East Queensland or Melbourne. Pick parcels by mining planning panel reports, council papers and state infrastructure plans. Lodge a proponent-led planning proposal or planning scheme amendment (NSW gateway to LEP amendment; Victorian PSA or precinct structure plan; SEQ scheme amendment) and sell zoned englobo land to master-planned community developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The step-up is already priced in. Land with any real chance of rezoning sits inside published growth or investigation areas and trades at hope value (Beveridge about $367k/ha unzoned versus about $1.5-2M/ha zoned). Developers hunt for exactly these parcels themselves. That leaves a 2-6x, multi-year, politically driven proving step, where the work is advocacy rather than discovery and ML adds only a modest edge.
scored.frame: The rung is optioning broadacre land and taking it through a proponent-led rezoning (NSW Gateway to LEP amendment, Victorian PSA/PSP, SEQ scheme amendment), then selling zoned englobo land. Inside that rung, picking the parcel ('discovery') is maybe 15-25% of the work. The other 75-85% is the proving step: technical studies (traffic, flood, biodiversity, heritage, servicing), consultant fees, council and state advocacy, infrastructure contribution negotiation and politics, over 3-10 years. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted, so it fails the 80%-discovery test. A capitalised buyer does exist: master-planned community developers such as Stockland, Lendlease, Mirvac and AVJennings.
scored.step_up: Unzoned land inside identified growth or investigation areas already trades at hope value. Prior evidence for Beveridge: about $367k/ha unzoned versus about $1.5-2M/ha zoned, a 4-5x step. Truly rural land outside the UGB or growth areas is cheaper (roughly $20-60k/ha), but its rezoning odds are very low. Zoned land also carries infrastructure contributions: GAIC/ICP-type levies of about $80-95k/ha in the Melbourne boundary changes, and much more under current ICP and PSP development contribution regimes. Searches found no current 2025 per-hectare comparison of zoned and unzoned land, so the step-up stays at the earlier 2-6x estimate, net of contributions and holding costs.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are rough industry estimates, not searched figures. A proponent-led planning proposal or PSP-style amendment costs about A$0.5-3M+ per attempt in studies and consultants, plus option fees and 3-10 years of holding. That clears the 'expensive' bar. Base hit rates depend on location. For land already in a growth or investigation area, approval is high-probability and the main uncertainty is timing. Out-of-sequence proposals on land outside those areas mostly fail or stall; NSW has rejected many at Gateway and Victoria guards the UGB tightly. ML on council papers and panel reports could plausibly improve parcel choice by about 1.2-1.5x. Most of the predictive signal, though, already sits in legible state documents: growth corridor plans, Regional Plans, the SEQ Regional Plan and infrastructure pipelines.
scored.data: Planning panel reports, council business papers, submissions and state infrastructure plans are public and partly unstructured, so there is some genuine illegibility. The outcome, however, is largely summarised in legible form: growth area and investigation area maps, UDP datasets that classify zoned versus unzoned englobo land, PSP schedules and Regional Plan maps. Developers, buyers' agents and land aggregators already read this material closely. The right can be bought, by option or put-and-call over farmland, but owners near growth fronts are routinely approached by developers and price in hope value. The sellers who cannot read the data are mainly owners outside the mapped areas, and their land is the land least likely to be rezoned.
scored.right_bought: Option or put-and-call agreements over freehold rural land, bought from farmers and lifestyle-block owners. These are bought, not free first-come rights. Owners near growth fronts are well informed and receive frequent developer approaches.
scored.buyer: Master-planned community developers and land developers (Stockland, Lendlease, Mirvac, Frasers, AVJennings, Satterley, Peet), along with land-banking funds. They are well capitalised, but they also run this exact rezoning playbook in-house, so they are competitors as well as buyers.
scored.ladder: The ladder is long and real: rezoning, then englobo sales, then subdivision and civil works, then lot sales, then house-and-land and built-form homebuilding, then whole master-planned communities and associated assets (retail centres, build-to-rent, infrastructure). The top of this ladder is occupied by multi-billion-dollar incumbents (Stockland, about A$10B+ market cap), so the end state is large. Climbing it is capital-intensive and competitive, with no technology moat.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is already priced in, and the proving step is advocacy, not discovery. Land with a real chance of rezoning sits inside published growth or investigation areas and trades at hope value (Beveridge about $367k/ha unzoned versus about $1.5-2M/ha zoned). Developers hunt these same parcels in-house. What remains is a 2-6x, multi-year, politically driven approval, net of large infrastructure contributions. Self-developing, as the round-6 C2 allows, only turns this into an ordinary land-developer return (about 15-20% IRR, well under 5x on capital), and ML gives at most a modest selection edge.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a large market with a long ladder and capitalised buyers, but rezoning is a years-long advocacy process rather than an 80%-discovery rung. The likely outcomes are already legible in state growth maps and priced into hope value, so ML adds only about 1.2-1.5x selection and self-development yields ordinary developer returns.
sources: prior round evidence: Beveridge ~$367k/ha unzoned vs ~$1.5-2M/ha zoned

scored.name: Texas ETJ-release plus MUD/WCID formation land
scored.one_line: Option fringe ranch and farm acreage near Texas metros, use SB 2038 (2023) to release it from a city's ETJ, form a MUD or WCID with a utility service agreement and development agreement, and sell the entitled, utility-backed tract to master-planned-community builders. The company also keeps reimbursement rights on the district's future bonds.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: This is the existing Texas land-entitlement business. The rung's work is legal, political and utility-negotiation execution, not discovery, and the step-up is only about 3-8x on land. Key status data (TCEQ district database, CCN shapefiles) is already legible, so ML adds at most a modest screening edge in a market where sophisticated incumbents compete for the same fringe tracts.
scored.frame: The rung is 'entitled, utility-backed raw tract sold to master-planned-community (MPC) developers or homebuilders'. A capitalised buyer exists: public homebuilders and MPC developers buy entitled MUD land. But discovery (picking the tract) is maybe 15-25% of the work. Most of the work is execution: filing the SB 2038 release petition and defending it (cities like Denton, College Station, Bastrop and Navasota denied petitions, and about 20 cities have sued), getting a TCEQ or legislative MUD/WCID created, negotiating a utility service agreement with a CCN holder or a wholesale water provider, and drafting the development agreement and engineering. This 'physical' step is legal, political and engineering work over 1-3 years. It is not trivial and it is not abstracted. The frame fails the 80%+ discovery test.
scored.step_up: TRERC puts the Texas rural average at about $5,214/acre (2025). Urban-adjacent fringe land runs about $9k-$20k+/acre because sellers already price in development potential. Entitled MUD land with utility commitments typically trades at roughly $30k-80k/acre in DFW, Austin and Houston fringe markets (broker norms; I found no exact source). The proven-value step-up on fringe land is therefore about 3-8x, not 10^3-10^4. Under round 6, holding the MUD bond reimbursement rights adds upside. Developers typically get about 70% or more of eligible water, sewer and drainage infrastructure reimbursed out of district bonds, but that money repays the developer's own capex rather than creating a spread. A realistic return on total capital is about 2-3x over 3-6 years. The prize across Texas fringe growth is multi-$B, but incumbents (Hillwood, Johnson Development, Howard Hughes and others) already capture it.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs roughly $0.3-2M in legal, engineering, district-creation and option payments and takes 1-3 years (estimate; no source found). That clears the 'expensive' bar. The base success rate of carrying an optioned tract to an entitled, utility-backed MUD is plausibly 40-70%. Failures come from city denial or litigation, the CCN holder refusing service, water-supply limits, and floodplain. Most of these failure modes are political or negotiated, so ML predicts them poorly. A model over CCN capacity, floodplain, city petition outcomes and approvals for nearby districts plausibly gives about 1.2-1.4x better cost per proven tract.
scored.data: The key data is legible and widely used: the TCEQ Water Districts database, PUC CCN shapefiles, county appraisal parcels, FEMA floodplain layers and city agendas listing ETJ petition outcomes. Land brokers and MPC developers already screen with GIS. Some illegible signal exists in scanned utility service agreements, district creation orders and city council minutes, but the outcome (district created, petition approved or denied) sits in legible records. ML's edge is modest.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought: you can option ranch land. But fringe sellers near metros are not data-blind. Brokers solicit them constantly and they price in development potential, so there is little purchase discount that comes from the buyer reading data the owner cannot.
scored.buyer: Public homebuilders (DR Horton, Lennar and others) and MPC developers buy entitled MUD tracts and finished lots. Bond-market investors buy MUD bonds, which supports the reimbursement rights.
scored.ladder: There is a strong ladder: entitled tract, then horizontal development and finished lots (financed by reimbursement), then the MPC developer role, then homebuilding. Owning the water and wastewater utility (a CCN, recurring revenue) is an adjacent rung. Full vertical integration is a large business, as Howard Hughes and Hillwood show, though they are not trillion-dollar companies.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is the existing Texas land-entitlement business. Inside the rung, the work is legal, political and utility-negotiation execution (SB 2038 petitions that cities deny and contest in court, MUD creation, utility agreements), not discovery. The status data (TCEQ district database, CCN shapefiles, city petition records) is already legible, and fringe sellers already price in development potential. ML therefore yields at most about a 1.2-1.4x screening edge and no real purchase-price spread over sophisticated incumbents.
scored.one_line_reason: Round 6 lets the company develop or hold the asset, and the expensive proving step meets the relaxed C3 bar. It still fails C1 and C4: execution dominates discovery, the data is legible, and incumbents compete for the same tracts with no information discount. The total stays at about 10/25.

scored.name: Orphan Hydro Relicensing Roll-up
scored.one_line: Buy small FERC-licensed hydro dams whose owners face relicensing (often given away or sold for near zero), push them through relicensing with ML-picked winners, then operate or sell the relicensed plants to hydro IPPs (Brookfield, Eagle Creek/Ontario Teachers, Rye) that pay full value for long-licence MWs.
scored.unproven_right: The dam and its expiring FERC licence (or a purchase option on it), bought for $0-1M from municipalities, mill owners and small utilities that would otherwise file to surrender because relicensing looks too costly.
scored.proving_step: FERC relicensing (ILP/ALP): 3-6 years and $1-5M in fish-passage, flow and environmental studies plus settlement with agencies. Roughly 40-60% of small projects get through on economic terms. ML predicts which ones get mandatory conditions they can afford.
scored.proven_buyer: Hydro IPPs and infrastructure funds (Brookfield Renewable, Eagle Creek, Enel, Rye Development) and utilities that need firm clean MWh or RECs.
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary (scanned study plans, Section 18 fishway prescriptions, 4(e) conditions, settlement agreements, surrender filings across decades), USFWS/NMFS biological opinions, USGS NWIS streamflow, EIA-923 generation, state 401 water-quality certification files. The outcome cost (the agency conditions) is buried in unstructured PDFs, not in a status field.
scored.rough_step_up: Bought at ~$0-0.3M/MW. A relicensed plant with 30-50 year term trades at ~$2-4M/MW. That is about 3-8x on all-in capital (purchase + relicensing), with roughly 1,000+ US licences expiring by 2035 (a multi-$B prize). Ladder: operate, uprate turbines, add storage, sell firm power directly.
scored.frame: The rung is "expiring FERC licence plus dam, carried through relicensing." Proving is regulatory work (studies, agency settlements), but it does not end with the paperwork. The relicence usually requires physical capex: fishways, minimum-flow changes that cut generation, and repairs to dam safety. Picking which project to take on is perhaps 30-40% of the work. The rest is a long negotiation with agencies (8-10 years in practice, not the nominal 5-6) and then construction to meet the conditions. Hydro IPPs and funds are capitalised buyers, but they buy operating cash flow, not licence status. The physical step is not trivial, so the rung fails the 80%-discovery test.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $0-0.3M/MW (surrender candidates, sometimes given away). Proven: the only clean comp is OPG buying Eagle Creek in 2018 for US$298M for 216 MW across 63 small plants. That is about $1.3-1.4M/MW, not the $2-4M/MW the pitch claims. Senate ENR testimony puts the median project at 2.5 MW. Brookfield says relicensing one project costs $0.75-1.5M in process costs alone, before any capex for mandated conditions. Take a 2.5 MW plant: buy it for about $0.3M, spend about $1-1.5M on the process and about $1-3M or more on fishway and flow capex. All-in is about $2.5-5M against a proven value of about $3.3M. That is roughly 0.7-1.5x on capital over about a decade. The pitch's 3-8x does not survive real comps.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive, clearing the C3 bar: Brookfield cites $0.75-1.5M per small-project relicensing (Senate ENR, about 2016), and hydro.org says more than $10M for projects over 10 MW. It is also slow: 8-10 years in practice. The 40-60% base rate of getting through on economic terms is plausible and fits the relaxed C3.
