ML reading the prescriptions and settlements of past Section 18 and 4(e) cases could pick projects with cheaper conditions better, maybe 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven asset. That gain is limited because the conditions are negotiated case by case, depend on the species and on the agency staff, and have only a small labelled set (a few hundred small relicensings).
scored.data: FERC eLibrary holds decades of scanned study plans, fishway prescriptions, 4(e) conditions and settlements, so the data is public and hard to read. That part holds. But the outcome is not hidden from the owner. Owners hire relicensing consultants who know the likely conditions for their own river, and the agencies flag their positions early, in scoping and study-plan comments. Small owners surrender mostly because the economics are bad: about 10 GWh a year earns roughly $0.5M in revenue, against relicensing plus capex. They do not surrender because they misread the data. Buying the rights cheaply is realistic. But the discount mostly reflects a real negative NPV, not an information gap the ML can close. Surrenders are also rare: about 41 in the last decade (hydro.org), so the pool of near-free assets is thin.
scored.right_bought: The dam and its licence, or an option on them, bought from municipalities, mill owners and small utilities. The right is transferable and can be cheap. But the licensee also takes on dam-safety and decommissioning liabilities, which can be large (Pierce Atwood warns decommissioning usually costs more than expected), so a 'free' dam can carry a negative price.
scored.buyer: Small-hydro aggregators and infrastructure funds: OPG/Eagle Creek, Brookfield Renewable, Rye Development, Enel. They are capitalised but pay only about $1.3-1.4M/MW for portfolios of small operating plants. Utilities or corporates buying RECs or firm clean power under PPAs can lift the price somewhat, but not by an order of magnitude.
scored.ladder: The ladder is: operate, uprate and modernise turbines, add pumped storage or batteries, sell firm power or RECs directly, then become a hydro IPP. That is real but bounded. Each site is about 2.5 MW, and the total US small-hydro fleet is a few GW. The best end state is a mid-size IPP like Eagle Creek, which sold for $298M, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proven asset is worth only about $1.3-1.4M/MW (OPG/Eagle Creek comp). Relicensing ($0.75-1.5M per project, 8-10 years) plus the mandated fishway and flow capex on a median 2.5 MW plant eat most or all of that value. Owners give these dams away because the relicensed economics are genuinely negative, not because they cannot read the FERC record. So ML-led selection has little spread to capture, and the physical step is not trivial.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive and the data is illegible, but relicensed small hydro trades at only about $1.3M/MW. Process plus mandated capex on a 2.5 MW plant leaves roughly 0.7-1.5x on capital over about a decade, and the discount reflects real negative NPV, not an information gap.

scored.name: Industrial sewer/water capacity reservation on idle plant sites
scored.one_line: Buy idle food-processing, paper or textile plants that hold large legacy municipal water and sewer capacity allocations. Prove the allocation can be transferred and requalified for a new heavy user, then sell the water-ready site to semiconductor, battery or data-center builders. ML over utility capacity records finds the allocations that still survive.
scored.unproven_right: Fee purchase of shuttered plants (often priced as scrap and land) whose owners do not realise their historic industrial wastewater and potable capacity reservation, connection fees, and pretreatment permits may transfer
scored.proving_step: A will-serve letter and capacity transfer agreement with the utility, a pretreatment permit modification, an engineering capacity study, and sometimes litigation or negotiation over lapsed allocations. Costs $100k-$600k and takes 1-2 years, with a base success rate of about 40-60%. ML could lift that 1.5x by reading which utility contracts and ordinances keep allocations alive.
scored.proven_buyer: Semiconductor and battery manufacturers, hyperscalers needing cooling water, and industrial site-selection funds, who pay heavily for sites with certain 1-5 MGD capacity
scored.public_data: Municipal utility council minutes, scanned industrial user agreements, capacity-fee ordinances, state pretreatment program files, NPDES/DMR historical flows (EPA ECHO), and utility master plans. The transferability of capacity is never a legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: A site bought at $1-5M becomes a water-ready mega-site worth $15-60M (about 3-10x on capital). The prize is in the low $B. Ladder: develop shell plants, then own industrial water reuse and treatment, then become a utility-scale water provider for industrial parks. Weaker than others: partly overlaps the powered-brownfield critique (cleanup cost).
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy an idle mill, get a will-serve letter and capacity transfer, sell it as a water-ready site'. Discovery and proving are maybe 30-40% of the work inside it. The rest is utility negotiation and politics, which ML does not do: Canton NC passed a 12-month data-center moratorium, there was organised opposition at Wisconsin Rapids, and Sentinel withdrew at Jay ME. The physical work is also large: demolition, environmental cleanup and running or rebuilding an on-site wastewater plant. The buyers (hyperscalers, fabs) are well capitalised, but they choose sites mainly on power. Water and sewer capacity is a secondary filter.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims $1-5M in becomes $15-60M out (3-10x). I found no verified closed sale prices. What I did find: Billerud sold its idled Wisconsin Rapids mill (about 220 acres, with an on-site wastewater plant and 32 MW) to a data-center developer. The Red River Mill in Campti LA is listed by CBRE with 'permitted, transferable water intake and discharge rights' at 'contact broker' pricing. Mills with water already sell as data-center sites, so the realistic uplift from proving the transfer is probably 1.5-3x, not 10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate estimates $100k-$600k and 1-2 years per attempt, with a 40-60% base success rate. These figures are not sourced, but the order of magnitude is plausible. Proving is expensive, so that part of C3 passes. ML is a weak lever, though. Whether capacity transfers depends on the utility's current headroom, a negotiation, and local politics such as moratoria. Reading old ordinances does not predict that, and the important facts (master plans, headroom such as 'about 8 MGD available' at Little Rock's utility) are already published. A realistic ML lift is about 1.1-1.3x.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned industrial user agreements and council minutes, plus EPA ECHO discharge monitoring report (DMR) flows. But the outcome-relevant facts are legible and well marketed. NPDES permits are public and transferable, state permit-transfer filings exist (the Canton permit went to TBD Utilities), and utility master plans state available capacity. The edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought as a fee purchase of the plant. The sellers are sophisticated corporates (Billerud, Pactiv Evergreen, Pixelle), and they hire industrial brokers like CBRE who explicitly market the water and discharge rights and on-site treatment plants. Municipalities and economic-development agencies also promote these sites. The premise that owners 'cannot read the data' fails for the 1-5 MGD sites that matter.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers and data-center developers (PCH WI Holdings, Nautilus, Sentinel), and semiconductor and battery makers. They have plenty of capital, but they decide on power first. Big fabs like Micron often get new purpose-built sewer districts from the state rather than buying a legacy allocation.
scored.ladder: There is a reasonable ladder above the first rung. First develop shell plants or powered shells. Then own industrial water reuse and treatment as a utility, then become the water provider for an industrial park. Industrial water-as-a-service is a large market, but regulators and politics sit on every rung, and incumbents like Veolia already occupy it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is not hidden. Transferable water and discharge rights at idle mills are already identified and actively marketed by brokers and towns. Utility headroom is published, so the purchase price already includes the water value. Whether a transfer succeeds depends on negotiation and local politics, which ML cannot read. This is the powered-brownfield failure again, with cleanup and demolition costs on top.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive, but sellers already know about and market their water and discharge rights, and the binding constraints (power, local politics, cleanup) are not something ML can find, so the spread is thin.

scored.name: Retired peaker gas turbines, overhauled and resold to data centers
scored.one_line: Buy aeroderivative and small frame gas turbines (LM6000, LM2500, 7EA, 6B) from retiring peakers and cogeneration plants at salvage prices. Use ML on the scattered operating and permit record to pick low-wear units. Pay for hot-section inspection and overhaul. Sell or lease the certified package to data-center and behind-the-meter developers stuck in a 5-7 year new-turbine backlog.
scored.unproven_right: Title to a retiring turbine package (turbine, generator, controls), bought at roughly $1-4M salvage; buyers cannot judge remaining hot-section life without a costly inspection.
scored.proving_step: Borescope and hot-section inspection, overhaul of combustor, HGP and blades, re-skid, run test and emissions recertification. About $3-12M and 6-12 months. Overhaul scope varies 3x; ML predicting cheap-scope units from starts, hours, fuel and permit history plausibly gives ~1.5-2x on cost per certified unit.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscaler and colocation developers, behind-the-meter power developers, oil and gas compression and international utilities, paying sharply higher prices for any available turbine capacity in 2025-26.
scored.public_data: EIA-860 and EIA-923, EPA CAMPD/Air Markets hourly emissions and operating data (starts and hours derivable with modelling), state Title V permits and stack-test reports (scanned), ISO deactivation notices, PUC dockets and bankruptcy auction records.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$5-15M against $15-40M sale or lease value per unit while the shortage lasts, roughly 2-4x, with shortage-duration risk. Multi-$B prize. Ladder: overhaul and resale, parts and repair shop, own-and-operate BTM plants (IPP), power developer.
scored.frame: The rung is "acquire a retiring turbine package, overhaul it, certify it, resell it". Picking the unit is maybe 10-20% of the work. Most of the work and capital is physical: hot-section overhaul, re-skid, run test and emissions recertification, at $3-12M against a $1-4M purchase price. This looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, where the physical build matters more than finding the right asset. There is a capitalised buyer (data-center and behind-the-meter developers), but discovery is well below 80% of the work.
scored.step_up: I found no verified secondary-market transaction data. Unproven: a dealer listing asks about EUR 433k for a 2002 LM6000 with ~38k hours, and the candidate assumes $1-4M salvage. New turbines: Wood Mackenzie projects $600/kW by end-2027, up 195% since 2019, with ~6-year lead times. That puts a new 48 MW unit above about $29M. Proven: ProEnergy sells refurbished PE6000 (LM6000-class) units to data centers for 2027 delivery, so a $15-40M sale or lease value is plausible. All-in cost is $5-15M, a step-up of about 2-4x, not 10^3-10^4. The spread depends on the shortage lasting, and new capacity is expected after 2028.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs $3-12M and takes 6-12 months per unit, so it is expensive. The base 'hit rate' is high: most packages can be overhauled, and what varies is the cost (scope varies up to ~3x, per the candidate). ML predicting low-scope units from CAMPD-derived starts and hours plausibly gives 1.2-1.5x on cost per certified unit, not 2x. The seller's own maintenance logs and borescope reports, shared in data rooms during due diligence, already tell a buyer most of what the model would. Sources: candidate estimate; industry practice of pre-purchase borescope inspection.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible. EIA-860 lists every unit's model, vintage and planned retirement in structured fields. EPA CAMPD hourly operating data comes through a clean API, so starts and hours are easy for any broker to derive. ISO deactivation notices are public and closely watched. The truly decisive data, the OEM maintenance records and borescope history, is private to the seller and is handed to every bidder. Only the scanned Title V stack-test reports are illegible, and they carry little signal on hot-section wear. The outcome (remaining life and inspection findings) is already in documents the seller holds.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not claimed first-come. But the sellers are sophisticated utilities and IPPs who know the turbine shortage well. Many are deferring peaker retirements because capacity prices are high, which shrinks supply. Auctions and brokers (ProEnergy, APR, Mitsubishi and PW Power Systems channels, used-turbine dealers) already price units near market. So there is little 'owner cannot read the data' discount.
scored.buyer: Strong and capitalised: hyperscalers, colocation and behind-the-meter bridging-power developers. ProEnergy reports selling 21 turbines (more than 1 GW) for two data-center projects as 5-7 year bridging power. Other buyers are oil and gas compression and international utilities.
scored.ladder: There is a credible ladder: overhaul and resale, then a parts and repair shop (MRO), then owning and operating behind-the-meter plants (IPP), then power developer. Owning and operating gas plants for data centers is a large business. But each rung is capital-heavy, crowded with incumbents, and does not build on any ML data edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is in physical overhaul and in a market-wide shortage, not in reading illegible data. The physical step costs 2-4x the purchase price and dominates the work. The decisive data (maintenance and borescope records) is held by informed sellers and given to every bidder. Incumbents like ProEnergy already run this exact refurbish-and-resell play. So ML creates almost no spread over what an informed buyer pays.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer demand is real and there is a real ladder, but this is a capex-heavy refurbish arbitrage on a temporary shortage, where discovery is under 20% of the work and the edge comes from legible data and the seller's own records.

scored.name: Orphaned 510(k)-cleared devices from defunct medtech firms
scored.one_line: Buy 510(k) clearances, design history files and tooling for cleared devices (including robotic and surgical) from bankruptcy estates and dissolved startups at liquidation prices. ML over 510(k) summaries, MAUDE and procedure-volume data picks clearances that remain valid with clean safety histories and recoverable design files. Pay for re-verification, supplier requalification and a quality-system build, then relaunch or sell the revived product line to a strategic.
scored.unproven_right: Transferable 510(k) clearances plus design history files, IP and tooling sold in Chapter 7 or ABC sales, often for $50-500k, by trustees who cannot judge clinical or commercial value.
scored.proving_step: DHF gap audit, design verification and validation re-run, supplier and CMO requalification, ISO 13485 QMS, check for whether a new or special 510(k) is needed, and first commercial lots. About $0.5-3M and 6-24 months; base success about 40-60%.
scored.proven_buyer: Mid-cap and strategic medtech (Integer, Teleflex, Merit Medical, Stryker and Medtronic tuck-ins), PE-backed device roll-ups and hospital GPOs, paying 2-6x revenue for a cleared line with live supply and early sales.
scored.public_data: 510(k) summaries and decision letters (unstructured PDFs), MAUDE adverse-event narratives, recall database, ClinicalTrials.gov, PACER bankruptcy dockets and asset-sale schedules, state dissolution filings, USPTO assignments, CMS procedure-code utilisation.
scored.rough_step_up: $0.1-0.2M right plus $1.5-2M proof leads to a $5-50M exit or operated line, about 3-20x. Prize small unless rolled up. Ladder: contract-manufacturing roll-up, then a multi-product device company.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a cleared but dormant device line and prove it can ship again." Picking which clearance to buy (discovery) is maybe 15-25% of the work. The rest is physical and operational: DHF remediation, V&V re-runs, CMO and supplier requalification, building an ISO 13485 QMS, first lots, and then the real hurdle, commercial adoption. FDA guidance says a transferred 510(k) usually needs no new submission unless the device changes, so the regulatory proof itself is cheap. The expensive part is rebuilding manufacturing and sales. That makes this the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: running the line is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: Comparable estate sales: the Vycor/NovaVision Chapter 7 deal (510(k)s, CE marks and IP) went for $0.9M. Therma Bright paid $425k for Saringer's products, tooling, technical files and QMS. MedLink bought Perseon out of Chapter 11 for about $4.4M. Proven lines sell to strategics at about 2-6x revenue, but most orphaned lines bring in under $5M a year in revenue, so exits are $5-20M. Against $0.1-0.5M for the right plus $1.5-3M of proof, gross is about 3-10x per success. At a 40-60% success rate and after commercialization spend, realistic return on capital is about 1.5-3x per line, and the prize is small unless rolled up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims a 40-60% base success rate and $0.5-3M over 6-24 months per revival, so proving is expensive. I found no source for the success rate. ML over MAUDE, recalls and 510(k) summaries mostly screens out safety and regulatory dogs. Those risks are already fairly legible in structured FDA databases. The dominant failure mode, no market pull (often why the startup died), is poorly predicted from public data. Plausible ML lift on cost per revived line is about 1.2-1.4x.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: 510(k) summary PDFs, PACER asset schedules and MAUDE narratives. But the key outcomes are legible. Clearance status sits in a structured FDA database, recalls and MAUDE are queryable, and clearances do not expire. Rights are genuinely bought, usually through 363 or trustee auctions. Those auctions draw informed strategic bidders: Zoll bought Vyaire's ventilator lines and Amgen paid $10M for Unilife's IP. Trustees cannot read the data, but the strategics bidding against you can, which compresses the discount.
scored.right_bought: Transferable 510(k) clearances bundled with DHF/DMR, IP, tooling and inventory, bought from Chapter 7 trustees, Chapter 11 363 sales or ABC assignees. Typical price is $0.2-1M per line. The buyer must re-register, list the device under the original K-number within 30 days, and relabel with its own UDI.
scored.buyer: Mid-cap and strategic medtech tuck-ins (Integer, Teleflex, Merit, Zoll, Stryker) and PE device roll-ups. They are capitalised, but they buy on revenue and supply continuity, not on clearance alone, typically paying 2-6x revenue.
scored.ladder: A credible ladder exists: serial revivals, then an in-house contract manufacturer and QMS platform, then a multi-product device company or distributor. This is a known PE roll-up model, and it plausibly reaches a $1B+ company, but not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Orphaned device lines usually failed commercially (no adoption, reimbursement or sales channel), not on regulatory grounds, and the clearance itself carries little value. Reviving a line means rebuilding manufacturing and a sales force, which is physical, bespoke operating work that ML discovery does not help with. Discovery is therefore a minor share of the rung.
scored.one_line_reason: The clearance is cheap and transferable, but the work is in manufacturing and commercial relaunch rather than discovery; prices come from auctions with informed strategic bidders, and returns are low single-digit multiples with a small prize per line.

scored.name: Mid-life aircraft engines selected for cheap shop visits, then leased or resold
scored.one_line: Buy mid-life CFM56-7B/-5B and V2500 engines, and the aircraft they come on, near part-out value. ML over public maintenance and registry records picks engines whose shop visit will be cheap and whose LLPs carry hidden remaining life. Pay for a performance-restoration shop visit, then lease or sell the green-time engine into the GTF/LEAP-driven spare-engine shortage.
scored.unproven_right: Title to a run-out engine or end-of-lease aircraft at ~$2-6M, priced at part-out value with no way to judge the next shop-visit cost.
scored.proving_step: Full performance-restoration shop visit (module overhaul, LLP replacement where needed, test cell) at $4-8M and 3-6 months. Nearly all pass, but cost varies 2x; ML predicting scope plausibly gives ~1.3-1.7x on cost per green-time engine.
scored.proven_buyer: Engine lessors (Willis Lease, AerCap Engines, SES), airlines grounded by GTF inspections and MRO pools, paying record lease rates and $12-20M for green-time mid-life engines.
scored.public_data: FAA registry and deregistration records, Service Difficulty Reports, FAA/EASA ADs, NTSB data, ADS-B flight histories (cycles, sector length, hot/sandy airports), lessor 10-K/ABS servicer reports (scanned), bankruptcy auction listings.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$7-13M against $12-22M value, roughly 1.5-2.5x (weakest multiple of the set), but multi-$B prize (~20k aftermarket engines). Ladder: engine shop, USM parts, engine lessor and MRO platform.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a mid-life engine, run its shop visit, sell or lease it as green-time". That rung is real and sellable: FTAI Aviation, AerFin, Willis Lease and Kellstrom all run it. Discovery is not 80%+ of the work, though. The physical step is the bulk of both the work and the capital: a shop visit costing $4-8M (which is as much as or more than the $2-6M asset), 3-6 months, and a limited supply of HPT blades and shop slots. Choosing the engine is maybe 10-20% of the value created, and execution (getting slots, sourcing used parts, workscope engineering) is most of the rest. It is close to the geothermal counter-example: the hard part is the physical step, not finding the asset.
scored.step_up: Unproven: run-out or mid-life CFM56-7B/V2500 at roughly $2-6M (teardown claims put exhausted engines at $0.8-1.2M against $1.6-2.2M of USM; unverified, Safe Fly). Proven: green-time engine at roughly $10-20M on the candidate's figures. IBA has CFM56-7B values up ~20% from 2023 to 2024 and lease rates up from ~$75k to ~$100k a month. All-in cost is roughly $7-13M, so the gross multiple is about 1.5-2.5x, with no 10^3-10^4 jump. The prize is multi-$B: WLFC puts CFM56 shop visits at a peak of ~2,200 in 2025, and FTAI shows the model can support a large company. The spread is a cycle-driven gap that FTAI, AerFin and others already compete for. Return on equity can reach 3-5x with leverage and lease income, but the extra margin that ML adds on top of informed buyers is thin.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Almost every engine passes the proving step (shop visit), so the base hit rate is about 95%+. The lever is cost variance, not the hit rate. Cost per attempt is $2-8M depending on scope: Safe Fly gives $1.8-3.5M for a CFM56-7B performance restoration or heavy visit without a full LLP stack, and $6-8M+ with LLP replacement on current list prices is my estimate. Scope swings with EGT margin, borescope findings, HPT blade scrap (AerFin says scrap can exceed 50% for mid-life blades) and LLP stub life. Those drivers sit in private trend-monitoring and borescope data, not public records. Realistically ML gives about 1.1-1.3x on cost per green-time engine, not the 1.3-1.7x claimed. Proving is expensive, so the lever is real but weak.
scored.data: This fails on both legs. The value-determining facts are LLP remaining cycles (back-to-birth traceability), EGT margin, the last shop visit's workscope and borescope findings. All of them sit in private technical records, and the seller hands those records to every bidder in the data room. They are the legible summary field that kills the ML edge. Public data (the FAA registry, ADS-B cycle and sector-length histories, SDRs, ADs) is a weak proxy for information buyers already get directly. Sellers are sophisticated (lessors, airlines, ABS servicers) and are advised by appraisers (IBA, mba, Oriel). Rights are bought, but not from owners who cannot read the data, so ML cannot create a purchase discount.
scored.right_bought: Title to a mid-life or run-out engine, or to an end-of-lease aircraft, bought at part-out value in a competitive bid or from a bankruptcy auction. Records are full and shared with all bidders.
scored.buyer: Well capitalised and real: engine lessors (Willis Lease, AerCap Engines, SES), airlines short of spares because of GTF and LEAP problems, and MRO pools. They pay record lease rates of about $100k a month for a CFM56-7B (IBA) and high values for green-time engines.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong and already proven by FTAI Aviation. It runs from used serviceable material (USM) parts trading to a module factory and engine shop, then to a lessor of engines and aircraft, then to an MRO and aftermarket platform. Each step is a large business. The catch is that incumbents already hold every rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal (LLP back-to-birth life, EGT margin, borescope, workscope history) is in private technical records that sellers give every bidder, and the most important of these (LLP life) is a legible summary field. Sophisticated incumbents like FTAI, AerFin and Willis already price assets from those records. So public-data ML creates no purchase discount, and most of the value comes from executing the costly physical shop visit, not from discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The market is real and large and the ladder is strong (FTAI shows it). But discovery is a small share of the work, the shop visit costs as much as the asset, and the signal sits in data-room records every informed bidder already sees. ML over public data adds little edge.

scored.name: Orphaned light-aircraft and engine type certificates
scored.one_line: Buy dormant FAA type certificates for discontinued aircraft, engines or propellers from estates and defunct OEMs. Pay for engineering data recovery and a production certificate. Then make spares and new units for the installed fleet, or sell the revived TC to an aerospace consolidator.
scored.unproven_right: Orphaned or abandoned TCs and their design data (FAA keeps an orphan-TC list), sold by estates for low six figures or less.
scored.proving_step: Recovery and digitisation of drawings, conformity work, a production certificate or PMA-based parts approval, and first articles. About $0.5-3M and 1-3 years, moderate success rate.
scored.proven_buyer: Aerospace aftermarket consolidators (TransDigm-style roll-ups, Textron, Continental and other GA OEMs) paying high multiples for sole-source TC-holder positions with a captive fleet.
scored.public_data: FAA TCDS sheets (scanned), FAA registry fleet counts and ages, Service Difficulty Reports, ADs, the orphan-TC list, scanned historical type-design data. ML ranks TCs by captive fleet, parts-scarcity pricing and data-recovery cost.
scored.rough_step_up: $0.2M right plus $1.5M proof leads to $1-5M/yr sole-source margin or a $10-40M sale, about 3-15x, but low $B total prize. Ladder: aftermarket roll-up, new-build production.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a dormant TC plus a working production approval'. Choosing which TC to buy is maybe 10-20% of the work. The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory: recovering drawings, rebuilding tooling, conformity and first articles, getting an FAA production certificate or PMA, setting up a supply chain, and carrying product liability. The physical step is bespoke and hard, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern, not the drill-hole pattern.
scored.step_up: There are real price points for unproven TCs. True Flight Holdings paid $925k for the Grumman Tiger TCs, tooling and equipment out of bankruptcy. The Navion and Commander TCs went at auction or 'bargain' prices that were not disclosed. Anecdotal asks run as high as $10M (Great Lakes). On the proven side, Viking bought the DHC-1 to DHC-7 TCs from Bombardier in 2006 and restarted the Twin Otter at a $3.9M base price. It had 40 orders by 2008 and built about 24 a year by 2014, which is roughly $100M+/yr of revenue, but only after about 4 years and heavy capital. Most light-aircraft TCs support only $1-5M/yr of parts margin. The realistic return is about 2-5x on $1-3M per asset and the total prize is low $B, so 1x-10x, not 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $0.5-3M and takes 1-3 years (candidate estimate; Viking took about 4 years from TC purchase to first delivery in 2010). The base hit rate is maybe 40-60%. Failure comes mostly from data that cannot be recovered, cost overruns, FAA production-approval delays, liability and thin demand. Those are execution risks that ML does not predict. The demand signal (fleet size and age) is a registry count, so ML adds perhaps about 1.2x over a spreadsheet triage.
scored.data: TCDS sheets, registry fleet counts, ADs, SDRs and the orphan-TC list are all public, but mostly legible: the registry is a structured download and TCDS are text PDFs. The key outcome variable, the size of the captive fleet, is already a legible field. The one illegible part is the scanned historical type-design data, but much of that is held privately by the TC holder rather than in public files. Data-recovery cost is the real unknown, and you only learn it after you have the files.
scored.right_bought: Yes. TCs are bought from estates, bankruptcy trustees and defunct OEMs, often for low six to low seven figures (Tiger $925k). But the sellers and their brokers know the fleet size, and type clubs and owner groups (the Commander owners' buyout) compete for the same assets. There is a mild information discount from distress, not a data-legibility discount.
scored.buyer: For a revived TC: aftermarket consolidators (TransDigm-style, though they target sole-source parts on larger fleets rather than tiny GA TCs), GA OEMs (Textron, Continental) and owner groups. For new aircraft: niche operators, as with the Twin Otter, whose buyers are bush and utility operators. Buyers are capitalised but thin at the light-GA end.
scored.ladder: Parts and PMA for the installed fleet, then MRO and upgrades, then new-build production, then a multi-TC roll-up. The Viking path shows this: TCs bought in 2006, Twin Otter production, then De Havilland Canada and the Longview group with the Dash 8 and the Canadair water bombers. The ladder is real but slow and capital-intensive, and each rung is manufacturing.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is bespoke engineering, manufacturing and FAA production certification, not discovery, so discovery is well under 80% of the rung (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode). The main signal, captive fleet size, is already a legible registry field, so ML has little edge in choosing which TC to buy.
scored.one_line_reason: The assets are real and bought cheaply (Tiger TCs for $925k; the Viking Twin Otter success), but the work is reviving manufacturing rather than reading illegible data, the demand signal is a legible registry count, and returns are about 2-5x on a low-$B prize.

scored.name: Commercial-to-residential by-right conversion sites (CA AB 2011/SB 6, TX SB 840)
scored.one_line: Buy underused strip malls, office parks and commercial parcels where new state laws allow ministerial multifamily housing. ML over scanned title reports, CC&Rs, deed restrictions, easements, prior use permits and environmental files predicts which sites truly qualify with no blocking covenants. Secure the by-right approval and sell shovel-ready multifamily sites.
scored.unproven_right: Options or purchases of distressed commercial parcels at commercial cap-rate value, from owners pricing the land as declining retail or office.
scored.proving_step: Design, site plan and ministerial approval application, plus title curative work to extinguish blocking covenants. About $200k-$1M and 6-18 months, about 50-70% success after ML screening.
scored.proven_buyer: Multifamily developers and REITs (Greystar, AvalonBay, Related) and build-to-rent capital, paying residential land value per entitled unit.
scored.public_data: Scanned recorded CC&Rs, easements and deed restrictions in county recorders, historic CUPs and variances, state GeoTracker/EnviroStor and TCEQ files, city planning records.
scored.rough_step_up: Commercial land at $30/sf becomes $60-150/sf entitled residential (2-5x on land), roughly 2-4x on capital. Multi-$B across CA, TX, FL and WA.
scored.frame: The rung is an entitled, shovel-ready multifamily site under AB 2011/SB 6 (CA) or SB 840 (TX). Discovery, meaning finding a parcel that truly qualifies, is only about 25-35% of the work inside that rung. Most of the effort goes elsewhere: architecture and site plan, the ministerial application, title curative work, community and city friction (DFW suburbs including Plano, Frisco, Irving and Arlington are already passing measures to constrain SB 840), and above all proving the project pencils. AB 2011 carries prevailing-wage and 13% affordability requirements, plus density floors of 50-75% of allowable density, so construction feasibility rather than eligibility is what usually kills a deal. The physical step is not abstracted away. Buyers with capital do exist (Greystar, AvalonBay, build-to-rent funds).
scored.step_up: The candidate's estimate is commercial land at about $30/sf becoming $60-150/sf entitled residential, roughly 2-5x on land and 2-4x on capital. That is unverified: searches found no post-enactment land-price data for AB 2011 or SB 840. Commentators already describe underused retail and office as 'acquisition targets' under SB 840 (Foley, Squire Patton Boggs, BSB Design). So sellers and brokers already know about by-right potential, and the discount at purchase is shrinking. Under prevailing wage, the residual land value for residential is often at or below commercial value in many CA corridors. A realistic expectation is about 1.3-2x on land for the best sites, not the claimed 2-5x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's proving cost is $200k-$1M and 6-18 months per site, which is expensive enough to qualify. Its claimed 50-70% success after ML screening is an estimate with no source. The ML lever is weak, though. The binding risks on qualification can be read cheaply and directly before signing an option. Covenant and title risks show up in a standard preliminary title report costing a few $k. Zoning, corridor frontage, parcel size and adjacency are statutory criteria on legible GIS layers. Envirostor/GeoTracker status is a database field. The failures that remain are economic or political, and ML over scanned documents does not predict them. My estimate is roughly a 1.1-1.3x gain in cost per proven site.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned CC&Rs, easements, and historic CUPs. But the outcome of eligibility is mostly already written into legible fields: zoning designation, street width or commercial-corridor status, parcel size, sensitive-site flags, and cleanup-site status on EnviroStor and GeoTracker. Title companies routinely extract the illegible covenant layer in every transaction, so incumbents already read it. The right is bought (options or purchase), not free first-come, which is good. However, owners and their brokers increasingly market by-right potential, so the asymmetry is thin.
scored.right_bought: Options or fee purchases of underused strip malls and office parks, bought from private owners at commercial or distressed-commercial value. Owners in large CA and TX metros are now broadly aware of by-right conversion potential.
scored.buyer: Multifamily developers, REITs and build-to-rent capital (Greystar, AvalonBay, Related), paying a residual land value per entitled unit. They are well capitalised but price-disciplined, and most source and entitle sites in-house.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from entitlement to vertical construction, then to owning and operating multifamily, then to a REIT or platform. It is a very large market, but it is commoditized and capital-intensive. Winning the entitlement rung gives no durable advantage on the higher rungs, so the path to the whole chain is weak.
scored.fatal_flaw: Eligibility and the covenant risk are already legible or cheaply resolved: statutory criteria sit in GIS and zoning fields, and blocking covenants show up in a standard preliminary title report costing a few $k. Sellers' brokers also already price in by-right potential. The remaining failure mode is project economics (prevailing wage, affordability set-asides, density floors, local resistance), and ML over scanned records does not predict it. So the ML-led proof creates no meaningful spread.
scored.one_line_reason: A real rezoning opportunity, but discovery is a minority of the work, eligibility is legible and already being priced in, and the real risk is construction feasibility, which ML over title records cannot reduce.

scored.name: Corridor Title / Orphan Easement / EasementGraph: dormant utility, pipeline and telegraph easement corridors
scored.one_line: Buy forgotten assignable easements in gross and corridor strips from successors of dissolved utilities, co-ops, interurbans, telegraph and pipeline companies; ML over scanned deed books stitches continuous corridors and proves scope (communications or any lawful purpose) and survival; sell insured corridors to HVDC and long-haul fiber developers.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: Scope and width overburden plus continuity. A dormant telegraph, telephone or pipeline easement is usually 10-33 ft wide and limited to its original use. In most states it cannot legally be expanded to carry an HVDC line, so fee owners will win overburden and abandonment suits. A corridor is only worth anything when unbroken, and every gap must be cured by negotiation or eminent domain, which the developer would do anyway. The hard part is legal assembly and survival, not discovery, so ML does n
scored.frame: The rung is a corridor proven insurable for HVDC or fiber use. Discovery (finding the dormant easement in deed books and stitching segments) is maybe 20-30% of that rung's work. The other 70-80% is legal: scope and overburden opinions, abandonment and survival analysis, curing gaps by negotiation or condemnation, quiet-title suits and getting a title insurer to sign off. The physical-step equivalent here is litigation, not drilling, and it is neither trivial nor abstracted. Buyers (HVDC developers like Invenergy, long-haul fiber builders) are well capitalised, but they buy assembled, unbroken, wide-enough corridors, not fragments.
scored.step_up: A dormant easement in gross bought from a dissolved company's successor costs close to zero. But the railroad-fiber class settlements show what fee owners get when an old easement is used beyond its scope: about $1-2 per linear foot (Sprint/Qwest/Level 3/WilTel 2003, $142.5M to about 360k landowners, $2/ft with proof of title, $0.33/ft without; Norfolk Southern/T-Cubed $6,000 per mile). So scope is a liability that fee owners collect on, not something the easement holder gets to monetise. HVDC lines need 150-200 ft easements, which Grain Belt Express pays fee owners above 100% of fair market value for (about $105M across roughly 1,500 Kansas landowners). A 10-33 ft telegraph or pipeline strip does not replace that, so the realistic step-up is small, perhaps a nuisance or holdout value against the fee owner.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving one corridor (title abstracting across many counties, legal opinions, and possibly a quiet-title or declaratory action) easily costs over $50k and takes years, so the expensive leg of relaxed C3 is met. The base hit rate for a dormant easement surviving and allowing HVDC-scale use is probably well under 10%. Fiber-only scope is more plausible in states with broad "communications" grant language. ML could plausibly screen grant language and continuity 1.2-1.5x better, but the outcome turns on state law and fee-owner litigation, which ML cannot change. These are estimates; I found no source for corridor-proving cost.
scored.data: The signal really is in illegible public data: scanned county deed books and recorded easement grants from defunct telegraph, interurban, co-op and pipeline companies, with no structured index of survival or scope. Incumbents do not systematically extract it, and no regulator status field records whether an easement survives, so C4's legibility test passes. The weakness is buying the right. Successors (bankruptcy trustees, merged utilities) are reachable, but chain of assignment is often uncertain and some easements are appurtenant or non-assignable. The fee owner holds the countervailing right and can sue.
scored.right_bought: Assignments or quitclaims of easements in gross from successors of dissolved utilities and railways, often for nominal sums. Whether the quitclaim conveys anything is uncertain (assignability, abandonment by non-use, merger into the fee).
scored.buyer: HVDC transmission developers (Invenergy Grain Belt Express, SOO Green, Clean Line successors) and long-haul fiber builders, plus title insurers as gatekeepers. All are capitalised, but they mostly prefer new negotiated easements or co-location in highway and rail ROW.
scored.ladder: In theory the company could climb from corridor assembly to developing transmission or fiber lines, then to operating them for regulated transmission or dark-fiber revenue, then to a national corridor utility. The rungs exist, but the bottom rung does not give a lasting edge on the upper ones, because developers acquire new ROW directly.
scored.fatal_flaw: Scope and width overburden. Dormant telegraph, telephone and pipeline easements are 10-33 ft wide and limited to their original use. HVDC needs 150-200 ft and fiber over-use has already produced fee-owner damages ($1-2/ft class settlements). The value is created by legal assembly and litigation against fee owners, not by ML discovery. Every gap must still be cured by negotiation or condemnation the developer would do anyway. Relaxing C3 does not touch any of this.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the right is cheap, but the asset legally cannot carry HVDC-scale use. Proof here is legal assembly rather than discovery, so ML moves little of the value, and the relaxed C3 only raises it slightly.

scored.name: Unclaimed emission reduction credits from shuttered industrial plants
scored.one_line: Buy the right to the unbanked emission reductions of closed or curtailed plants in ozone nonattainment areas, certify them as emission reduction credits (ERCs) with the air district, then sell them as offsets to new gas plants, data-center backup generation and industrial projects. ML finds eligible reductions that are still inside the lookback window.
scored.unproven_right: Contractual assignment of shutdown and curtailment reduction rights from owners of idle or closed plants (paper mills, refineries, foundries, peakers), who usually do not know the reductions are bankable or have treated them as worthless
scored.proving_step: ERC banking application: reconstruct baseline actual emissions, prove the reductions are surplus, permanent, quantifiable and enforceable, surrender permits, and go through district review and any challenge. Costs $75k-$500k and takes 1-3 years. Many applications fail on baseline documentation. ML that reconstructs baselines from historic records could lift the approval rate and certified tonnage 1.5-2.5x.
scored.proven_buyer: New or expanding major sources in severe nonattainment areas (gas peakers, data-center generator fleets, chip fabs, refineries) in South Coast AQMD, SJVAPCD, Bay Area, Houston-Galveston-Brazoria and Dallas-Fort Worth
scored.public_data: Scanned historic Title V and state permit files, annual emissions inventory submissions, EPA NEI facility history, CEMS and Clean Air Markets data, district permit-surrender and shutdown notices, and state business-closure records. Whether a reduction is still bankable is not written in any field.
scored.rough_step_up: Rights acquired for near zero to low six figures become certified NOx/VOC ERCs at $50k-$300k+/ton in severe areas (often more than 5x on capital per site). The prize is several $B, limited by the size of the offset market. Ladder: offset bank, then own permitted generation sites, then develop gas or hybrid power for large loads.
scored.frame: The rung is an ERC bank: you get the shutdown-reduction rights, certify the credits and sell offsets. There is a capitalised buyer: new major sources in severe nonattainment areas that cannot get a permit without offsets. But discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work inside this rung, not 80%+. Finding the shutdowns is easy, because shutdowns and permit surrenders are public notices. The real work is timing, contracting before the filing deadline, documenting the baseline under the district's rules, and getting through review and any challenge. That is regulatory paperwork more than discovery.
scored.step_up: Per site the spread is real. South Coast AQMD's CY2024 transaction report gives an average NOx ERC price of about $418k per ton/year, roughly $76k per lb/day (CY2023: about $380k per ton/year). Shutdown rights might be acquired for near zero to low six figures. But the market is very thin: South Coast had only 4 NOx ERC trades in 2024, moving 79 lb/day (about 14 tons/year, about $6M), and 2 trades in 2023. Houston-Galveston-Brazoria (HGB) ERCs are described as 'rapidly consumed', but I found no public price. Per-deal returns above 5x on capital are plausible, but the prize is in the tens to low hundreds of $M across all districts, not multi-$B.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is not reliably expensive. San Joaquin Valley's (SJVAPCD) ERC filing fee is about $1,066 (instructions marked Rev July 2026), plus consultant work of tens of thousands of dollars. The candidate's $75k-$500k figure is high-end and unsourced. Base approval rates for timely, well-documented shutdown applications look high. Failures come mostly from late filing or reductions that are not surplus, and ML does not fix either. Baselines come from annual emissions inventory and CEMS data that are already structured. I estimate ML gives under 1.2x on cost per certified ton.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible and the window is short. South Coast Rule 1309(b) requires the ERC application within 180 days of the reduction. San Joaquin Valley Rule 2301 sets the same 180-day limit, and Antelope Valley and Mojave Desert allow 6 months. So the core thesis fails in the main California districts: 'unbanked reductions still inside the lookback window' that ML finds in old scanned permits mostly do not exist there. Anything old enough to be hidden is past the deadline, and anything recent is a public shutdown or permit-surrender notice. Baseline emissions are in structured inventory, National Emissions Inventory (NEI) and Clean Air Markets data. Texas 30 TAC 101 allows longer windows, but those reductions are equally visible in TCEQ's inventory. The right can be bought, but the sellers who matter (refineries, utilities, peakers) know ERCs are worth $400k per ton/year, and ERC brokers already chase every shutdown. Only small owners such as foundries or small mills may not know, and their tonnage is small.
scored.right_bought: A contractual assignment of the shutdown/curtailment reduction rights plus permit surrender, bought from the plant owner before the 180-day (California) or roughly multi-year (Texas) filing window closes.
scored.buyer: New or modified major sources in severe or extreme ozone nonattainment areas, such as gas peakers, data-center generator fleets, fabs and refineries in South Coast, San Joaquin Valley, Bay Area, HGB and Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW). They have the capital and must hold offsets before they operate.
scored.ladder: There is a plausible ladder: offset bank, then holding offset-backed permitted generation sites in nonattainment areas, then developing gas or hybrid power for large loads such as data centers. It is credible but capped by local offset scarcity. The upper rungs are mainstream power development, where this company would have little edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The filing windows are short (180 days under South Coast Rule 1309(b) and San Joaquin Valley Rule 2301). So eligible reductions are recent, publicly noticed shutdowns whose baselines sit in structured emissions inventories. There is no hidden backlog in illegible records for ML to find. Brokers and informed owners already capture the value in a thin market (about 4 NOx trades a year in South Coast).
scored.one_line_reason: The per-ton ERC price is high, but the 180-day banking windows and legible inventory data leave ML nothing to discover, the proving step is cheap paperwork, and the offset market is too thin for a multi-$B prize.

scored.name: Salvaged large power transformers, refurbished and certified for resale
scored.one_line: Buy decommissioned or retiring large power transformers (100-500 MVA) from utility surplus, retiring generator step-up units and plant closures at near-scrap prices. Use ML on condition evidence scattered through PUC rate cases to pick the units that will pass. Pay for factory teardown, rewind if needed and certified retest. Sell into a 3-4 year lead-time shortage to utilities, data-center developers and IPPs at close to new price. The company owns the unit end to end and keeps the uplift.
scored.unproven_right: Title to a retired or soon-retiring LPT, or GSU transformer at a closing coal or gas plant, bought at scrap or salvage value (about $150-500k) because the seller cannot show its insulation or core condition and treats it as a disposal cost.
scored.proving_step: Removal, transport and factory tear-down inspection, then rewind or repair, re-oil and full IEEE C57 factory acceptance testing (impulse, heat run, partial discharge). About $0.5-2M and 4-9 months per unit. Base pass rate without rewind maybe 40-60%; ML over the condition record could plausibly lift the share that pass cheaply 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities, data-center developers and IPP/renewable developers facing 120-200 week lead times for new LPTs, already paying $3-10M per refurbished or certified unit to get power on early.
scored.public_data: State PUC rate case and IRP exhibits (scanned asset-condition reports, DGA summaries, replacement-justification memos), FERC Form 1 plant accounts, EIA-860 generator retirement schedules, ISO/RTO deactivation filings, utility surplus auction listings, DOE/NERC transformer reliability reports. The condition signal sits in scanned exhibits, not a legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$1-2.5M against a $3-10M sale, roughly 3-5x on capital. Multi-$B prize (US LPT market ~$10B+/yr). Ladder: certified-used broker, in-house rewind and remanufacturing, new transformer and GOES/core supply, grid-equipment OEM.
scored.frame: The rung is a certified used LPT ready for resale, and it is sellable: buyers exist. But discovery (knowing which retired unit is good) is maybe 15-25% of the work. The rest is physical, slow and bespoke: de-energising, draining, heavy-haul transport ($100k+ for 150-250 t units), factory teardown, rewind, re-oil, IEEE C57 FAT, then matching a buyer whose voltage, impedance and footprint fit. RESA says remanufacture returns a unit for 60-70% of new cost, so the factory work is the value. Structurally this is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the physical step is harder than finding the asset.
scored.step_up: New 200+ MVA unit: about $3.5-4.5M with lead times up to 5 years (RESA/PARC 224 MVA GSU case). Woodmac: 80-210 week lead times, prices up 60-80% since 2020. Remanufactured units sell at about 60-70% of new (RESA), and reconditioned equipment generally goes 10-40% below new (CB Insights). Realistic sale is about $2.5-4M, not $3-10M. All-in cost: acquisition $0.15-0.5M (rising, since owners now know about the shortage), haul $0.1-0.3M, remanufacture often 40-60% of new ($1.5-2.5M when a rewind is needed), plus carry and the risk of finding no buyer. Net is roughly 1.2-2x on capital per unit. Step-up at proof is about 2-3x the purchase price only if the purchase really is at scrap.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $0.5-2.5M and 4-9 months per unit (RESA reman ~60-70% of new cost; ABB TRES Duke Beckjord 260 MVA GSU reman took 15 weeks with core requalified and nearly everything else replaced). Base pass-without-rewind is maybe 40-60%. The ML lift is weak. The decisive condition evidence (DGA trend, furan/DP, FRA, through-fault history) is in the owner's own maintenance records, not in PUC exhibits, which give only summary replacement justifications. Teardown is still decisive. Plausible lift is about 1.1-1.3x on cost per certified unit.
scored.data: The public data is genuinely illegible: scanned PUC rate-case condition exhibits, IRP replacement memos, EIA-860 retirement dates, ISO deactivation filings. EIA-860 and deactivation filings legibly flag which plants are retiring, and that is the main discovery input; anyone can read it. Condition detail is fragmentary in public filings. The sellers are utilities and IPPs with transformer engineers who hold the full DGA history, so they are not unable to read their own asset. In a known shortage they sell to or consign through RESA/PARC, SPX, Hitachi TRES and others, or keep the unit as a fleet spare. The scrap-price purchase premise is mostly gone.
scored.right_bought: Title to a retiring GSU or substation LPT. You can buy it, but not cheaply from uninformed owners. Utility asset managers and surplus brokers price in the shortage, utilities increasingly hold retired units as strategic spares (EEI STEP / spare-sharing programs), and specialised remanufacturers already compete for them.
scored.buyer: Utilities, IPPs and data-center developers are capitalised and short of transformers, so a real buyer exists. But they buy against tight specs (voltage class, impedance, BIL, footprint, tap range), and a retired GSU often fits only some sites. They demand a warranty and vetting, which puts a discount on used units.
scored.ladder: The ladder is reasonable: certified-used broker, then an in-house rewind and remanufacturing shop, then new transformer manufacture, then GOES/core supply, then grid-equipment OEM. It is a real ~$10B+/yr US market with a long shortage. But each upper rung is capital-heavy manufacturing where Hitachi, Siemens Energy, HD Hyundai and others are entrenched, and the ML discovery edge does not carry upward.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step (heavy-haul removal, factory teardown, rewind and certification, at 60-70% of new cost) is the work and the value, not discovery. The spread is already being arbitraged by informed incumbents (RESA Power/PARC, SPX, Hitachi Energy TRES) buying from sellers who hold the full condition data, so ML over PUC exhibits gives little edge. It fails the same way as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Real shortage and real buyers. But the work is factory remanufacturing, not discovery. Resale is only 60-70% of new, sellers and incumbent remanufacturers already know unit condition, and that leaves roughly 1.2-2x returns and a weak ML lever.

scored.name: Shuttered FDA-registered sterile and API plants, remediated and re-certified
scored.one_line: Buy idle or distressed FDA-registered pharmaceutical plants (sterile fill-finish, oral solids, API) at a deep discount to replacement cost. Use ML over FDA inspection documents to pick plants whose compliance problems are cheap to fix. Fund remediation through a clean re-inspection. Sell the certified plant to a CDMO or pharma company, or run it as a CDMO.
scored.unproven_right: Plant real estate, equipment and site registration, bought from a closing owner or out of bankruptcy at ~10-25% of replacement cost, discounted because an open warning letter or 483 history makes regulatory standing unknowable.
scored.proving_step: cGMP remediation (quality systems, environmental monitoring, equipment requalification, process validation), then an FDA inspection with an NAI/VAI outcome. $5-40M and 12-30 months; base success maybe 40-60%. ML over 483 and EIR text identifying procedural vs structural observations plausibly gives 1.5-2x on cost per certified plant.
scored.proven_buyer: CDMOs (Thermo/Patheon, Lonza, Catalent's acquirer, onshoring Asian CDMOs), big pharma reshoring under tariff and BIOSECURE pressure, PE CDMO roll-ups. Certified US sterile capacity trades at $100-500M per site.
scored.public_data: FDA Form 483s and EIRs (FOIA reading room, scanned), warning letters, FDA Data Dashboard inspection classifications, establishment registration and DECRS, drug shortage lists, state environmental permits and bankruptcy dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: All-in ~$20-80M against $100-400M certified value or CDMO cash flow, roughly 3-5x. Multi-$B prize. Ladder: re-certified plant, CDMO operator, owned shortage-drug portfolio, integrated manufacturer.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a distressed FDA-registered plant and getting it to a clean (NAI/VAI) inspection. In that rung discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work: reading the 483s, warning letters and EIRs to choose a plant. Most of the work is physical and organisational: rebuilding quality systems, requalifying equipment, environmental monitoring, process validation, rehiring a skilled aseptic workforce, and securing products or ANDAs and customers to run. The FDA does not 'certify' plants. Inspections are tied to applications and products, so a re-inspection usually needs a product filing and a running operation. This looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: running the plant is much harder than finding it. Buyers with capital do exist (CDMOs, onshoring pharma, PE).
scored.step_up: The purchase discount is real. Rising Pharmaceuticals (H.I.G. Capital) bought Akorn's Decatur, IL sterile production plant out of Chapter 7 for about $1.2M, plus $50k for the packaging site (Fierce Pharma, citing the Herald & Review, 2023). That 230,000 sq ft site had received a $25M upgrade in 2018. Rovi bought BMS's operating Phoenix plant property for $18.5M (2026). The other idle-site deals found (Xellia buying the idle ex-Ben Venue Bedford site; Lilly buying Nexus's Pleasant Prairie plant) did not disclose terms. The proven value of a plant is mostly product portfolio, ANDAs, customers and workforce, not the building. Hikma's ~$300M Bedford deal bought a product portfolio. Generic sterile-injectable plants close mainly because the economics are bad (rock-bottom generic prices, per the 2023 NPR/KAXE shortage reporting), not because their regulatory standing is unknowable. A re-qualified empty plant is not obviously worth $100-400M. Realistic all-in return on $20-80M is roughly 1.5-3x, and highly uncertain.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $5-40M and 12-30 months per plant (candidate estimate; consistent with Akorn's multi-year failure to clear warning letters at Decatur and Somerset). Base success is maybe 40-60%. The ML lever is weak. Only dozens of distressed plants come up each year, so n is too small to train on. Experienced cGMP remediation consultants already sort procedural from structural observations by reading a 483 in an afternoon. FOIA'd 483s and EIRs are heavily redacted, and the decisive failure modes (aseptic culture, cleanroom design, workforce loss) show up in the text and are read by every bidder. Plausible gain is around 1.1-1.3x on cost per re-qualified plant.
scored.data: The data is public but partly illegible: FDA 483s and EIRs come from the FOIA reading room, scanned and redacted. But the outcome is already in legible fields. The FDA Data Dashboard gives NAI/VAI/OAI classifications, and warning letters and close-out letters are published. The sellers are pharma companies, lenders and bankruptcy trustees whose QA staff know their own plant better than any outside model. The right is bought, not free, and sold cheaply, but that is mainly because the plant has no economic use. It is not because the seller cannot read the data. The Akorn auction drew about 130 bidders, which is not an illiquid, uninformed market.
scored.right_bought: Plant real estate, equipment and site registration, bought from a closing owner or out of bankruptcy for well under replacement cost (Decatur: $1.25M for a site with $25M of recent capex). Buying the asset cheaply is achievable. The owner's lack of information is not the reason it is cheap.
scored.buyer: CDMOs (Thermo Fisher/Patheon, Lonza, Novo/Catalent), pharma reshoring under tariff and BIOSECURE pressure, and PE CDMO roll-ups. These buyers mostly pay for running operations with customers and validated products, not for re-inspected empty shells. Several of them (H.I.G./Rising, Xellia, Lilly) already buy distressed plants directly, competing away the spread.
scored.ladder: The ladder is decent: re-qualified plant, then CDMO operator, then an owned shortage-drug ANDA portfolio, then an integrated US manufacturer. A real onshoring tailwind exists, but every rung is operations-heavy, low-margin generic manufacturing rather than repeated discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Distressed sterile and API plants are cheap because running them is uneconomic and remediation is a hard, operations-heavy rebuild of quality culture and workforce. Their regulatory standing is not hidden. Inspection outcomes are already legible (FDA Data Dashboard classifications, warning letters), and sophisticated sellers and around 130 informed bidders read the same 483s. So ML over the text buys little, and the physical step is the dominant cost and risk.
scored.one_line_reason: The plants really are cheap ($1.2M for Akorn Decatur), but they are cheap because running them is uneconomic. Remediation and operations, not picking the plant, are 80%+ of the work, and inspection outcomes are already in legible FDA fields, so the ML edge is small.

scored.name: Unexploited public germplasm and expired-PVP crop lines, trialled into licensed varieties
scored.one_line: License, cheaply or free, under-used public breeding lines and expired-PVP accessions from universities and USDA. ML predicts line-by-environment performance. Pay for multi-location yield and quality trials, then release and own a commercial variety or sell it exclusively to seed companies.
scored.unproven_right: Non-exclusive or exclusive releases of university and USDA breeding lines, plus germplasm whose PVP has lapsed, licensed for nominal fees by programmes that cannot run large trials.
scored.proving_step: 2-3 seasons of multi-environment yield, disease and quality trials plus seed increase. About $100k-$1M per line over years. Base hit rate about 10-30%; ML may give roughly 1.5-2x lift.
scored.proven_buyer: Regional and national seed companies (Corteva, Syngenta, regional independents) and food processors needing specific traits (malting barley, pulses, specialty wheat), paying royalties or $1-20M for exclusives.
scored.public_data: USDA GRIN-Global phenotype records, decades of scanned university variety-trial reports and extension bulletins, NCBI and public genotype panels, PVP certificate database, crop acreage and price data.
scored.rough_step_up: $20k licence plus $0.5M trials leads to a $2-20M variety value or royalty stream, about 3-10x on winners. Ladder: own seed production, vertically integrated specialty-crop supply chain.
scored.frame: The rung would be "licensed line becomes a released variety". Discovery, meaning picking the line, is perhaps 20-30% of the work inside that rung. Most of the work is physical and slow: 2-3 seasons of multi-location trials, disease and quality screening, seed increase, registration and PVP filing, then marketing to seed growers. None of that is trivial or abstracted. There is a buyer for the proven output (seed companies, intermediaries such as the Kansas Wheat Alliance, food processors), but the rung is not discovery-dominated.
scored.step_up: Unproven: public and university lines license for nominal fees. Montana State's exclusive term sheets ask only for reimbursement of PVP and AOSCA fees, about $5,500-5,750. Expired-PVP germplasm is free to anyone. Proven: royalties are small. Kansas Wheat Alliance charges 1 cent/lb (about $0.60/bu) and WSU charges 2 cents/lb of certified seed. University of Idaho has collected about $3M in total royalties from its LCS sales to date. A whole public breeding programme like Oklahoma State costs about $0.5M/yr. A typical winning public variety is worth roughly $1-5M in lifetime royalties, so winners return maybe 2-5x, and that falls below 2x across the portfolio at a 10-30% hit rate. That fails the round-6 bar of at least 5x on capital with a multi-$B prize.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheaper than the candidate claims. A Canadian oat study puts a field plot at CAD $40-50, and 30 entries x 10 locations x 4 reps at $48-60k, which works out to about $1.6-2k per line per trial-year. Three years plus seed increase and quality testing comes to roughly $20-150k per line. That only marginally reaches the ~$50k "expensive" threshold. Hit rates for advanced public lines becoming commercially successful varieties are about 10-30%. ML predicting genotype-by-environment performance could give about 1.5x, but breeders already use genomic prediction and G×E models, so the gap the lever exploits is narrow.
scored.data: The data is largely legible and the outcome is already written down. University variety-trial reports publish yield, test weight and disease tables by location and year. That is exactly the outcome the ML would predict, and it is summarised in structured or semi-structured tables that every seed company reads. GRIN-Global phenotypes are structured. Rights are weak on two counts. First, expired-PVP germplasm is open to everyone, so it cannot be owned exclusively, and it is 20+ years old genetics that has lost roughly 15-25% in yield to genetic gain since. Second, good university releases are offered competitively through tech-transfer calls (Guelph, Montana) to informed seed companies, so the sellers are not owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: Exclusive licence to a university or USDA advanced line for about PVP-fee reimbursement ($5-20k) plus royalty share. Alternatively, free non-exclusive use of expired-PVP germplasm, which cannot be owned.
scored.buyer: Regional and national seed companies and sublicensing intermediaries (Kansas Wheat Alliance, NU Horizon Genetics, SeCan), plus food processors needing traits such as malting barley or pulses. They pay per-pound royalties rather than large lump sums. $1-20M exclusives are rare outside major crops held by Bayer and Corteva.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from variety ownership to seed production and conditioning, then to an identity-preserved specialty-grain supply chain such as malting or pulse ingredients. A real ladder exists, but specialty-crop chains are mid-sized and commodity seed is dominated by Bayer, Corteva and Syngenta. A trillion-dollar path is implausible, though a $1B+ specialty seed and ingredient company is conceivable.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no ownable information asymmetry. The outcome the ML would predict, line performance by environment, is already published in university variety-trial yield tables. The best public lines are licensed competitively to informed seed companies for nominal fees. Expired-PVP germplasm is obsolete and cannot be held exclusively. Per-line trials cost only about $2k per location-year, so incumbents already run them, which leaves no cheap-to-proven spread, and winners earn only $1-5M in lifetime royalties.
scored.one_line_reason: Trialling dominates the work rather than discovery, the outcomes are already in published trial tables, and royalty-scale prizes ($1-5M per variety) make portfolio returns under ~2x.

scored.name: Grandfathered billboard permits converted to digital
scored.one_line: Buy legally nonconforming static billboard structures and permits from mom-and-pop owners, use ML over scanned state DOT outdoor-advertising permit files and municipal sign-code variance decisions to predict which can win digital conversion or relocation, obtain approvals, then operate or sell to the majors.
scored.unproven_right: Static billboard structure plus grandfathered permit, about $50-200k each from small owners
scored.proving_step: Digital conversion or relocation approval (variance, sign-code amendment, DOT permit): $50-300k and 1-3 years, often litigated. About 30-50% succeed; ML lifts that by targeting jurisdictions and permit histories.
scored.proven_buyer: Outfront, Lamar and Clear Channel Outdoor, paying $1-3M per digital face in good markets
scored.public_data: State DOT outdoor advertising permit inventories and scanned files, municipal sign-code amendments, board of adjustment minutes, traffic counts
scored.rough_step_up: 5-15x per site at digital approval. Operating a digital network is the ladder; smaller prize (low $B).
scored.frame: The rung is a static structure plus its grandfathered permit, taken through digital-conversion approval. Discovery (finding which sites can be converted) is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of it is political and legal: variances, sign-code amendments, cap-and-replace swaps (removing several static faces to win one digital face), and lawsuits such as Lamar v. Knoxville (lost) and Lamar v. Lexington-Fayette (federal suit). The physical step is a $200-250k LED build. That is not trivial, though contractors can do it. A capitalised buyer does exist (the majors, at 10-14x cash flow).
scored.step_up: Static face: about $3k/month revenue, roughly $20k/yr billboard cash flow, selling for $150-250k at 8-12x (Stark Capital/Billboard Insider). Digital face: about $15k/month (Lamar CEO Sean Reilly) after about $200-250k capex (Outfront). That is worth about $1-1.5M at 10-14x (CCO's US sale was valued at 12.8x). So the step-up is about 5-7x on the structure's value, but only about 2-2.5x on all-in capital (purchase plus $50-300k approval plus $250k build). Majors report 20-43% IRRs on conversions, which is ordinary infrastructure return, not a 10^3 jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each approval attempt costs $50-300k and takes 1-3 years (candidate estimate, consistent with how long the Knoxville and Lexington cases ran). Base success rate is about 30-50%. ML might lift it about 1.2-1.4x by targeting jurisdictions whose sign codes already allow digital or have a record of settling (Rapid City settled with Lamar, repealed its ban and paid $100k). But outcomes depend on local politics and litigation more than on patterns hidden in documents.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. Whether digital is allowed is written in the municipal sign code, which is public, searchable text, and DOT permit inventories are often structured databases. Lamar, Outfront and CCO run local real-estate and legal teams that track every convertible site in their markets. Small owners sell through brokers at standard 8-12x multiples and usually know their local code. The right is bought, not free, but there is little information gap: the main signal (is digital permitted, or does a cap-and-replace path exist) sits in a legible field.
scored.right_bought: Bought: the static structure plus its site lease or easement plus a nonconforming permit, from mom-and-pop operators at 8-12x billboard cash flow (about $50-250k). The structure is cheap only relative to its digital value, and only in jurisdictions where conversion is uncertain. Where conversion is clearly allowed, sellers and the majors already price that in.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront Media and Clear Channel Outdoor, plus regional consolidators, paying about 10-14x cash flow for digital faces, roughly $1-3M per face in good markets. They are well capitalised and acquire constantly.
scored.ladder: Short ladder: run a regional digital network, sell ads programmatically, then consolidate into a mid-size outdoor-advertising company. Total US OOH is about $9B in revenue, Lamar's market cap is about $13B, and there are only about 10-12k US digital roadside faces. A $B outcome is possible as a roll-up, but not a trillion-dollar chain. Billboards are a capped, regulation-constrained asset class (the Highway Beautification Act freezes supply).
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving here is a political and legal fight, not a discovery problem. Whether a site can go digital is written in the public sign code and known to the majors' local permitting teams, and approval turns on variances, cap-and-replace swaps and litigation, which ML cannot read. So there is no information gap for ML to exploit, and the spread on all-in capital is only about 2x.
scored.one_line_reason: Billboard conversion is a well-understood regulatory and political game that the majors already play with full information. ML adds little edge, and the realistic return of about 2x on capital (static board plus approval plus $250k LED build, against a 10-14x cash-flow exit) is too thin.

scored.name: Former SCIF and secure-facility buildings re-accredited for cleared tenants
scored.one_line: Buy or master-lease buildings that once housed SCIFs or SAPFs (left behind by contractor exits and agency moves) at ordinary office prices. ML finds surviving build-outs from scanned permits. Re-accredit to ICD 705 and lease as turnkey secure space to cleared defense and AI-security firms at 2-3x normal rent, or sell the stabilised asset.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase or master lease of an office or flex building whose RF shielding, acoustic build-out and alarm infrastructure survive, priced as distressed office
scored.proving_step: TEMPEST and RF shielding tests, acoustic remediation, intrusion detection and sponsor-led re-accreditation. About $0.3-2M per site over 6-12 months; the proof is the accreditation.
scored.proven_buyer: Defense primes, cleared startups (defense tech, AI labs) and REITs buying stabilised secure-office assets
scored.public_data: GSA lease inventory, scanned building permits mentioning RF shielding or ICD 705, USAspending and SAM.gov award locations, contractor WARN and relocation notices, county assessor improvement records
scored.rough_step_up: Distressed office at $80-150/sqft becomes $400-700/sqft stabilised secure space, about 3-5x on capital, portfolio prize of a few $B.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy or master-lease an office or flex building with a surviving secure build-out, then re-accredit it". Finding the building is maybe 20-30% of the work. The rest is physical and administrative, and none of it is trivial: TEMPEST and RF testing, bringing an old build-out up to current ICD/ICS 705 tech specs (an inactive Herndon SCIF listing notes that reactivation needs modifications), intrusion detection, and above all getting a government sponsor. A SCIF can only be accredited, or co-used by a contractor, when an agency sponsors it for specific classified work. A landlord cannot obtain accreditation on spec. Buyers exist: cleared contractors and secure-office REITs. But the "proof" is not in the company's hands. It depends on a tenant's sponsor, so this is not a discovery-dominated rung.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims $80-150/sqft distressed office rising to $400-700/sqft stabilised secure space. The public comps don't support the top end. Northern Virginia Class A office trades at about $184-280/sqft (8111 Gatehouse at $184/sf; 4075 Wilson Blvd sold for $52.7M on 189k sf, about $279/sf, after a $6M renovation). The JLL sale of Independence Center II in Chantilly marketed tenant-installed SCIFs as a feature, but the price was not disclosed. Building a new SCIF costs about $350-1,000/sqft, so a surviving build-out does carry replacement value. However, it is often tenant-owned, it is already marketed, and it has to be upgraded to current specs. Shared and coworking SCIF space already exists in Virginia. I found no public SCIF rent premium. A realistic outcome is perhaps 1.5-2.5x on capital per site, not 3-5x, and the prize is a niche of a few hundred million to low $B, concentrated in the DC, Huntsville, Colorado Springs and San Diego corridors.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $0.3-2M per site over 6-12 months, which is expensive enough to clear the threshold. Real costs: new SCIF construction runs $350-1,000+/sqft (Strategic Solutions Unlimited, Adamo Security), and even basic facility security adds at least $50/sqft (CSO Online). The base rate for a surviving build-out becoming re-accreditable is unknown, but it is probably 30-60% once a sponsor is in hand. Most of the residual failure is about sponsors and specs, which ML does not predict. ML over permits can find candidate buildings, but brokers already flag SCIF space as a listed attribute, so the lift in cost per proven asset is likely about 1.2-1.4x.
scored.data: Scanned county permits mentioning RF shielding or ICD 705 are illegible, but the outcome is largely legible elsewhere. Brokers list "SCIF space" as a marketed amenity (the JLL Chantilly listing, the commercialcafe Herndon listing that says a SCIF is inactive and no longer accredited). Owners and leasing agents know exactly what is in their buildings. Accreditation status sits in the DNI SCIF Repository, which is not public but is known to sponsors. GSA lease inventory and SAM.gov locations are structured and widely mined by federal real estate brokers. Purchase is possible, since rights are bought, but the sellers are sophisticated office landlords who price the infrastructure in or pitch it to cleared tenants. There is little discount available from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: Fee purchase or master lease of an office or flex building with residual SCIF or SAPF build-out. Because the right is bought, there is no first-come claim. The seller is usually an institutional landlord who knows about, and markets, the secure infrastructure, so it is not priced as plain distressed office.
scored.buyer: Defense primes and cleared contractors (as tenants who need their own sponsor), classified coworking and SCIF-as-a-service operators, and secure-office REITs such as COPT Defense Properties buying stabilised assets. They are capitalised but few, and they already understand the space well.
scored.ladder: The possible path runs from re-accredited secure office to SCIF-as-a-service operator, then ground-up classified campuses, then secure and classified data centers for AI and IC workloads. That is a real but niche ladder, and the end state is COPT-like: about a $3-4B REIT, not a trillion-dollar chain. The DoD is also launching mobile secure workspaces for contractors (ClearanceJobs, Sep 2026), which competes at the bottom rung.
