scored.fatal_flaw: The landlord cannot produce the proof. ICD 705 accreditation, or contractor co-use, requires a government sponsor tied to a specific classified contract, so a SCIF cannot be accredited on spec. And the surviving build-out is a known, broker-marketed feature, not hidden in illegible data, so there is no purchase discount for ML to unlock.
scored.one_line_reason: Accreditation needs a tenant's government sponsor, owners already market their SCIF build-outs, and comps put stabilised value well below $400-700/sqft. The result is thin spread, weak ML edge and a niche prize.

scored.name: Captive Scent (natural odorant discovery from public GC-MS spectra)
scored.one_line: Mine public GC-MS and NMR spectra of plant, fungal and insect volatiles for unassigned peaks whose predicted structure is a high-impact odorant (musk, ambergris, sandalwood). Make a few mg and run an odour panel. File composition-of-use IP and sell the captive molecule to a fragrance house, which pays $5-50M for a patented captive.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: There is no defensible owned asset. Natural odorants found in public spectra are generally unpatentable as compositions (natural products in the US) and may be anticipated by the publication itself. So the "captive" is a weak use patent, not a cheaply bought right. And Osmo ($130M raised) already owns ML odorant discovery using synthetic novel scaffolds, which avoids that patent problem.
scored.frame: The rung is a single molecule, from an unassigned spectral peak to a patented captive odorant. Discovery (picking the peak, predicting the structure, panel-testing the odour) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is physical and regulatory and not trivial: finding a scalable synthesis (Givaudan tried 19 routes for Pomarose), stability and performance in finished products, IFRA/RIFM safety testing and REACH/TSCA registration. Capitalised buyers exist (Givaudan, IFF, Symrise, dsm-firmenich), but they make about 2,000 new molecules a year in-house and rarely buy outside captives.
scored.step_up: Under the round-6 rubric the step-up multiple matters less. The candidate assumes $5-50M for a patented captive, but I found no public deal comps for an outside captive being sold. Givaudan says the cost of individual molecules is 'not cheap' but undisclosed. A captive that gets into products can earn for years or decades, but the value only exists with exclusivity, and a natural product found in public spectra gives weak exclusivity.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Mg synthesis plus an odour panel costs roughly $10-50k per candidate, which is at or below the ~$50k threshold. The truly expensive steps (tox, REACH, scale-up, likely $0.5-2M+) are not ones ML improves much. Houses report about 2,000 molecules made per year for a handful of commercial captives, a hit rate well under 1%. ML structure and odour prediction could plausibly raise the odour-hit rate 1.5x+, but the cheap proving step weakens the lever. Source: Givaudan innovation page, Wikipedia 'Captive odorant'.
scored.data: Public GC-MS/NMR spectra (GNPS, MassBank, supplementary data in the literature) are semi-structured and already mined by metabolomics tools, so they are only partly illegible. Odour outcomes are not recorded in those datasets, which is good for the ML edge. But there is no right to buy: a molecule in a public spectrum belongs to no one, publication may anticipate any claim, and natural compositions are largely unpatentable in the US (Myriad/Funk Bros). IP is first-to-file on use or synthesis, not a right bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: Nothing is bought. The asset is a self-filed use or synthesis-route patent on a possibly natural, possibly published molecule, which is weak and easy to design around.
scored.buyer: The big four fragrance houses (Givaudan, IFF, Symrise, dsm-firmenich), which are capitalised but have strong not-invented-here habits and their own discovery pipelines. A secondary option is selling the ingredient directly to indie perfumers, a much smaller market.
scored.ladder: Molecule IP, then ingredient manufacturing (aroma chemicals), then a fragrance compounding house. Each rung is real, but the fragrance ingredients market is about $15-20B with entrenched oligopolists. It is a path to a mid-size specialty chemicals company, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no defensible owned asset. Natural odorants identified from public spectra are largely unpatentable as compositions and may be anticipated by the source publication, so the 'captive' is at best a weak use patent, not a right bought cheaply. Meanwhile the incumbents (about 2,000 new molecules a year each) and Osmo already do ML odorant discovery on novel synthetic scaffolds that can be patented.
scored.one_line_reason: Relaxing C3 does not rescue this. Proving an odour is cheap, the expensive steps (safety tox, REACH registration, scale-up) are not ones ML speeds up, there is no right to buy, and a natural molecule in a public spectrum has weak IP, so the value cannot be captured.

scored.name: US mitigation-bank sponsor (hunt 9)
scored.one_line: Buy drained hydric farmland, win IRT approval, restore and sell wetland credits.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: Bank NPV ~1-1.5x land; approval almost always succeeds; demand is the hidden state.
scored.frame: The rung is a single bank: option drained hydric farmland, get IRT/Corps approval of a banking instrument, restore it, then sell credits as each milestone releases them. Discovery (choosing the site and service area) is maybe 10-20% of the work. Most of it is physical and regulatory: restoration construction, a prospectus and instrument negotiated over 2-7 years, about 7 years of monitoring, financial assurances, and perpetual management. That physical step is the business, not a trivial one. Buyers are 404 permittees, who pay for credits, not for an approved but unbuilt bank. Some sponsors do sell entitled banks, but that resale market is thin.
scored.step_up: Before approval, the land trades at roughly farmland value (~$5-15k/ac). After approval and restoration, credits sell for ~$40k-$100k+ per credit/acre in the Willamette Valley and Nebraska, and up to $30k-$360k per impact acre in Florida (broker figures). That gross gap is mostly eaten by restoration, monitoring, assurance and endowment costs, plus 5-10 years of carry while credits release in tranches (~20% at easement). Nebraska's Glacier Creek bank priced credits at $100k/acre and expected only a 15% total return on a $4.77M project. Realistic return on capital is about 1.15-2x over a decade, inside a US compensatory-mitigation market of a few $B a year that is split into many local service areas.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive. It costs roughly $0.3-1M+ in consultants, design and negotiation before construction, and takes 2-7 years (the Corps' 225-day review limit is routinely blown; Army 2024 memo; Florida consultant cites ~7 years federal). But approval almost always succeeds once a sponsor commits to a hydric site, so ML has little failure to remove. The real unknown is whether local demand absorbs the credits, and RIBITS ledgers and 404 permit flow already make that fairly legible. Under the relaxed C3, ML site and service-area picking might give ~1.1-1.3x on cost per sold-out bank, short of the 1.5x for full credit.
scored.data: The signal is mostly LEGIBLE and already used by sponsors: SSURGO hydric soils, NWI, drainage tile and ditch layers, RIBITS credit ledgers and prices, and Corps 404 permit notices. The outcome (credits released, sold, remaining) sits in RIBITS ledger fields. Land is bought, not claimed first-come, from farmers who sell at farmland value. That discount exists, but it is an ordinary entitlement arbitrage that established sponsors (RES, Ecosystem Investment Partners, Westervelt) already run. ML does not create it.
scored.right_bought: A fee purchase or option on drained hydric farmland at ag-land prices, typically $5-15k/acre, from farmers. The owners can see the opportunity, and incumbent sponsors actively work these areas.
scored.buyer: Section 404 and state permittees (DOTs, developers, utilities, pipelines) buying credits inside the bank's service area. Occasionally a large sponsor or infrastructure fund buys a whole bank. Capitalised, but demand is lumpy and local.
scored.ladder: From a single bank you can build a multi-bank portfolio, add stream, species-conservation and nutrient/water-quality credits, then full-delivery and turnkey mitigation for DOTs, and possibly land and conservation-easement management at scale. That is RES-scale (~$1B-class) at most. The market is capped by regulated demand, with no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proof is not where the risk or the value sits. IRT approval of a well-chosen hydric site almost always succeeds. The work is years of restoration and perpetual stewardship. The data and the demand state (RIBITS ledgers) are already legible, and the realistic return is only ~1.15-2x over a decade in a few-$B, fragmented market.
scored.one_line_reason: Under round 6, owning and operating the bank is allowed, but returns are ~15%-2x over 5-10 years. Approval rarely fails, so ML has little hit rate to lift. The data is already legible, and restoration plus stewardship, not discovery, dominates the work.

scored.name: Distressed Legacy Wind Repowering
scored.one_line: Buy end-of-PPA or bankrupt 2000s-era wind farms at salvage value, use ML to find the ones where full repowering (new taller turbines on the existing permitted footprint and interconnection) clears economically, prove the repower plan, then operate or sell the repowered asset.
scored.unproven_right: The aging wind farm plus its land leases, county permits and existing interconnection rights, bought at about $50-150k/MW from owners whose PPA is ending or whose turbines are failing.
scored.proving_step: Repower feasibility: LiDAR/met campaign, FAA re-determination for taller tips, county permit amendment, interconnection material-modification study and PTC/ITC requalification. $1-3M and 1-3 years. Base success about 50%. ML picks farms where wind resource and permit headroom support it.
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities and IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy, utility-owned rate base) that pay full value for repowered MW with tax credits and existing grid access.
scored.public_data: EIA-860/923 monthly generation by plant (read against ERA5 reanalysis to separate resource from failure), scanned FAA OE/AAA obstruction filings, county conditional-use permits, ISO interconnection agreements, USGS US Wind Turbine Database.
scored.rough_step_up: Bought at about $0.1M/MW. A repowered farm with a new 20-year PPA is worth about $1.2-1.6M/MW against about $0.9M/MW repower capex. About 2-4x on capital, with roughly 30 GW of pre-2012 US wind (a multi-$B prize). Ladder: operate, add storage at the interconnect, sell power.
scored.frame: The rung is 'aging wind farm plus a proven repower plan'. The proving work is a $1-3M feasibility package (met/LiDAR, FAA, permit amendment, interconnection study), and it is only about 10-20% of the work. New turbines at about $1.0-1.5M/MW (IRENA new-build onshore about $1,041/kW in 2024) are the dominant step. This is a bespoke physical build, close to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Discovery is not 80%+ of any sellable rung.
scored.step_up: The candidate assumes purchase at about $0.1M/MW. Real end-of-life wind deals are far higher. TRIG sold 35 MW of end-of-life Irish wind for EUR25M (about EUR0.7M/MW, a 26% premium to book) explicitly as a repowering opportunity. Galp paid EUR420M EV for 361 MW of 21-year-old merchant Spanish wind (about EUR1.16M/MW). Younger US wind traded at $1.8M/MW (EDPR, Illinois). The candidate's proven value is $1.2-1.6M/MW against $0.9M+ capex. With a realistic entry of $0.5-1.0M/MW, all-in cost is about $1.5-2.0M/MW, so the spread is roughly 0 to 1.1x, not 2-4x. The OBBBA also ends wind 45Y/48E credits for projects that began construction on or after July 4, 2026 unless placed in service by end-2027. A 1-3 year proving step starting now therefore misses the credits the plan relies on, which lowers proven value further.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate assumes a 50% base success rate at $1-3M and 1-3 years per attempt. That is expensive enough to meet the rubric. ML lift is weak because an operating farm already has 15-20 years of measured generation (EIA-923) and SCADA history. Wind resource and turbine failure are already well characterised, and the owner holds the data. Most remaining uncertainty is in FAA, county and interconnection decisions, which ML predicts poorly. Plausible lift is about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven repower.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible and already summarised. EIA-860/923 give plant-level capacity and monthly generation in structured form. The USGS USWTDB lists every turbine with model, hub height and date. ISO interconnection agreements are public and structured. Owners such as NextEra, MidAmerican, RWE, Pattern, Clearway and Xcel are sophisticated fleet operators with better private SCADA data than any public dataset. Many have already repowered: GE repowered 4 GW at 36 farms for NextEra and MidAmerican by 2019, and Siemens Gamesa repowered Rolling Hills. Scanned FAA and county filings add little. Rights are bought, but not from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: The right is the aging farm plus its leases, permits and interconnection rights, bought from end-of-PPA or distressed owners. In practice the interconnection position is scarce, given multi-year queues, and sellers and buyers both price it. End-of-life assets trade at about EUR0.7-1.2M/MW, not salvage value. Truly distressed sellers are rare and are auctioned to informed bidders.
scored.buyer: Utilities and IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy, utility rate base), and infrastructure funds. They are capitalised, but they are also the current owners and repower in-house.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but conventional. It runs: operate the repowered fleet, add storage or solar hybrids at the existing interconnect, sell power or data-centre PPAs, then become an IPP. That is a large prize, but it is the existing IPP business, with no ML-specific moat at higher rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no purchase discount, so no spread. Aging wind farms and their interconnection rights already trade at about EUR0.7-1.2M/MW to informed buyers who price repowering upside, not $0.1M/MW salvage. The owners hold better data (SCADA, measured output) than any public dataset, and the dominant cost is the physical turbine replacement, not discovery. The OBBBA credit sunset compounds this by removing the tax credits the proven value depends on.
scored.one_line_reason: Sophisticated owners already price repowering into end-of-life wind (TRIG at about EUR0.7M/MW, Galp at about EUR1.16M/MW), the physical rebuild dominates the work, and public data is legible, so ML creates no spread.

scored.name: NRHP-Eligible Building Rehab with Historic Tax Credits
scored.one_line: Buy overlooked older commercial and industrial buildings in secondary cities at land-plus value, get them listed on the National Register and win NPS Part 1/2 approval, then sell the certified project to tax-credit developers or redevelop it to capture the 20% federal plus 20-25% state historic credits.
scored.unproven_right: Fee ownership or options on vacant mills, warehouses and downtown blocks priced as teardowns by owners who do not know the building qualifies.
scored.proving_step: Register nomination, SHPO review and NPS Part 1/2 certification (historian report, documentation, design). $75k-$300k and 12-24 months; human-picked approval around 50-60%, ML ranking by significance evidence and integrity lifts it about 1.5x.
scored.proven_buyer: Historic tax credit developers and syndicators, and bank tax-equity investors (US Bancorp CDC, PNC, Enterprise).
scored.public_data: Scanned Sanborn fire insurance maps, state SHPO reconnaissance survey forms, local newspaper archives, city directories, NRHP nomination PDFs of comparable sites, historic photos. Eligibility is a narrative judgement, not a field.
scored.rough_step_up: Teardown $10-20/sf to credit-eligible project value 2-3x; credits worth about 40% of qualified rehab spend. About 2-4x on equity if developed in-house. $B-range prize across Rust Belt and Southern cities.
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is "certified-eligible building" (Part 1 approved, optionally Part 2 approved), which is sold to HTC developers. Inside that rung, discovery and proving are the historian report and the nomination, a small share of the cost and effort of the realised asset. The credit is earned only on qualified rehab spend that has to be substantial (more than the adjusted basis), so construction, financing and the Part 3 sign-off are most of the work, probably 85-95% of capital and effort. A Part-1-only building has a thin market: developers do eligibility screening themselves and pay for the rehab-able building, not for the certificate. So the frame where discovery is 80%+ either does not exist or does not have a buyer paying a premium. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: building the bespoke project is much harder than finding the site.
scored.step_up: I found no price for an unproven building versus a Part-1-certified one. The candidate's own figure is a 2-3x project value uplift and 2-4x on equity if developed in-house (unsourced). The credit stack, 20% federal plus 20-25% state of qualified rehab spend, priced at roughly $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar, mostly fills the financing gap on buildings that otherwise do not pencil. It is not a windfall on top of market value. The national prize is real but bounded: NPS certified 939 completed projects with $9.6B of qualifying rehab cost in FY2025, about $1.9B a year in federal credits, already worked by an established developer and syndicator industry. Realistic returns are developer-fee plus value-add real estate economics (about 1.5-2.5x equity over 3-5 years), not 5x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate's $75k-$300k per attempt merges Part 2 architectural design into proving. Part 1 and a National Register nomination typically cost tens of thousands of dollars, and many buildings sit in already-listed districts where Part 1 is close to a formality. NPS approved 1,463 Part 1s and 1,187 Part 2s in FY2022, and the volumes point to high approval for professionally prepared applications (I found no published denial rate). The cheap Part 1 step is below the ~$50k threshold and already has a high hit rate, so ML lift on cost per proven asset is small. The expensive, risky part is rehab execution and pencilling the deal, where ML adds little.
scored.data: Some of the signal is illegible: scanned Sanborn maps, city directories, newspaper archives and comparable nomination PDFs. But much of the answer is already in legible fields. Historic district boundaries are GIS layers, SHPO survey databases carry eligibility and contributing-status codes, and NRHP listings are structured. That is the regulator-writes-the-answer problem the rubric warns about. Rights are bought rather than taken first-come, and some rural or secondary-city owners do price buildings as teardowns. However, "historic tax credit eligible" is a common broker marketing line, and the main reason old buildings are cheap is that rehab costs more than they are worth, not that the owner missed their eligibility.
scored.right_bought: Fee simple or options on vacant mills, warehouses and downtown blocks, bought from private owners and municipalities or land banks. These are bought rights, so this criterion is met.
scored.buyer: HTC developers and syndicators, plus bank tax-equity investors (US Bancorp CDC, PNC, Enterprise). They are well capitalised, but they buy credits from projects that are being rehabbed or are complete. They do not buy eligibility certificates. Developers buying buildings pay for location and rehab economics.
scored.ladder: Above the eligibility rung sit rehab development, syndication, and owning and operating the property, and possibly a vertically integrated adaptive-reuse platform. These are real rungs, but they lead into fragmented, local, low-margin real estate development with policy risk on the credit. That is a decent real estate company at most, not a path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical rehab is most of the work, capital and risk, and the credit is earned only on qualified rehab spend. Discovery (finding an eligible building) is a small, cheap step whose answer is often already legible in SHPO survey status and historic district GIS, so no rung exists where ML-led discovery is 80%+ of the work with a buyer paying for the proof. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example applied to real estate.
scored.one_line_reason: The credit rewards rehab spend, not discovery, and Part 1 eligibility is cheap, high-hit-rate and often already in legible SHPO and district data, so ML buys little spread and the company becomes an ordinary real estate developer.

scored.name: Powered brownfields (hunt 8)
scored.one_line: Buy contaminated former industrial and power-plant sites near substations, price cleanup from California GeoTracker records with ML, remediate and develop as powered industrial / data-centre land.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: No purchase discount in LA assessor data (+5.4%); ML added +0.004 AUC over a buyer heuristic; gas-station cleanups cost ~10x the closure uplift.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a contaminated parcel near a substation, price and carry out the cleanup, get regulatory closure, then sell or develop it as powered land. Discovery (picking the parcel and estimating cleanup cost) is maybe 10-20% of the work. The physical step, remediation, is the biggest cost and risk, and from earlier hunts it costs about 10x the uplift that closure brings. This fails the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example does: the physical step is harder than the finding.
scored.step_up: Powered land does trade at a large premium. Altus Group's study of 80 US deals found committed utility load is the main price driver: Northern Virginia median $2.8M/acre, Columbus/Phoenix/Atlanta about $100k-$460k/acre, markets with little committed load down to about $28k/acre. One Loudoun deal paid $6.33M/acre. Land without a power path sells for about $10k/acre and can reach six figures once power is in place. That premium comes from committed power, not from cleanup proof. The earlier hunt's own test of the cleanup step: LA assessor data showed only a +5.4% discount on contaminated parcels, and cleanup cost about 10x the uplift from closure. So the step-up the ML would create is about 1.05x, not a large multiple.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving means a Phase II site assessment plus remediation. A Phase II alone is roughly $20k-$100k+ (my industry estimate; no source found this round) and remediation takes years, so the step clears the 'expensive' bar under the relaxed C3. But ML added only +0.004 AUC over a simple buyer heuristic in the earlier hunt, so cost per proven site improves about 1.0x, well short of the 1.5x needed. Base closure rates may well be in the 30-70% range the relaxed rule allows. That does not help when the model cannot tell good sites from bad ones better than buyers already do.
scored.data: California GeoTracker is public and partly structured. It records case status (open / closed / no further action) in a legible field, which is exactly the 'regulator writes the answer into a status field' problem. Scanned case documents add little beyond that field, as the +0.004 AUC shows. Power proximity is legible from substation maps and queue data, and queue-position lookups are already known to match ML.
scored.right_bought: Fee title can be bought, but there is no informational discount. Sellers and buyers both commission Phase I reports, and assessor data showed only a +5.4% difference. Sellers who own sites near substations know their power value, because data-centre land brokers now contact them directly. Land deals for data centres rose 141% in Q1 2026, and about 30% of development-site spending went to data-centre land (Bisnow / Avison Young). That is a crowded, well-informed market.
scored.buyer: There are capitalised buyers with plenty of money: hyperscalers, data-centre developers (and their REITs) and industrial developers. They pay for powered, entitled, clean land. That price reflects committed load and entitlements, not the cleanup estimate.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: land, then entitlement and power commitment, then a powered shell, then a data centre or industrial facility, then operations or leasing. The steps above the land are worth very large sums, but none of them depends on the cleanup-ML edge. Each rung is won through power and utility relationships and capital, which incumbents already hold.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up in value comes from committed utility power, which is legible and widely competed for, not from the cleanup estimate. The cleanup-pricing ML adds nothing (+0.004 AUC over a buyer heuristic), contaminated sites sell at almost no discount (+5.4%), and remediation costs about 10x the uplift from closure, so the physical step dominates and the spread created by discovery is negative.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 and the operate/develop C2 do not rescue it: the value is in power, not in the hidden cleanup cost; the ML edge is essentially zero and remediation, the physical step, costs far more than the uplift it unlocks.
sources: Prior hunt 8 results: LA assessor +5.4% discount, +0.004 AUC, cleanup about 10x closure uplift

scored.name: Idle fab shells requalified for trusted/defense microelectronics
scored.one_line: Buy or option idle or bankrupt 150/200mm fab buildings, whose cleanrooms, ultrapure water, gas systems and permits are still intact, at shell prices. Requalify the utilities and cleanroom class, then sell to a CHIPS-funded or defense-trusted foundry or run it as a specialty foundry for MEMS, RF and photonics.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase option on a dormant fab building and its utility plant from a bankruptcy estate, REIT or liquidator, priced as industrial real estate (about $50-150/sqft)
scored.proving_step: Utility and cleanroom requalification: particle-class certification, ultrapure water and abatement restart, renewed air and wastewater permits, structural vibration survey. About $2-10M and 9-18 months per site; success likely when the plant was mothballed rather than stripped.
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty and trusted foundries (SkyWater-type), defense primes building secure supply chains, and CHIPS-funded photonics or MEMS startups; or operate it directly.
scored.public_data: EPA Title V air permits and TRI chemical-release filings (showing which hazardous-gas and UPW systems ran recently), state wastewater discharge permits, PACER dockets and auction asset schedules (scanned), county building permits, OSHA records, liquidator equipment catalogs
scored.rough_step_up: Shell at about $10-30M becomes a requalified fab worth $100-300M (vs $1B+ new), about 5-10x on proving capex. ML picks the roughly 1 in 4 dormant fabs that are mothballed, not gutted, plausibly doubling the hit rate.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a dormant fab shell and requalifying it. Finding the fab is maybe 10-20% of the work. Requalification, putting in tools (a 200mm line needs tens to hundreds of $M), and above all winning customers and qualifying processes make up the rest. A requalified empty cleanroom is not a sellable finished product: buyers pay for tools, process IP, staff and customer qualifications. Here the physical and operating step is the hard part, the same pattern as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.step_up: Recent 200mm fab sales, mostly as working fabs with tools and staff: SkyWater bought Infineon Fab 25 for $110M headline ($80M transaction price, ~$30M working capital, plus $25M in wafer credits; closed June 2025). SkyWater bought Cypress Fab 4 for $30M (2017). Littelfuse bought the Elmos Dortmund fab for about EUR 93M (2023). Silex is buying onsemi Mountain Top for $40M (2026). These are full operating fabs at $30-110M. That undercuts the claim that a bare shell at $10-30M becomes $100-300M through utility requalification alone. Realistic step-up for an empty, requalified shell is about 1.5-3x before tool capex, not 5-10x. One dealer quote says a cleanroom costs $200-300/sqft to build but sells for ~$10/sqft if relocated; that is a discount on moving it, not on in-place value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive ($2-10M and 9-18 months per site, the candidate's own figures), which passes the cost leg. The ML lever is weak. Only a few dozen idle 150/200mm fabs exist in the US. Each is marketed by specialist brokers (ATREG handled onsemi Pocatello and Elmos, and is now listing the former SK hynix Eugene fab with 170k sqft cleanroom and infrastructure largely intact). Whether a site was mothballed or gutted shows up in the broker package and a one-day site tour. Base hit rate among listed shells is probably 30-60%, and ML adds perhaps 1.1x over a broker call plus a walkthrough.
scored.data: Title V, TRI, wastewater permits and PACER dockets are public and somewhat illegible. But the outcome (cleanroom class, UPW and gas status, tool set) is written plainly in broker offering memoranda and liquidator catalogs. Sellers are sophisticated IDMs (Infineon, onsemi, SK hynix, Cypress) using specialist brokers, with process-run auctions and a limited but informed buyer pool. They do not fail to read their own data. The right is bought, not free, but not cheaply relative to what an informed buyer pays. CFIUS and trusted-foundry rules also restrict who can buy.
scored.right_bought: Purchase or option on a fab building and utility plant from an IDM, bankruptcy estate or REIT, usually via ATREG-style brokered sales. Comparable fabs have traded at $30-110M with tools.
scored.buyer: Specialty and trusted foundries (SkyWater, Silex, Littelfuse, LA Semiconductor), defense primes and CHIPS-funded startups. They are capitalised, but they already buy directly from IDMs through the same brokers, so the company sits between informed parties and adds little.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: shell, then requalified cleanroom, then tooled specialty foundry (MEMS, RF, photonics), then trusted-foundry accreditation, then a multi-fab specialty foundry roll-up (SkyWater is roughly a $1B+ company). Each rung up is operations-heavy, not discovery-heavy.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is not a discovery problem. The universe is a few dozen brokered fabs sold by sophisticated owners to informed buyers. The price already reflects mothballed-vs-gutted status, so ML creates no spread. The value comes from tooling and running a foundry and winning customers, the hard physical and operating step, as in the geothermal counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Comparable 200mm fabs trade at $30-110M through specialist brokers to informed buyers, and the hard part is running a foundry, not finding the shell. ML has neither an illegible signal nor a naive seller to exploit.

scored.name: Cold War hardened sites converted to EMP-hardened sovereign compute
scored.one_line: Buy decommissioned hardened sites (Nike and Atlas missile sites, AT&T Long Lines bunkers, FAA and DoD communications bunkers) cheaply from GSA, counties or private holders. Prove structural integrity, dryness, power and fiber reach and HEMP shielding, then sell or operate as hardened colocation for defense and AI-security tenants.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or option on the bunker parcel, usually $0.3-3M from private owners or GSA disposal auction
scored.proving_step: Structural and corrosion survey, HEMP/MIL-STD-188-125 shielding test, utility power study and fiber diversity study. About $300k-1.5M and 6-12 months per site; likely to pass where the site stayed dry.
scored.proven_buyer: Hardened data center operators, defense and intelligence agencies, sovereign-AI or classified-cloud tenants paying premium rates per kW
scored.public_data: Army Corps FUDS records and scanned property reports, HABS/HAER drawings at the Library of Congress, Long Lines route archives, county assessor and deed scans, GSA disposal notices, utility substation maps
scored.rough_step_up: Bought for ~$1M, certified for under $1.5M, worth $20-60M as a 5-20MW hardened shell (vs $150M+ new): about 10x on capital, prize under $1B unless 20+ sites are rolled up.
scored.frame: The rung would be "buy the bunker, certify it as a hardened shell, sell or lease it". A proven site does not sell as a finished asset, though. A tenant pays for powered, cooled, connected capacity. Getting there means a bespoke underground fit-out: 5-20 MW of utility service and substation, cooling, MEP and fiber builds, waterproofing, and MIL-STD-188-125 shielding retrofit (the original shielding has usually decayed or been stripped). That fit-out costs far more than finding and surveying the site. On a $20-60M valued asset, discovery and proving ($1M purchase plus about $1.5M certification) is perhaps 5-15% of the work, nowhere near 80%. This has the same structure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. No liquid buyer market exists for a "certified but unbuilt hardened shell".
scored.step_up: Unproven: Atlas F and E sites have asking prices of about $0.18-1.3M (Abilene Atlas F at $380k in 2022, later $179k at half price on missilebases.com; Lincoln KS 8.5 acres at $1.3M in 2025; Kansas Atlas E at $750k; an Adirondacks converted silo cut from $4.6M to $750k). Proven: the candidate's own $20-60M figure is not backed by any comparable sale. The one public bunker colo comparable, InfoBunker in Iowa, charges about $750-875 per rack per month and $2,900 per month for a suite. That is a small niche business, not evidence of $20-60M shells. The large asking-price cuts suggest the market does not pay a big hardening premium. Each realised dollar requires the heavy fit-out first. On total capital including fit-out, a realistic return is under about 2x, and the prize is under $1B.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs $300k-1.5M per site and takes 6-12 months, which counts as expensive under the relaxed C3. The base pass rate is probably 30-60% on dryness and structure, but much lower on power and fiber reach for remote rural silos. ML over FUDS records, HABS/HAER drawings and water-table data could plausibly screen out wet or flooded sites and those far from substations, perhaps a 1.2-1.5x gain in cost per proven site. The pool is small, though: a few hundred Atlas, Titan and Nike sites plus some Long Lines bunkers, many already converted or flooded. A good human screener with GIS (substation distance, fiber routes, listing photos) captures most of that edge. Sources: the listings above. The pass rate and ML lift are my estimates.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: FUDS scans, HABS/HAER drawings and Long Lines archives. But the key fact, that the site is a hardened bunker, is entirely legible. These properties are marketed as missile silos and bunkers on missilebases.com and Zillow, often tagged "data center", and sellers price them as novelty bunkers. The value-limiting unknowns (power reach, fiber, water ingress) come from utility maps and physical inspection, not from hidden signal in scanned files. The right is bought, not claimed, which passes. But owners are not ignorant of what they hold, so the information asymmetry is thin.
scored.right_bought: Fee simple title or a purchase option from private owners, counties or GSA disposal. Listed prices run about $0.18-1.3M.
scored.buyer: In theory: hardened and defense colocation operators, DoD and intelligence-community agencies, sovereign or classified cloud tenants. In practice, DoD builds or leases its own accredited SCIF and HEMP facilities and buys finished, accredited capacity, not raw shells. Commercial hardened colo demand is niche (InfoBunker, Bahnhof Pionen, Iron Mountain's limestone-mine site), and those operators favour large mines over small silos. No capitalised buyer pays a step-up for a certified-but-unbuilt shell.
scored.ladder: Shell, then fit-out and operating colocation, then accredited classified-cloud operator, then roll-up of hardened sites. A ladder exists, but every rung is a capital-heavy physical build. Rural silo sites have limited power, and their small volume (an Atlas F silo is about 52 ft across) caps any single site at a few MW. That limits how far the climb goes.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates, as in the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Turning a small, often wet, rural bunker into powered, cooled, fiber-connected, HEMP-certified 5-20 MW capacity is a bespoke build costing far more than finding or certifying the site. No buyer pays a large premium for a certified-but-unbuilt shell, and whether a site is a bunker is already legible in public listings.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the value chain, the fit-out is the hard part, the "hardened bunker" fact is already legible and priced, and the prize stays under $1B.

scored.name: Natural Pearls in Estate Jewellery (Nacre / NaturalPearl / Nacre Lab)
scored.one_line: Buys antique pearl strands and jewels sold as 'cultured', 'costume' or generic 'pearls' at US, European, Indian and Gulf provincial estate auctions, uses ML over catalogue photos and text (pre-1930 dating, clasp hallmarks, drilling, lustre, size gradation, provenance words) to pick likely natural saltwater pearls, gets GIA/SSEF/Gübelin/LFG X-ray reports, and resells at Christie's and Sotheby's Geneva/Hong Kong.
scored.old_fatal_flaw: The market is too small, and the value of a typical hit ($3-30k) does not scale. The signal that decides a hit (internal structure) is not in the public data at all. Only a $50 X-ray reveals it, and expert dealers already apply the visible priors. So ML adds little over a dealer's eye plus cheap blanket testing, and the 10^3x hits are rare cases with known provenance that big houses already catch.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a mislabelled strand, get a lab report, consign it to a top house. Inside that rung, discovery (picking which strand to test) is about 80% of the work, and the physical step (a pearl X-ray, a lab report, consigning) is trivial. Buyers with capital do exist: Christie's, Sotheby's and Gulf collectors. The rung is real but tiny, and anyone can run it, because the proof is cheap and gets done routinely.
scored.step_up: Unproven to proven runs about 3-10x per strand, not 10^3. Example: Nadeau's Lot 565, a natural saltwater strand from the John L. Hughes estate, was estimated at $10-20k and realised $70,150 in Jan 2026. Even a provincial room already sold it with a GIA natural report, so the spread was captured before any arbitrageur got to it. The rare real 'cultured to natural' finds go from about $200 to $5-30k. Sotheby's Geneva SSEF natural strands carry estimates of CHF 100-200k, but those come with provenance and are already identified.
scored.hit_rate_capex: A GIA/SSEF/LFG pearl identification report costs about $100-$1,000 per strand and takes days to weeks. That is far below the ~$50k-per-attempt bar. The base hit rate among strands loosely catalogued as 'pearls' at provincial sales is low (probably well under 5%). But because proving is cheap, blanket testing beats ML triage, so C3 scores 0 even under the relaxed rule. These figures are from lab price lists I remember, not checked this round.
scored.data: Catalogue photos and text are public and scattered, but they are not illegible in the Terranox sense. The deciding signal (internal growth structure) is invisible in photos, and only an X-ray reveals it. Dealers already apply the visible priors (antique clasp, drill holes, gradation, period). Sellers often write the answer into the lot anyway ('natural, GIA report'). The right is bought cheaply at auction in open competition with specialist dealers, so it is not a right that only an ML reader can see.
scored.right_bought: You buy auction lots outright. Buying is competitive against specialist pearl dealers, who scan the same provincial sales and bid up anything that looks antique.
scored.buyer: Christie's and Sotheby's Geneva/Hong Kong natural-pearl sales, Gulf collectors, and high-end dealers. All have capital, but the total market is small, roughly low hundreds of $M a year.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are pearl dealing, high jewellery and retail. None of them compounds toward a very large company, natural pearl supply is fixed and shrinking, and a 'whole chain' worth billions does not exist.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is cheap. A pearl X-ray or lab report costs a few hundred dollars, and the deciding signal (internal structure) is not in the public photos or text. So blanket testing plus a dealer's eye matches ML triage. On top of that, the prize is a niche worth low hundreds of $M, with per-hit spreads of $5-50k that do not scale.
scored.one_line_reason: Under round 6 the step-up rule no longer bites. But proof costs about $500, so ML has no lever (C3=0), the signal is not in the data, and the market is far too small to give a multi-$B prize or a ladder.

scored.name: Irrigation Canal Conduit Hydro
scored.one_line: Buy lease-of-power-privilege rights and canal-drop agreements from irrigation districts, use ML to find drops with year-round head and flow, prove them via conduit exemption, then build and operate a portfolio of small hydro.
scored.unproven_right: Lease of Power Privilege (Bureau of Reclamation) or irrigation-district canal-drop leases, negotiated cheaply with districts that do not know their drops' generation value.
scored.proving_step: Conduit exemption or LOPP contracting, NEPA, interconnection and flow verification: $0.2-1M and 1-3 years per site. Many fail on seasonal flow. ML over flow records lifts the hit rate.
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities and community-solar/REC buyers, plus small-hydro IPPs; or hold and sell power under PURPA.
scored.public_data: Scanned BOR project data books and canal operations reports, state water-master daily diversion records, FERC conduit exemption filings, BOR Site Inventory reports.
scored.rough_step_up: Rights about $10-50k/MW. Built plants worth about $3-5M/MW against about $2.5M/MW capex: about 1.5-3x on capital, a small prize (sub-$1B). Weak ladder.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted canal-drop site (LOPP or conduit exemption plus interconnection), and there is no sellable rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work. Finding the site is maybe 10-20% of the work and well under 10% of capital. The bespoke low-head civil works and turbine (~$2.5-5M/MW, with small units costing more per kW) are most of the job. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern: building the plant is harder than finding the drop. Buyers of permitted but unbuilt sites (small-hydro IPPs) are thin and small.
scored.step_up: Using the candidate's own numbers, rights cost ~$10-50k/MW and a built plant is worth ~$3-5M/MW against ~$2.5M/MW capex. Return on total capital is therefore ~1.2-2x, and likely under 2x once you count the 1-3 year proving time and seasonal capacity factors (often 30-50%, since irrigation canals run only April-October). No source showed a large markup on a permitted, unbuilt LOPP site.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs $0.2-1M and takes 1-3 years per site (conduit exemption or LOPP, NEPA EA/FONSI, interconnection; e.g. Reclamation's 1.1 MW C-Drop on the Klamath C-Canal needed a full EA). That meets the expense bar. But the main cause of failure, seasonal flow, can be read straight from the daily diversion records, which are already legible. ML adds maybe 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven site, not 1.5x. Reclamation figures from 2016: 12 LOPP sites operating (43 MW) and 17 in development (51 MW). NREL: 23 of 36 LOPP projects (76 MW) reached some phase of development, so base success is already moderate.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible, and the answer is already summarised. Reclamation and NREL/ORNL resource assessments already list candidate dams and conduits with estimated MW (more than 360 MW identified across Reclamation-owned dams and conduits). State water-master diversion records are structured daily time series. FERC conduit exemption filings are indexed. Scanned project data books add only small margins. Some head and flow detail is buried in scanned documents, but the outcome field (MW potential) is already written down by the agency, which is the pattern that killed earlier hunts.
scored.right_bought: Weak. A Reclamation LOPP is awarded through a public solicitation in which the irrigation district or water users' association holding the operating contract usually gets preference. It is not bought cheaply from someone who cannot read the data. Districts know their drops and increasingly develop them themselves (e.g. North Unit Irrigation District's 3.24 MW in-conduit system on its Main Canal, Oregon, using Natel turbines; Farmers Conservation Alliance programs), so a private canal-drop lease means negotiating with an informed counterparty that already has preference.
scored.buyer: Utilities and REC buyers through PURPA QF contracts at avoided-cost rates (low in most Western states), plus a handful of small-hydro IPPs. Buyers exist but have little capital and pay thin margins. There is no buyer comparable to a mine developer paying a large markup for a proven site.
scored.ladder: Short ladder. Above canal-drop hydro sit a turbine-equipment line and maybe utility-scale hydro or pumped storage, but those are separate businesses with different discovery dynamics. Total conduit and canal potential is in the hundreds of MW to low GW, a prize of well under $1B in asset value. Nothing points toward a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates. Building and operating bespoke low-head hydro is most of the work and capital, and the sites are already inventoried by Reclamation and NREL with MW estimates and held by informed districts with LOPP preference, so there is no discovery-dominated rung and no cheap right for ML to unlock.
scored.one_line_reason: This repeats the geothermal-in-mines failure: building the plant is harder than finding the drop, returns are about 1.5x on a sub-$1B prize, and federal assessments already publish the site potential.

verified.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
verified.one_line: Option farmland next to substations ML predicts have load headroom; prove with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter; sell powered land to data-center developers. Rescore of powered brownfields with a real purchase discount.
verified.old_fatal_flaw: Proving here is not a cheap discovery event that the landowner then owns. Utility capacity is allocated to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the data first. The study result is non-binding and decays as others queue. Rising tariffs specifically target speculative flippers. And well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen the same public grid data. So the 10^3x step-up needs heavy capital commitment and network upgrades, not an ML-fou
verified.frame: The rung is a farmland option plus a utility large-load study or will-serve letter, sold as 'powered land'. Picking the site from public grid data is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is site control, rezoning, study deposits, and above all committed capacity. Committed capacity needs a signed ESA, collateral and network upgrades, and it goes to whoever commits capital, not to whoever reads the data first. Altus (80 transactions, 2026) finds that committed utility load, not a study result, is the strongest predictor of price. The physical and capital step is not trivial. A capitalised buyer does exist: hyperscalers and developers like QTS, Amazon and Tract.
verified.step_up: Farmland runs about $9.5k-23k/acre (PA average $9,560; NE Wisconsin $23k). Data-center land runs a $28k/acre median in markets with limited committed load, $60k/acre offered for 261 PA acres, about $330k/acre paid by QTS in Salem Twp PA (35x farm value), and a $2.8M/acre median in N. Virginia. Sites within half a mile of a high-voltage substation trade at about 2x sites 2-5 miles away. So the realistic step-up is 3-35x and only arrives with committed capacity; a study alone earns far less. Sources: Altus Group, Fortune, farm press.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $75k-600k plus 6-24 months. Examples: AEP Ohio charges a load study fee of up to $100k per 100 MW plus a deposit and an 8-year minimum term. Xcel Colorado has a $120k study deposit, about $600k upfront in total. EKPC charges $75k plus $1k per MW. Option payments come on top. Proving is expensive, so it passes the relaxed C3. I estimate the base rate that a chosen substation shows usable headroom on a reasonable timeline at about 30-50%. ML over hosting-capacity maps, FERC 715 data and IRPs plausibly lifts that 1.2-1.5x. Earlier work found lookup tables and queue data match ML on grid siting, so 1.5x+ is doubtful.
verified.data: The signal is semi-legible. Utility hosting-capacity maps, FERC Form 715 data, IRPs, queue data and large-load tariff dockets are public and partly structured. Well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen them. Some illegible pieces exist, such as scanned IRP appendices and substation one-lines, but the outcome (available MW) is increasingly published in hosting-capacity fields.
verified.right_bought: Yes, the option is bought from farmers. But owners near substations are now informed and pricing up: a PA farmer rejected $15M at $60k/acre, NE Wisconsin farmland doubled in 3 years, and the 'powered land' rebrand is widespread. The purchase discount is shrinking quickly and is being arbitraged by many players.
verified.buyer: Hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Google), colocation and data-center developers (QTS, Vantage, Aligned), and land platforms (Tract). They are heavily capitalised and paying $60k-330k+/acre for sites with committed capacity.
verified.ladder: Strong ladder: powered land, then entitled and energized land with committed capacity, then powered shell or build-to-suit, then data-center development and operation, then owned on-site generation or PPAs. Tract shows that the land-to-campus path supports a multi-$B company.
verified.fatal_flaw: The proof is not a cheap discovery event the landholder then owns. Value comes from committed utility capacity, which goes to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral (large-load tariffs at 36+ utilities now require study fees, deposits, minimum bills and exit fees designed to screen out speculators). The grid signal is semi-legible and already screened by well-funded incumbents. Farmers near substations are already pricing in the premium, so the ML read does not create the spread.
verified.one_line_reason: There is a real buyer and a big ladder, and relaxed C3 lets an expensive study count. But the step-up requires capital-committed capacity rather than ML discovery, grid data is semi-legible to incumbents, and the farmland purchase discount is eroding fast. Total 14/25.

verifiers.evidence:
BUYER: real and well capitalised. US data-center land purchases were about $6B in H1 2026, up 79% YoY (Avison Young via DCK). Q1 2026 alone was about $3.3B, up 141% (Bisnow). The average deal is 224 acres (Cushman), and Altus verified 80 transactions. So the market is a few hundred deals a year at most.

STEP-UP: well under 10^3 and mostly under 30x.
- Raw farmland is about $6k-23k/acre. DCK puts low-cost markets at about $10k/acre with no power path, rising to "six figures" with infrastructure and utility relationships, so roughly 10x.
- JLL's Holcomb: land goes from $2 to $25 per sq ft once transmission is secured, about 12x, and he calls that step neither easy nor cheap.
- Ambrose: $20k/acre farmland is pitched at $400k/acre once zoned, about 20x.
- QTS Salem Twp paid $330k/acre, 35x PA's $9,560 average. QTS bought directly from 96 families, so the farmers captured that spread, not an intermediary. The site already had transmission and substations serving a gas plant and a nuclear plant.
- Altus: the median is $28k/acre in limited-committed-load markets. Being within half a mile of a substation is worth only about 2x versus 2-5 miles away.
- In NoVA, entitled-unpowered land is about $4M/acre and powered land at least $6M/acre, so power itself adds only about 1.5x where entitlement already exists.

WHAT THE BUYER PAYS FOR is the executed ESA or final interconnection, not a study.
- Plug Power sold its Graham TX project to Stream for $50M up front plus up to $26.5M contingent on the load capacity in the final interconnection agreement (164 MW reference, $6.5M utility deposit). The payment is gated on the final agreement.
- Kidder Mathews: land with an executed ESA trades at many times land with only a queue position. Capacity rights need utility consent to transfer. Minimum bills and exit fees of 12-19 years can exceed the land's value.
- Acres (vendor heuristic): confirmed capacity is worth about $150k-400k per MW.
- No published comp prices a load study or will-serve letter on its own.

CAPITAL AND RISK:
- ERCOT requires a $50k/MW deposit just to start review.
- An LOI that once cost a few hundred thousand dollars now takes hundreds of millions in real capital for a formal power commitment. Utilities ask for investment-grade credit to pass a large-load study.
- Cloverleaf raised $300M (NGP/Sandbrook) and handed its Port Washington site to Vantage at an undisclosed price. Commercial Observer, citing the NYT, says Cloverleaf spent $300M and sold for $200M; I could not confirm that independently. Cloverleaf also abandoned Greenleaf WI.
- About 50% of Texas large-load requests come from wildcatters (400+ GW requested against a ~100 GW grid). Hyperscalers are trying to bypass middlemen, and experts say the wildcatting window is closing.

So a capitalised buyer exists, but the step-up is 10-35x, it arrives only after capital-heavy ESA commitments, and much of it goes to informed farmers or to whoever posts the collateral.
verifiers.killer: The step-up is roughly 10-35x, not 10^3-10^4x. It is paid only for an executed ESA or final interconnection capacity: Plug/Stream's price was contingent on the final interconnection agreement, and Kidder says land with only a queue position is worth many times less. Getting there takes deposits ($50k/MW at ERCOT) and commitments in the hundreds of millions, with minimum-bill liabilities that can exceed the land's value. No comp prices a study or will-serve letter on its own. The cleanest big comp, QTS at 35x, went straight to farmers with no intermediary. The best-funded wildcatter, Cloverleaf ($300M raised), reportedly sold for less than it spent and abandoned another site, so the ML-picked option-plus-study rung has no proven spread.

verifiers.evidence:
DATA LEGIBILITY: The key signal, which is substation offtake (load-serving) headroom, is already pulled out of power-flow models and sold as a ready-made field. LandGate says it has "nationwide proprietary offtake capacity data", "offtake capacity data for every substation in the US", and 98% coverage over more than 84,000 mapped substations, along with substation-level queued projects and modelled upgrade costs. Its transmission engineers build DC and AC models across multi-year scenarios, which is the same FERC 715 / ISO-case work the finalist proposes to do with ML. Enverus Site & Screen sells "parcel-level MW feasibility" plus withdrawal capacity and load-serving ceilings at each substation, across 156M parcels and 43,500 substations. Its April 2026 report maps 272 GW of buildable data-center potential on 136,000 acres. Acres.com sells AI tools to qualify powered land, plus a 2026 site-selection playbook. Ascend Analytics and Cleanview sell headroom and siting analytics. So the outcome sits in a legible field you can buy from a vendor. The only illegible data left is utility-internal and cannot be read by anyone outside the utility.
COMPETITION: Tract controls 20-30k+ acres (8,590 acres in Reno for $65M; 2.1k acres in Buckeye for $136M) and Fleet DC reportedly raised $3.8B of debt in 2026. Scale ($300M from NGP/Sandbrook) bought Reload, a firm that specialises in finding and permitting powered land. Silver Lake and Commonwealth run a $400M powered-land platform. Exowatt launched ExoRise for powered land after a $50M raise. Others in the space: Quinbrook's Rowan (5 GW+ pipeline, $4B+ of debt), CBRE IM, Harworth, and Landpower in the UK (founded 2026). The space is crowded with well-capitalised buyers who already use the same vendor data.
HIT RATE AND PROVING: Proving is expensive ($75k-600k in study fees and deposits, 6-24 months), so it passes the relaxed C3 on cost. But what usually fails is commitment, not discovery. Wood Mackenzie puts requested load at about 1,066 GW, with about 12% firm and about 28% expected to be served. The rest is speculative or duplicate requests that never put up money. ERCOT showed 1.8% of 226 GW operational. Utilities are now demanding upfront financial commitments to screen out exactly this kind of speculation. ML over public grid data can at best match commercial offtake products, so the lift in cost per proven powered site is probably under 1.2x against a competitor who just subscribes to LandGate or Enverus.
VALUE CAPTURE: Farmers near substations already price in the premium (PA $60k/acre offers turned down; NE Wisconsin land doubled). Altus finds committed load drives price. So the spread goes to whoever puts up ESA collateral, not to whoever reads the data. Operating the asset (powered shell or campus) is still a real path, which is why C5 stays strong. But C2 shrinks because there is no information-driven purchase discount.
verifiers.killer: The edge this idea depends on, finding substation load headroom before others do, is already a commercial data product. LandGate sells modelled offtake capacity for every US substation (98% coverage), and Enverus sells parcel-level MW feasibility. Tract, Scale/Reload, Silver Lake/Commonwealth, Exowatt and Rowan all use that data with billions of dollars behind them. The step that actually decides who gets the power, a signed ESA with posted collateral, depends on capital, not on reading data. So ML adds under 1.2x and leaves no purchase discount over informed sellers and buyers.

verifiers.evidence:
The right is legally buyable, and the finalist hits no hard exclusion: there is no drilling and the company owns the option. The frame fails on the proving step, which is a large, forfeitable capital commitment rather than cheap paperwork.

(1) Legal right holds. The Texas PUCT draft large-load rule (16 TAC 25.194, March 2026) accepts "a signed purchase/lease option" as site control, alongside a deed or a lease of 5+ years (Foley). SB 6 requires site control as "ownership, lease, or legal interest" for loads above 75 MW.

(2) The physical/capital step dominates. Before the ERCOT formal study, the same draft requires a $100k-300k study fee plus $50,000/MW of financial security. A 200 MW site therefore needs about $10M posted, as cash, a BBB- or better guaranty, or an A- or better bank LOC. If the project is withdrawn or misses milestones, 80% of the remaining security is forfeited. A full refund requires 5 years of operation at contracted demand. Applicants must also disclose duplicate requests, explicitly to curb speculative line-jumping. The finalist's sources say a September 2026 White & Case alert reports the adopted rule keeps $50k/MW as posted security, with size-tiered study charges on top of a $100k flat fee. I could not open that alert (HTTP 403), so the final rule is unconfirmed. Elsewhere, AEP Ohio requires a minimum bill of 85% of claimed load, which cut its queue from 30 GW to 13 GW. Dominion GS-5 requires 14-year contracts and collateral from January 2027. I&M requires 12+ year terms, exit fees and collateral. FERC show-cause orders (June 2026) push network-upgrade costs onto large loads. Like the bespoke geothermal plant, the capital-at-risk step to make the land "powered" is far bigger and riskier than finding the substation.

(3) A spread exists, but it is old and thin. Claros (Bisnow, pre-SB6) puts power-ready Texas land at about $800k/acre versus $2.5k-10k/acre for unstudied sites. It also notes that only 10-15 Texas sites had completed both scope ($50-100k) and infrastructure ($100-300k, up to $1M) studies, and that operating without secured demand "makes this type of bet extremely risky." Avison Young puts entitled unpowered land in N. Virginia at about $4M/acre versus $6M+ powered, only about a 1.5x premium for power. It also finds 230/500 kV-tied sites trade at about 2.4x sites at 138 kV or below. Both of those signals are legible from public maps.

(4) Owners can read the signal. Landowners now see on-site infrastructure as valuable. Brokers such as Greenwood field about 100 landowner calls a week. A Kentucky family rejected an offer at about 10x local farm value, and a PA farmer rejected $15M. Data-center land spend was $3.3B in Q1 2026, up 141%, and $6B in H1 2026, up 79%. Developers such as Thor Equities already use purchase-option structures on farmland (Urbana OH).

(5) Rezoning risk is outside the ML read. Saline Twp MI denied rezoning of 575 acres, and the developer settled for 250. The C2 spread survives only for a well-capitalised player who posts security and holds the asset. That makes the startup a capital-heavy developer competing with Tract and others, not an ML-discovery rung.

Not covered: my web-search budget ran out (the turn-wide limit was reached) before I could check local moratorium counts and whether study-only or will-serve sites sell at a discount to committed-capacity sites. I also could not confirm the adopted Texas rule text.
verifiers.killer: The option on the land is cheap and legally buyable, but the step that makes land "powered" is not a cheap discovery event. In Texas the draft PUCT rule requires $50k/MW of posted security, with 80% forfeitable, plus an investment-grade guaranty or LOC, before the formal study even runs: about $10M at risk per 200 MW site. Other utilities use minimum bills, 12-14 year contracts and exit fees built specifically to screen out speculators. The capital-at-risk step dominates the ML site read, which is the geothermal failure mode. The landowners and incumbents can also read the substation signal, so ML does not create the purchase discount.

verified.name: Entitlement arbitrage on exurban residential land (ML over planning records)
verified.one_line: Option raw agricultural or exurban parcels at farm value on the Sun Belt growth fringe. ML over scanned planning-commission and council minutes, meeting video transcripts, staff reports, comp plans, sewer and water master plans, CIPs and past rezoning votes predicts which parcels will get utility service, annexation and rezoning. Push entitlements through and sell entitled acreage or finished lots to national homebuilders, who pay the step-up.
verified.unproven_right: Purchase options or contingent contracts on 50-500 acre farm parcels at ag or unentitled value ($5-30k/acre), from farm families, estates and local brokers who do not read utility master plans or council voting patterns.
verified.proving_step: Annexation, rezoning, PUD or preliminary plat approval with utility will-serve letters: engineering, traffic, drainage and environmental studies plus hearings. About $150k-$2M and 1-4 years per project, base approval roughly 40-65%. ML trained on thousands of hearing outcomes and staff-report language plausibly lifts hit rate 1.5-2x and drops doomed options before deposits go hard.
verified.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, NVR, Toll) running land-light strategies through land bankers (Millrose, Varde), paying cash for entitled land and finished lots.
verified.public_data: Scanned and PDF city and county planning-commission and council agendas, minutes and staff reports (Granicus/Legistar archives, YouTube video), municipal Capital Improvement Plans, sewer and water master-plan PDFs, annexation agreements, comprehensive and future land-use plans, past rezoning case files and votes, county GIS parcel, zoning, assessor and deed records. Approval odds are in no legible field.
verified.rough_step_up: Raw land at $10-30k/acre becomes $80-300k/acre entitled (3-10x on land); about 3-8x on cash at risk with an option structure. Multi-$B prize (US homebuilders buy $50B+ of land a year). Ladder: horizontal development, build-for-rent or vertical homebuilding, master-planned community operator.
verified.frame: The rung is clear and sellable: an entitled parcel or finished lots, sold to a homebuilder or land banker. But discovery is not 80%+ of the work. Finding a parcel in the path of sewer and water is maybe 25-40% of the work. The rest is the entitlement campaign itself: engineering, traffic, drainage and environmental studies, negotiating with staff, managing neighbors, hearings and offsite utility commitments. That is a 1-4 year political and engineering job, the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: doing the proving step is harder than picking the site.
verified.step_up: Entitled land sells for about 2-4x equivalent raw land (acres.com), or about 2x (allieddev). The candidate's 3-10x figure is optimistic for the US Sun Belt; the 22x UK green-belt figure comes from a much more restrictive planning system. Realtor.com/MortgagePoint: raw-land price per acre fell 2.4% YoY into 2026 against 1.1% for build-ready land, so the spread is real but modest. With an option structure the return on cash at risk might be 3-5x on winners, but entitlement spend of $150k-$2M per project plus carry, spread across the failures, pulls the blended return on total capital toward about 2-3x. The prize is multi-$B: builders buy tens of $B of land a year, and Millrose alone took 24,000 homesites from Rausch Coleman for about $900M.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs about $150k-$2M and takes 1-4 years, so the expensive-proving leg is met. The base rate is moderate: projects that reach a hearing are usually approved, because staff negotiate them first, while early-stage parcel picks fail more often (the candidate's own 40-65%, no hard source found). Staff recommendations and the comp plan's future land-use map already predict outcomes well. The only ML precedent I found is a Frederick County MD logit study, which found rezonings largely follow the ordinance and staff. So ML's realistic gain on cost per entitled parcel is about 1.2-1.5x from dropping doomed options early, not 2x+.
verified.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned minutes, meeting video, CIP and master-plan PDFs. But many cities now publish searchable Legistar/Granicus records, and staff reports carry a legible approve/deny recommendation that summarises much of the outcome. Comp-plan future land-use maps and sewer service-area boundaries are often already GIS layers. ReZone AI (now part of Shovels) already extracts rezoning decisions from US council and planning minutes, so the extraction edge is being commoditised.
verified.right_bought: The right is bought via options or contingent contracts, as Dhruv's rubric requires. But Sun Belt fringe farmland is an informed market. Builder land-acquisition teams, land brokers, land bankers and local entitlement developers all read the utility master plans. Fringe sellers routinely ask hope-value prices well above ag value; WSJ/Land.com: Sun Belt vacant land per acre more than doubled in two years through Q2 2022. Sellers who truly cannot read the plans exist, but at the margin, not at scale.
verified.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and active: public homebuilders (D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte, NVR, Toll) and land bankers such as Millrose, which earned $185M of option fees in Q1 2026 and went from 11 to 18 third-party partners. Millrose describes its assets as having 'limited entitlement and development risk', which confirms that buyers pay up for entitled land and avoid raw-land risk.
verified.ladder: The ladder above is strong: entitlement, then horizontal development and finished lots, then build-for-rent or vertical homebuilding, then master-planned community operator (Howard Hughes, Forestar-style). The chain is very large, but every rung is crowded with well-capitalised incumbents.
verified.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Entitlement is a political and engineering campaign of 1-4 years and $150k-$2M per project. It runs in an informed, competitive land market: builder land teams, brokers and land bankers already read the master plans, and fringe sellers price in hope value. The approval signal is also largely legible already, in staff recommendations and future land-use maps. So ML neither makes discovery 80% of the rung nor buys the land at a deep discount to its proven value.
verified.one_line_reason: The buyer, ladder and prize are real, but the rung is an execution-heavy entitlement campaign in a market of informed bidders, so ML-led discovery gives only a modest ~1.2-1.5x edge, not a Terranox-style frame.

verifiers.evidence:
The web search budget was used up after my first call (200-search cap shared across the workflow). So this rests on fetches of the finalist's own sources plus arithmetic from known figures.

(1) acres.com says entitled land sells for 'two to four times' raw land in the same market. That is a 2-4x step-up, against a lens threshold of about 30x. The figure is credited to Land Partner Group, but that source is not shown on the page.

(2) Realtor.com via MortgagePoint: raw-land median price per acre is up 86.5% since 2019, against 53.3% for build-ready lots. Year over year, raw land fell 2.4% and build-ready lots fell 1.1%. Raw land is appreciating faster than build-ready land, so the raw-to-entitled spread is narrowing. Sellers are pricing in hope value.

(3) The allieddev page cited for '~2x' contains no uplift figures; its only timeline is a testimonial describing an 8-month process.

(4) The Millrose/Rausch Coleman deal was about $900M for about 24,000 homesites, roughly $37.5k per homesite (the press release returned 403, so the figure comes from the finalist's summary). Sun Belt fringe raw land at $10-30k/acre with 3-5 lots per acre works out to about $2-10k of raw land per lot. Much of the gap to $37.5k is horizontal development cost (typically $40-80k+ per finished lot, so many of these homesites must be partly finished or entitled-only), not entitlement value.

The gross land step-up at proof is therefore about 2-5x, and the candidate's own optimistic figure is 3-10x. That is two to three orders of magnitude below 10^3-10^4 and well under the 30x refute line.

The buyer is real and capitalised. Public builders and land bankers (Millrose: $185M of option fees in Q1 2026, 18 partners) buy tens of $B of land a year, so transaction volume is high: many thousands of parcel deals a year across Sun Belt markets.

Under round-6 C2 (value capture by operating), a blended 2-3x on total capital after failed entitlements and $150k-$2M of studies per project gives C2 about 2.5. The spread is thin because fringe sellers already price in hope value, so the asset is not bought cheaply relative to its proven value.
verifiers.killer: The step-up at proof is about 2-4x (acres.com), not 10^3-10^4x. Raw fringe land prices are rising faster than build-ready land (Realtor.com: +86.5% vs +53.3% since 2019), so sellers already capture much of the entitlement option value. verified.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)

It is political and legal work (hearings, organising against opponents, lawsuits) and, above all, proving power through utility will-serve letters and interconnection, which planning records cannot show. The rung does have capitalised buyers (hyperscalers and developers such as Tract, QTS and Vantage). Developer offers on likely data center sites: $35k/acre in Mason County KY (2025), about $60k/acre in Lancaster PA (2026), and $26M for a Kentucky farm, about 10x farm value. Sources: Fortune Feb 2026, TweakTown, Dairy News Today.
verified.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not sourced: each rezoning or special-exception attempt costs roughly $100k-$500k (legal, engineering, traffic and noise studies, option fees) and takes 6-18 months, so the proving step is expensive enough to qualify. Base approval rate was an estimated ~60-80% for rezonings and special-use permits, but it is falling. Data Center Watch counts about $64B of projects blocked or delayed in the two years to March 2025, $98B in Q2 2025 alone, and at least $152-156B (48+ projects) in 2025. Hundreds of opposition groups were active in 42 states. Saline Township MI denied a 575-acre rezoning. If approval falls toward ~50%, ML that reads meeting minutes and opposition signals plausibly gives about 1.3-1.6x on cost per entitled parcel. That is close to full strength under the relaxed C3, but it is capped because power is the real gate.
verified.data: Planning commission minutes, hearing videos and transcripts, comprehensive plans, overlay districts and public comment records are public, illegible and scattered across about 3,000 counties. That is genuinely hard data that incumbents extract only by hand or through brokers. The outcome is not pre-written in a status field before the vote. Legibility is falling, though: Data Center Watch and others already track opposition with LLMs, and the power signal (utility IRPs, interconnection queues) is the main driver and is already semi-legible.
verified.right_bought: The right is bought: options are taken on private farmland, not claimed first-come. But sellers can now read the opportunity. Nationwide press coverage of $35k-60k/acre offers means farmers ask for data center premiums before any rezoning, and land trusts compete (Lancaster Farmland Trust bought development rights). The cheap-buy spread is mostly gone in hot counties and survives only in counties nobody is watching yet, where power is often missing.
verified.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) and developers or REITs (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, Tract, CyrusOne) have large budgets for sites. They pay most for land that is both powered and entitled.
verified.ladder: Option, then entitled parcel, then powered land (substation and interconnection), then powered shell, then a built and leased data center campus, then operator or REIT, possibly with self-generated power. The ladder runs to a very large company: Tract-like land banking leads to QTS-scale operators. Each rung above entitlement needs large capital and power access, which the ML edge does not supply.
verified.fatal_flaw: What makes the land valuable is power availability, not zoning. Planning records cannot prove power, and the zoning premium is already widely known: farmers are offered $35k-60k/acre before rezoning, and Tract and brokers run this playbook. So the ML-led proof of approval leaves little spread between the purchase price and the proven price.
verified.one_line_reason: The ladder is real and well funded, and ML on illegible minutes can lift approval odds about 1.3-1.5x on an expensive step. But power, not zoning, drives the 5-10x premium, and sellers already know it, so there is little cheap-buy spread to capture.

verifiers.evidence:
The search budget ran out after 4 web searches (a shared limit), so the rest of this rests on 4 page fetches. Real transaction prices put the step-up at about 3-11x, roughly 10^0.5 to 10^1. That is well under the lens's ~30x threshold and nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
(1) Loudoun, Twin Creeks. JK Land Holdings (Chuck Kuhn) paid $57M, mostly in 2021, and sold 97 acres to SDC Capital Partners in Nov 2025 for $615M ($6M/acre). That is about 10.8x gross over about 4 years. The land was approved for five data centers, and a 13.3-acre substation parcel was sold to Dominion for $45M, so power was part of the value. This is the best case, and it took years plus power work. It was not an instant jump at proof.
(2) Prince William County. Data center land rose from $266k/acre (Digital Realty, 2018) to $903k/acre (AWS, 2021), about 3.4x across different parcels. Overlay-district land sold for $441-711k/acre in 2020.
(3) Digital Gateway, Pageland Lane. One home-site parcel was assessed at about $2.6k/acre. QTS and Compass contracted directly with landowners at about $1M/acre, contingent on rezoning. The 4-3 rezoning passed, but a court voided it in Aug 2025 for improper notice, the Court of Appeals upheld that, and the project is dead. So the largest headline step-up was never paid. The buyer went straight to the owners, so the owners, not a middleman, would have captured the premium. It also shows that approval, the 'proof', can be reversed.
(4) Monroe County GA. Google paid $42.5M for 948 acres (about $45k/acre) after a Nov 2024 C-1 rezoning. Against rural Georgia farmland, my estimate of $4-8k/acre gives about 6-10x.
(5) Tonopah AZ, May 2026. Arizona Land Consulting paid $25M for 956 acres (about $26k/acre) before any rezoning or utility deals. An incumbent entitler is already paying speculative prices for unentitled land, which shrinks the cheap-buy spread.
The buyers are real: hyperscalers and data center investors such as AWS, Microsoft, Google, SDC, QTS and Compass. But they typically contract with landowners directly, contingent on rezoning, and they pay most for power. There are perhaps dozens of large deals a year in the US, a multi-$B market. Under the relaxed round-6 C2, a Kuhn-style ~10x over 4 years can be done, but only where power exists and incumbents already compete. In unwatched counties without power, the realistic return is under ~2-5x after option, legal and political costs and the risk that approval is reversed. C2 is cut to 2.
verifiers.killer: The proven step-up is about 3-11x, not 10^3-10^4, and it builds up over years of entitlement plus power work rather than arriving at once. Capitalised buyers (QTS, Compass, Google, AWS) contract directly with farmers on rezoning-contingent terms, so the owner captures the premium, not an intermediary entitler. The largest example, Digital Gateway at $1M/acre, was voided in court after approval and never paid out.
