verified.name: UK land promotion / grey-belt freehold (hunt 9)
verified.one_line: Buy or option edge-of-settlement farmland, win outline consent, sell to housebuilders or build.
verified.old_fatal_flaw: Hope value priced in; LandTech scores grey belt; promoter keeps 5-25%.
verified.frame: The rung is strategic land promotion: option or buy a field and win outline consent, without building anything. This rung is discrete and sellable, and housebuilders are capitalised buyers. But "discovery" (picking the right site) is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is the proving step itself: a contested planning, legal and political process of local-plan representations, technical reports, committee and appeal. That step is hard and is not abstracted away.
verified.step_up: Bare farmland is about £10k/acre. With detailed consent it reaches about £500k/acre, and up to £1m/acre in the south of England (£600k/acre in the north), per Farmers Weekly. A York benchmark paper (June 2025) cites a Leeds residential site at £523k/ha. That is a raw ~50-100x, but edge-of-settlement and grey-belt land already trades or options at hope value (often £25-100k/acre, or a 75-90% share of proceeds to the landowner). Under a promotion agreement the promoter keeps about 10-15% (one promoter says 10-15%; a law-firm case study says about 15% of net proceeds). Realistic return on promotion capital is a few-x, not 10^3-10^4.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs roughly £100k to £1m+ of planning, technical-report and appeal costs, and takes 3-7 years. Sources: law-firm guidance (planning costs run to tens of thousands of pounds or more; the promoter is not reimbursed if consent fails) and an appeal case study (often several years). Base rate: a 2018 CPRE briefing found 54% of promoter-led appeals allowed, against about 28% for housing appeals generally. That puts the base rate inside the relaxed 30-70% band. ML's lift on picking sites is plausibly 1.2-1.5x, because outcomes depend on politics, the 5-year housing land supply position and the planning inspector, which data predicts only partly.
verified.data: The data is public and semi-illegible: planning portals, appeal decisions, SHLAA/HELAA assessments, local-plan evidence bases, Green Belt reviews and committee minutes, scattered across more than 300 local authorities as PDFs. But LandTech, Searchland and Nimbus already extract it and score grey-belt sites. The key outcome signals (HELAA suitability ratings, plan allocations, 5YHLS status) are written into legible fields, which is the regulator-writes-the-answer problem.
verified.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. Options and promotion agreements are negotiated with farmers. But landowners are usually advised by land agents who know about hope value and grey belt, so the purchase discount relative to proven value is limited.
verified.buyer: Volume housebuilders such as Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey and Vistry, plus regional builders and registered providers. They are deep-pocketed and buy consented land routinely.
verified.ladder: The ladder is strong: promotion, then land servicing and infrastructure, then housebuilding (the UK volume builders are £3-6B companies), then build-to-rent and other operated assets. A path to a large company is real, though it is a UK-only prize.
verified.fatal_flaw: It is an informed, competitive market. Hope value is already priced in by agents and established promoters (Gladman, Catesby, Richborough), and grey-belt scoring is already sold by LandTech and Searchland. The proving step is a political and legal process, not a hidden-data discovery. So ML adds only a marginal hit-rate edge and does not create a spread that informed buyers miss.
verified.one_line_reason: Real capitalised buyers and a large ladder, but site discovery is a minority of the work, hope value is already priced, data incumbents already score grey belt, and ML's lift on consent odds is about 1.2-1.5x at best.

verifiers.evidence: REAL PRICES. Unproven right: farmland sells for about £9,366/acre (£23k/ha), ranging £6.8-17.1k/acre (Harborough land market review). Hope-value land on an edge-of-village field is about £25k/acre (Savills 'In plain English: hope value'). Proven right: with permission, land reaches about £200k/acre (Savills). Large greenfield consented sites have agreed threshold land values of £135-170k/acre, and the review's sample of transacted sites averaged £274k/acre, ranging £82-424k/acre (Harborough). Knight Frank (2024) gives about £200k per GROSS acre against an existing-use value of £10k/acre, so roughly 20x, and calls that the MINIMUM for promotion to work. Higher figures (£500k-£2m/acre, or £1m/acre in the south per Farmers Weekly) are per net acre or for detailed consent and top locations. They are not what a promoter sells an outline-consent gross acre for. STEP-UP: about 15-30x from farmland value and about 5-10x from the hope-value price an informed seller actually asks. That is one to two orders of magnitude below the 10^3-10^4 claim, and below this lens's ~30x refutation line. COST OF PROVING: Knight Frank says promotion rarely costs under £25k per gross acre and often reaches £40k per gross acre. That is more than the farmland is worth, so the physical/legal proving step dominates and discovery does not. VALUE CAPTURE: the promoter takes only about 10-20% of net proceeds once costs are reimbursed. A law-firm case study says about 15%, and Savills via a West Oxfordshire CIL document says promoters expect 10-20% of land value. Knight Frank says promoters need about 5x on promotion spend to justify the risk. Its new-settlement case study planned 5x and realised 1.3x: costs rose from £7.5m to £12m over 14 years. BUYER: real, capitalised and immediate. Volume housebuilders buy consented sites on the open market at the consent date, and options are priced at market value less a discount. MARKET SIZE: promoters secure 41% of homes on 100+ unit sites outside London (Lichfields/LPDF). But the largest promoter, Gladman (Barratt-owned), consented about 2,760 plots on 15 sites in FY21 (£6.9m pre-tax profit) and made £44.4m turnover / £14.3m pre-tax profit in the 15 months to June 2023. That suggests about 15-20 large-site sales a year for a market leader and a UK promoter fee pool in the low hundreds of £m a year. Hope value is already priced: landowners are actively soliciting grey-belt promotion bids (e.g. a Cheltenham Landsale listing), and options carry minimum prices per gross acre.
verifiers.killer: The real step-up from farmland to outline consent is about 20x per gross acre (Knight Frank: about £200k against a £10k existing-use value), not 10^3-10^4. Measured from the hope-value price informed landowners already demand, it is only 5-10x. The promoter keeps just 10-20% of net proceeds. Proving costs £25-40k per gross acre, more than the farmland itself, and the promoter target of 5x has been realised as low as 1.3x. The buyer is real, but the spread is thin, competed for, and created by planning and legal process rather than hidden data.

verifiers.evidence:
1) The outcome drivers are legible fields, and a vendor already scores them. LandTech's Grey Belt Favourability score is built from two inputs. The first is how a parcel contributes to Green Belt purposes (a), (b) and (d), taken from council Green Belt reviews, plus a check on whether the developable area is under 0.1ha. The second is a presumption-in-favour estimate for each local authority, computed from its Housing Land Supply, its Housing Delivery Test score and the adoption date of its latest local plan. Users can filter site sourcing by this score (support.land.tech article 9915221). LandInsight also ranks sites on existing use, agricultural land classification, affordability and connectivity. Those are the same variables a new ML entrant would rely on, so the "regulator writes the answer" problem holds.
2) The base hit rate is already high from a lookup alone, which caps any ML lever. Marrons/LPDF data to 28 Feb 2026: 50% of 224 grey belt appeals were allowed, and 18 of 24 major residential appeals (about 75%). The August 2025 cut showed 57% overall and 80% for major residential. CPRE's December 2025 analysis found 13 of 15 qualifying major housing appeals allowed (86%). With the policy filter alone at 75-86%, the maximum possible lift is about 1.15-1.33x, which is below the 1.5x full-strength threshold. Green belt appeals generally rose from about 25% to 33% in 2025.
3) A direct ML entrant has already tried this and failed. Tract (London; pre-seed £744k in April 2024 plus a round co-led by Ada Ventures and Concept Ventures in September 2024) built a planning engine to find sites and predict outcomes from past applications. It tested Tract Source, Attract, Editor and also "tech-enabled land promotion" itself. It shut in March 2025 with no meaningful revenue and returned the remaining capital. Its founders cited the market's low willingness to pay and fragmentation, as well as their own mistakes.
4) The space is crowded. Data vendors include LandTech, Searchland (an AI Land Sourcing Assistant), Nimbus Maps and Urban Intelligence (ML appraisal of every parcel in Birmingham). Established promoters include Gladman, Catesby, Richborough and the LPDF members. Councils such as Chorley report an "unprecedented number" of speculative green belt applications, so landowners in grey belt areas are already being courted.
5) The proving step is genuinely expensive: £100k to £1m+ and 3-7 years per site. That part of C3 survives. But value capture is compressed. The promoter's share is about 10-15% of net proceeds. The Golden Rules (50% affordable housing on released green belt, benchmark land values) and the December 2025 NPPF draft's tighter land value capture cap the spread on exactly the grey belt sites the ML would pick.

verifiers.evidence:
Exclusions: none apply. There is no drilling or prospecting. The company holds the option or freehold itself, so it is not selling a service.

1. The right can be bought, legally and at scale, but the standard contracts tie its price to the proven value. A cheap unproven right does not exist here.
   - Promotion agreements: the promoter's share is typically 5-20% and the landowner keeps the rest (Farrer and other landowner law-firm guides). These agreements usually add a minimum land price the landowner can veto on, plus caps on promotion costs (HCR Law, Lodders).
   - Option agreements: the price is set at market value at the time of exercise, less a 10-30% discount (Law Society of Scotland journal; Savills says a percentage discount off market value at exercise). Landowners can also demand a floor price per net developable acre. So the buyer captures only a 10-30% spread, which is fixed by contract, not by better information.
   - Outright purchase of edge-of-settlement farmland: sellers routinely attach overage clauses, which give the seller a share of any later uplift in land value from planning consent. Overage now appears in more than 25% of land transactions. A typical clause takes about 25% of the uplift for 10-30 years, and Strutt & Parker says buyers resist anything over 35%. It is "normally used where land is adjacent or close to a built-up area" (Strutt & Parker; Farmers Weekly).
   - So in all three structures the "owner who cannot read the data" is contractually protected against exactly the uplift that ML would find.

2. Owners are not data-blind. Richborough sends Green Belt / Grey Belt brochures to landowners. Turley has published a 'Grey Belt Assessment for Land Promotion'. Bidwells and LRG publish NPPF December 2025 guidance aimed at landowners. LandTech and Searchland score grey-belt sites. Agents advise farmers on hope value, which is the price premium for possible future planning consent.

3. Is the proving step trivial? No, but it is not physical either. It is a contested planning, legal and political process that costs £100k-£1m+ and takes 3-7 years. This is unlike the bespoke geothermal plant, because nothing is built inside the rung. But discovery is still a minority of the work, so C1 fails the 80% test and drops to 2.

4. Base rates are too high for a large ML lift.
   - Grey-belt appeals from December 2024 to August 2025: 57% allowed overall (74 of 129) and about 55% for residential. Major schemes of 10 or more homes were allowed at 80% (16 of 20) (Marrons and LPDF analysis, via HBD Online).
   - At an 80% base rate, the theoretical maximum lift is 1.25x. At 57% it is 1.75x. A realistic ML lift is 1.1-1.3x, so C3 = 2.

5. Policy also squeezes the value captured. The golden rules require 15 points of extra affordable housing on top of existing policy, capped at 50%. The December 2025 NPPF draft tightens controls on land value capture. Barratt pulled four applications over viability under the earlier 50% proposal (Building; Lichfields; Bidwells).

6. Economics of the best-in-class operator. For the three years to March 2019, Gladman averaged £52.5m in sales and £18.9m profit before tax, consenting about 4,230 plots a year. For the year to March 2021 it made £6.9m profit before tax on £212m of gross assets. Barratt bought it for £250m.
   - That is roughly 3-9% a year on gross assets, which is a good business but not 5x on capital.
   - The promotion rung's prize is hundreds of £m. Multi-£B value only comes from housebuilding.
   - C2 = 2.

7. Ladder: real, as before. It runs promotion, then land servicing and infrastructure, then housebuilding (the UK volume builders are £3-6B companies), then build-to-rent. C5 = 4.

verified.name: Senior surface water right change-of-use decrees (Colorado and Western prior appropriation)
verified.one_line: Buy senior agricultural surface-water rights and ditch shares at ag prices, use ML over scanned diversion records, ditch-company ledgers, past decrees and Landsat ET to predict which rights keep the most transferable consumptive-use yield, win a water-court change-of-use decree, then sell or lease the firm municipal yield. Front Range and Utah cities (and data-center or fab developers) pay the step-up. Surface rights only, no groundwater or drilling.
verified.unproven_right: Senior direct-flow rights and mutual ditch company shares (South Platte, Arkansas and Colorado River basins), bought at about $5-15k per acre-foot of raw entitlement from farmers and estates who cannot reconstruct their own 50-year diversion history or know their transferable yield
verified.proving_step: A change-of-use case in Colorado water court (or state-engineer transfer in NM/UT): historic consumptive-use engineering, return-flow modelling, opposer settlements and dry-up covenants. Costs $150k-$3M and takes 2-7 years. Yield haircuts of 20-70% are common. ML predicting decreed yield per share plausibly gives 1.5-2x more decreed acre-feet per dollar.
verified.proven_buyer: Municipal water providers (Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Parker, Denver Water, St. George area and Utah districts), homebuilders needing water for new development, data-center and semiconductor developers, and water investment funds, paying about $30-80k+ per acre-foot of firm decreed municipal yield
verified.public_data: Colorado CDSS/HydroBase diversion records (decades of handwritten and scanned ditch-rider logs and water commissioner field books), historical water court decrees, resumes and case files with prior change-case engineering reports, ditch company bylaws, minutes and share ledgers, Landsat ET history 1984+ and historic aerial irrigation imagery, NRCS soils. Transferable consumptive use is never a legible field and has to be reconstructed case by case.
verified.rough_step_up: Ag $5-15k/AF becomes decreed municipal yield at $30-80k+/AF, about 3-6x on total capital after the yield haircut and legal costs. A single 2,000 AF portfolio is worth about $100M; the prize is multi-$B across western states. Ladder: storage (gravel-pit reservoirs), augmentation plans and conveyance, then a wholesale water utility.
verified.frame: The rung is owning ag ditch shares and getting a water-court change-of-use decree. Rebuilding historic consumptive use (HCU) from records is maybe 40-50% of that work. The rest is the physical and legal step, which is not trivial: opposer litigation and settlements, return-flow replacement and augmentation, dry-up covenants and revegetation. Under the anti-speculation doctrine, extended to change cases in High Plains A&M v. Southeastern (Colo. 2005, 120 P.3d 710), you also need a named end user before the court will decree. So the buyer often has to be locked in before you can prove the asset. A capitalised buyer exists (Front Range cities, homebuilders, funds), but discovery is well under 80% of the rung.
verified.step_up: Proven (decreed municipal) side: Colorado-Big Thompson (C-BT) water, the most liquid Front Range benchmark, traded at about $85k/AF in 2025, down from $101k/AF in 2022 (WestWater, reported by the Colorado Sun in 2026). A 2024 Northern Water auction averaged about $74.6k/AF. Unproven (raw ag) side: the candidate's own figure is $5-15k/AF of raw entitlement. A Box Elder Ditch valuation put HCU credit at about $4.8-5.2k/AF in the 2000s. In 2003 Greeley offered $6k/AF, about twice the going ag rate, and still found no sellers. After a 20-70% yield haircut, $150k-$3M in legal and engineering costs, and 2-7 years of carry, the realistic return is about 2-3x on capital. That is a step-up of a few times, not 10^3. The gap is mostly the known cost and risk of the change case, and informed buyers already price that in.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost: $150k-$3M and 2-7 years per change case, using the candidate's figures; I could not find a sourced total, but this range matches practitioner experience. Base rate: most change cases do end in a decree, but with yield haircuts. The 'hit' is decreed acre-feet per dollar, not decree versus no decree. ML that ranks shares by likely decreed HCU before purchase could plausibly give 1.2-1.5x. It could reach 1.5x where ditches have had no prior change case. However, experienced buyers' engineers already run HCU screens on HydroBase before buying, so the claimed 1.5-2x is optimistic.
verified.data: This partly fails the rule that the outcome must not already be summarised in a legible field. CDSS/HydroBase diversion records are largely digitised as structured daily and annual series. For any ditch that has already had a change case, the per-share HCU is written into the decree; a 2009 Colorado Springs Chilcott Ditch filing, for example, quantified 24.61 AF/share. The market prices ditch shares off those numbers. The illegible edge (scanned ditch-rider logs, ledgers, historic aerial imagery and Landsat ET) is real only for ditches that have never been through a change case. Those are also the ones with the most opposer risk.

Caveat: this turn's shared web-search budget was already used up, so no new searches ran. Several fetches also failed: CDSS StateCU returned 403 and the Colorado Sun returned 429. The findings below rest on the two pages I could fetch, the sources the finalist cited, and background knowledge that I could not re-verify this turn.

(1) The outcome is legible, and a data vendor already sells it. WestWater Research's own site lists transaction advisory ('buy, sell, or manage complex water assets'), valuation and appraisals, asset management, and a proprietary transaction-price database (Waterlitix), plus exclusive data supply for the Nasdaq-Veles water index. The price spread between ag and municipal water is therefore already sold to buyers. It is not hidden.

(2) The state already reconstructs historic consumptive use (HCU). Colorado's CDSS runs StateCU and StateMod models that estimate consumptive use for each structure. It also publishes irrigated-acreage GIS snapshots for most basins, at roughly 5-10 year intervals from the 1950s to 2020. HydroBase holds diversion records as structured daily and annual series (background knowledge; fetch blocked). OpenET now gives free field-level ET from Landsat across the West. The 'illegible scanned ditch-rider logs' therefore add little beyond what is already modelled and released. On top of that, any ditch that has had a prior change case has its per-share HCU written into the decree (e.g. Chilcott Ditch, 24.61 AF/share, 09SA178).

(3) The space is occupied. Change-case engineering firms (Leonard Rice, Wilson Water Group, Martin & Wood and others) run HCU screens on HydroBase/StateCU before purchase. Municipal buyers (Aurora, Thornton, Greeley, Castle Rock) have in-house water acquisition teams. Brokers like WestWater are active. Investor buyers already exist: the 2020 Colorado legislative work group (SB20-048) was formed in response to 'investment group purchases of farmland and their senior water rights on the West Slope and in the San Luis Valley' (coyotegulch, Nov 2020). Known players include Water Asset Management (West Slope farmland), Pure Cycle/Rangeview, the former Two Rivers Water & Farming (which struggled and collapsed), and Vidler.

(4) The anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains A&M v. Southeastern, 2005) requires a named end user, so the asset cannot be proven on spec.

(5) The proving step is expensive ($150k-$3M, 2-7 years), and the yield is uncertain at the margin. But decree-versus-no-decree success is high, and the cost per decreed acre-foot is mostly legal and dry-up work that ML cannot shrink. The realistic ML lever is about 1.1-1.3x, not 1.5-2x.

(6) Value capture: C-BT traded at about $85k/AF in 2025, against an ag entry of $5-15k/AF. After haircuts, legal costs and carry, the return is about 2-3x. That spread is already competed for by informed buyers.
verifiers.killer: The supposed ML edge, reconstructing transferable consumptive use from illegible records, is already done in legible form. The state's CDSS StateCU/StateMod models estimate consumptive use for each structure, it publishes irrigated-acreage GIS, and OpenET gives free field-level ET. Prior change decrees state per-share HCU outright. WestWater's Waterlitix sells transaction prices. Specialist engineering firms, municipal acquisition teams, brokers and investor buyers (Water Asset Management, Pure Cycle, earlier Two Rivers) already work this brokered market. So the ag-to-municipal spread mostly reflects the known legal cost and dry-up risk of the change case, which ML does not reduce. The anti-speculation doctrine also blocks proving on spec.

verifiers.evidence:
Search budget note: the shared web-search budget was used up after the round started, so this verification relies on direct fetches of the finalist's own cited sources plus text extracted from the Colorado Supreme Court opinion. No new independent searches were run.

1) The right cannot be proven on spec. The opinion is High Plains A&M v. Southeastern Colo. Water Conservancy Dist., 120 P.3d 710 (Colo. 2005), 04SA266/267, text extracted from the coloradojudicial.gov PDF. Key passages:
- "the change applicant must show a legally vested interest in the land to be served by the change of use and a specific plan and intent to use the water for specific purposes."
- The applicant satisfies this only if it "is a governmental agency, or a person who will use the changed water right for his or her own lands or business or has an agreement to provide water to a public entity and/or private lands or businesses."
- High Plains argued it "cannot enter into contracts with end users until it has court approval." The court said this "reverses the well-established methodology" and upheld dismissal.

High Plains had bought about 30% of the Fort Lyon Canal shares and proposed more than 50 possible uses across 28 counties. Its investment was stranded (Coyote Gulch/SB20-048 article; Quimbee). The decree is the 'proof' in this rung. Because it needs a contracted buyer first, the price is negotiated before proof with a sophisticated municipal counterparty who prices in haircut risk. The Terranox pattern (buy blind, prove, sell at proven value) is legally barred in Colorado.

2) Sellers are not blind, and the core market is benchmarked. Northern Colorado C-BT trades at about $60k per unit, roughly $85k/AF (CREJ). "Many high-value ditch company shares also are priced relative to CBT units" (CREJ). Buyers are mostly municipal providers using developer cash-in-lieu. Investor buy-and-dry on the West Slope and in the San Luis Valley is already a political target: SB20-048 created an 18-member speculation work group (Coyote Gulch 2020). Cheap rights exist mainly in remote basins, where conveyance and transbasin politics bind.

3) The physical and legal step dominates the rung. The work is opposer litigation, return-flow replacement (often needing storage or augmentation infrastructure), dry-up covenants and revegetation, plus 2-7 years and $150k-$3M per case, using the finalist's own figures. Reconstructing historic consumptive use from records is perhaps 40-50% of the work. This is not drilling-trivial, though it is less bespoke than a geothermal plant.

4) Hard exclusions: not hit. These are surface rights with no groundwater drilling, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service. It is adjacent to the groundwater exclusion only in spirit.

Revised scores:
- C1 = 2: a capitalised buyer exists, but proof cannot occur before the buyer is locked in, and discovery is well under 80% of the work.
- C2 = 2: about a 2-3x transaction-cost spread, compressed by pre-proof contracting.
- C3 = 3: proving is expensive, but the ML lever is about 1.2-1.5x, since buyers' engineers already screen HydroBase.
- C4 = 2: prior change decrees publish per-share consumptive use, and sellers are informed.
- C5 = 3: storage, augmentation and a utility (the Pure Cycle precedent) make a regional-scale ladder.
verifiers.killer: Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine, applied to change cases in High Plains A&M (Colo. 2005), requires the applicant to have its own use or a contract with an end user before a change decree can issue. The court explicitly rejected the argument that an investor "cannot enter into contracts with end users until it has court approval." So you cannot buy ag shares cheaply, prove them, and then sell at proven value. The buyer must be signed before proof, at a price an informed municipal buyer sets with the haircut risk priced in. The ditch-share market is already benchmarked to C-BT at about $85k/AF and politically hostile to investor buy-and-dry. The legal and physical change-case work (opposers, return flows, dry-up, augmentation) dominates the rung.

Unlike a drill hit, the manufacturing step is neither trivial nor abstracted. A buyer with capital exists (DLA, the services, and roll-ups like TransDigm), but what they buy is a running, cash-flowing production line, not a proven right sitting there to be picked up.

DLA Competition Advocates exist to break sole-source pricing: a SAR is by definition a request to become an additional source, and a 2014 DLA slide (possibly no longer current) says a new source can get 40% of an award even when it is not the lowest bidder. Award history, prices and AMSC/AMC codes are already legible in DIBBS and FPDS, and incumbents and brokers already mine them. verified.data: The signal is partly illegible: scanned TDPs, SAR rejection narratives, PACER and UCC liquidation records. But the outcome is largely written into legible fields. DIBBS award history, unit prices, AMSC codes (which flag sole-source or restricted status) and the approved-source CAGE lists already show which NSNs are sole-source and how often they are bought. That is the regulator-writes-the-answer problem the rubric warns about. On the right: assets of shuttered shops do sell cheaply at auction and from estates. But the buyer often does not get an ownable right. A build-to-print shop's drawings usually belong to the OEM or the government, approved-source status is tied to the CAGE code and facility and may not survive an asset sale, and the government can compete the NSN anyway. The right is weak and not exclusive.
verified.right_bought: Tooling, inventory, legacy drawings and part-number history of a closed or exiting small defense supplier, bought in liquidation for ~$100k-2M. Legal title to the technical data and transfer of approved-source status are uncertain.
verified.buyer: DLA Land and Maritime, Aviation and Troop Support; the services' sustainment commands; primes buying under IDIQs. Exit buyer: aftermarket roll-ups at 15-20x EBITDA (TransDigm, and private-equity defense aftermarket platforms).
verified.ladder: There is a strong ladder: single part lines, then a roll-up of hundreds of proprietary or sole-source NSNs (the TransDigm playbook, worth ~$70B+ in market value), then subsystem OEM and design authority, then platform sustainment prime. This is the strongest criterion.

Requalifying and then running a defense production line (first articles, AS9100, years of making parts) dominates cost and risk, so no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. The sole-source status the margin depends on is legible in DIBBS, AMSC codes and award fields, and DLA's competition program exists to erode it. This is the same flaw that killed FAA PMA parts.
verified.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough to pass the relaxed C3, and the roll-up ladder is real. But manufacturing dominates the work, the sole-source signal sits in legible DIBBS and AMSC fields, and the bought right often carries no transferable technical data or source status. So it fails C1 and C4, much as FAA PMA did.

The search budget ran out after the first query, so this rests on two fetched DLA/NDIA briefings and one Defense News article.

1) DLA SAR briefing, FY17 metrics (NDIA 2018): 282 packages received, 111 approved, 114 rejected, 144 pending, $35.5M potential annual savings. Approved over closed is about 49%, which matches the candidate's 40-60%. But savings come to about $320k a year per approved NSN, so each approved part carries only a modest annual buy.

The program sets a "Minimum $10K annual buy value" and is "not available on NSNs with less than $10,000". FY16: 211 packages received, 55 approved, $2.35M potential annual savings, about $43k a year per approved NSN. Typical full approval takes 12 to 18 months.
3) Both briefings quote DAG 17.7501-6, Retention of Newly Approved Sources: for 1 year from approval or first award, 40% of the award may go to the newly approved source. That makes the proven right a time-limited share of an award as an ADDITIONAL, competing source. It is not a sole-source franchise. The SAR process exists to break sole-source pricing; its output is counted as government "savings", i.e. lower prices.
4) TransDigm's excess profit came from OEM-proprietary sole-source parts. The DoD IG 2021 report via Defense News found $20.8M of excess profit on 105 parts across 150 contracts. TransDigm's FY2020 defense revenue was $2.18B (43% of total). That margin comes from design-authority ownership, which a liquidation buyer does not get.

Step-up implied by the numbers: ~$100k-2M in liquidation plus $50-500k per SAR, against per-NSN annual buys in the tens to low hundreds of thousands. Run at shared, competitive prices, that is a 1-3x return over several years, far under 30x and nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own 3-5x already fails the lens threshold. The SAR data suggests even 3-5x is optimistic, because approval turns a sole-source price into a competitive one.

Transaction count: one DLA site approves about 55-111 SAR packages a year. No public record of sales of orphaned defense lines priced as liquidation-then-sole-source exists in what was retrieved.
verifiers.killer: The proven right is not a sole-source line worth $5-20M. DLA's own SAR metrics show it is an additional-source approval that lowers the price. The DAG 17.7501-6 guarantee is only 40% of awards for one year. Approved NSNs carry about $43k-320k a year in government savings: FY16 had 55 approvals for $2.35M and FY17 had 111 approvals for $35.5M. Casting and forging contracts average about $740 each, against a $10k minimum annual buy. So the step-up from a ~$0.1-2M liquidation purchase plus a $50-500k SAR is roughly 1-3x, not 10^3x. The only buyer paying sole-source multiples (the TransDigm-style roll-up) pays for OEM-proprietary design authority, which an estate or liquidation purchase does not transfer.

3) The economics are anti-sole-source by design. Under DAG 17.7501-6 (2014), a newly approved source gets a multi-source award clause for at least one year. In 7 cases the item moved to fully competitive government drawings. A SAR therefore earns a share of a competed buy, not sole-source margins. Rejection reasons include "can't validate part (no government data to compare)", "application upgrade and/or discontinued" and "not in the best interest of the government". All of these come from DLA engineering judgement, so they are poorly predictable from public text.

4) Competition: Ontic, the "become the OEM for parts others developed" model, has about 10 group companies, licensing deals with Hamilton Sundstrand, Honeywell, Parker and Safran, and supports "thousands of essential parts". TransDigm, HEICO and Loar run the same proprietary-aftermarket roll-up. A long tail of small DIBBS bidders already uses Haystack and SERVA for exactly this NSN screening. The DoD IG reports (DODIG-2022-043) show that TransDigm-style sole-source margins draw IG and congressional clawback scrutiny.

The bought "right" (tooling and drawings) usually does not carry approved-source status or data rights. I scored C4 at 1 and C2 at 2 because the realistic return is about 2x, on a competed 40% share, with small NSN values.
verifiers.killer: DLA itself publishes SAR candidate lists of obsolete and limited-competition NSNs, AMSC codes already flag restricted status, and DLA tells bidders to screen with DIBBS, Haystack and SERVA. So the demand and sole-source signal is legible and commercially sold, not illegible. A successful SAR makes you an additional source that can win as little as 40% of a competed award, not a sole-source owner. FY17 approvals averaged only about $320k a year of savings per NSN (111 approved, $35.5M total), and the space is occupied by Ontic, TransDigm, HEICO, Loar and thousands of Haystack-using DIBBS bidders.

verifiers.evidence:
Lens: right and frame. The search budget for this turn ran out after my first call, so the evidence comes from one primary source I fetched directly and parsed (the DLA Land and Maritime SAR briefing to NDIA, June 2018), plus the DoD IG figures already in the candidate.

1) The candidate's "right" is not the right that creates the spread. Per DLA's SAR briefing, a SAR is a package that any prospective new supplier assembles to show it can make an NSN currently bought as other than full-and-open (AMSC B, C or D). It can come from OEM data or from reverse engineering an OEM part. DLA tells contractors to find candidate NSNs themselves in DIBBS, Haystack and SERVA, and it even publishes a "DLA candidate list" of obsolescence and limited-competition items. The valuable right, approved-source status, is therefore granted free by the government, open to anyone, first come, through reverse engineering. It is not bought from owners who cannot read data. Liquidation tooling and drawings are at best a cost-saver for the SAR package, not an exclusive right. Any competitor can file on the same NSN without buying the estate. This fails the C4 requirement that "rights are bought, not free first-come".

2) Approval does not create sole-source margins. It does the reverse: it is DLA's sole-source breakout tool. Under the 2014 DAG 17.7501-6 procedure, a newly approved source gets a multi-source award clause for at least one year, and up to 40% of an award if it is "not low but fair and reasonable". NSNs are also pulled from long-term auto-solicitation contracts. The new source becomes an additional competitor, so prices fall toward competitive levels. The briefing reports FY17 savings to the government of $35.5M across 111 approved packages, about $320k a year per NSN. That is consistent with small per-NSN prizes. The TransDigm-style excess margins (DoD IG: $16.1M excess profit on 46 parts; $20.8M on 105 parts) belong to incumbent proprietary or sole-source holders, not to newly approved second sources.

3) The proving step is expensive and close to a coin flip, which passes the relaxed C3. In FY17 there were 282 packages: 111 approved, 114 rejected and 144 pending, so about 49% of decided packages were approved. That supports the candidate's 40-60% guess. Listed rejection reasons include weapon criticality, item upgraded or discontinued, no government data to validate the part, and "need to complete qualification testing". The review chain (CAO, then VE in 15 days, then ESA in 90 days, plus data requests) runs months before any first article. ML over rejection narratives could plausibly give about 1.2-1.5x, so C3 scores 3.

4) Physical step: after approval the company must still run an AS9100 or MIL-spec production line for years, at partial award share. Manufacturing dominates the work, so no frame exists where discovery is 80%+. That is the same failure as the geothermal counter-example and the killed FAA PMA idea.

5) Outcome legibility: AMSC codes (B, C, D) and the approved-source CAGE lists are legible fields that already state sole-source status. DLA itself publishes the candidate list. So the regulator writes the answer into a field, which kills most of the ML edge.

6) Unverified (I could not search): under DoD qualification rules (SD-6), a change of plant location generally requires requalification, so approved status bought out of an estate probably does not carry over to a new facility.

7) Hard exclusions: none triggered. It is not drilling, and the company would own and operate the line.
verifiers.killer: The approved-source status that creates the spread is not a right anyone can buy. DLA grants it free, first come, to any supplier that files a SAR, reverse-engineered packages included. DLA even publishes the candidate NSNs. Approval is DLA's sole-source breakout tool: the new source gets a multi-source clause and as little as 40% of an award, and prices fall toward competitive levels instead of sole-source margins (FY17: about $320k a year of government savings per approved NSN). Liquidated tooling buys nothing exclusive, and running the line, not discovery, dominates the work.

verified.name: Reviving zombie subdivisions (lapsed or antiquated plats)
verified.one_line: Buy or option distressed parcels in stalled or antiquated pre-recession subdivisions where vested plat rights have lapsed or are uncertain and REO desks price them as raw land, re-entitle or confirm vested rights and secure will-serve letters, and sell finished-entitled lots to national homebuilders.
verified.old_fatal_flaw: The jump from paper lot to finished lot comes mostly from horizontal development: physical construction at $40-100k+ per lot, which is hard, bespoke and capital-heavy. Entitlement or vested-rights proving on its own gives only about a 2-5x step-up, and land brokers and builders already price entitlement status reasonably well. So discovery is not 80%+ of the value creation in any rung a builder pays a jackpot for.
verified.frame: The rung is the entitled paper lot: confirmed or re-won vested plat rights plus will-serve letters, sold to builders or land developers. Inside that rung, finding which plats still hold legally defensible rights is perhaps 30-40% of the work. The rest is political and legal: hearings, utility negotiations, impact fees, re-platting to current code, and often re-engineering. A buyer exists (Forestar, Lennar and others buy paper lots), but builders mostly pay for FINISHED lots. Getting from paper to finished means horizontal construction at about $40-65k per lot. That step is physical, bespoke and costs as much as or more than the land.
verified.step_up: Distressed raw or stalled plat land trades at about 15-25% of finished-lot value. Entitled paper lots fetch more, but still well below finished value. That comes from one forum source, a Southern California land dealer on BiggerPockets, so treat it as anecdotal. The 2025 US median finished-lot value is about $59k (NAHB), and Forestar's average lot price is about $106.6k. Entitlement alone is roughly a 2-5x step-up, not 10^3-10^4. Going to finished lots adds about $40-65k per lot of horizontal cost.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt is expensive. Re-entitlement or vested-rights litigation plus engineering and utility studies costs about $50k-$500k+ per subdivision and takes 1-3 years, so the expense test passes. This is an estimate; no single source gives it. The base success rate for reviving rights is moderate, maybe 30-60%. ML that reads scanned plats, development agreements, council minutes and utility capacity filings could lift it by about 1.2-1.5x, by spotting where vesting survives and where water or sewer capacity is real. It is unlikely to reach 2x, because the outcome turns on local politics rather than hidden facts.
verified.data: The data is public but partly illegible: scanned plats, recorded development agreements, extension ordinances, council minutes and utility will-serve history. Vesting status is a real legal ambiguity that incumbents don't parse systematically, and Lincoln Institute work documents how widespread zombie subdivisions are. But the plat itself is a legible recorded instrument. County planners, land brokers and the REO desks at banks and servicers routinely know whether a plat is recorded, expired or in a moratorium. The rights can be bought rather than claimed free, which passes that part of the test. The sellers, though, are banks, funds and HOAs or lot-owner groups with advisors. They are moderately sophisticated, and fractured ownership of scattered paper lots makes assembly costly.
verified.right_bought: Fee title or purchase options on stalled plats, distressed REO tracts, or assembled lots inside antiquated subdivisions. These are bought from banks and servicers, tax-deed sales and scattered individual owners. Assembling fragmented antiquated lots means many small transactions and holdouts.

They are well capitalised, and 64% of builders rated developed-lot supply low or very low in 2025. But they pay mainly for finished lots on takedown schedules, not for proven rights. Under the round-6 rubric the company could instead develop the lots itself, which makes it a Forestar-style lot developer.
verified.ladder: The ladder runs: revived entitlement, then horizontal lot development, then lot banking, then homebuilding, then build-to-rent or master-planned communities. These rungs are real and large. DR Horton and Lennar are each worth tens of billions of dollars. So the path to a big company exists, but every rung above the first is capital-heavy construction where discovery is not the edge.
verified.fatal_flaw: Most of the value comes from horizontal construction and local politics, not discovery. Entitlement-only proof gives about a 2-5x step-up that land brokers and REO desks already roughly price. Operating the lots yourself turns the company into a Forestar-style developer with about 20% gross margins. On that path, ML-led discovery is a minor input rather than 80%+ of the work, so the round-6 C2 (returns from operating) does not rescue it.
verified.one_line_reason: Rescored under round 6, little changes. Proving is expensive, so C3 earns a moderate score, and the ladder is large. But discovery is a minority of the work in every sellable rung, and plat status is fairly legible to sophisticated sellers. Self-development returns look like ordinary lot-developer margins of about 20% gross, under 2-3x on capital, not a 5x+ ML-created spread.

2) NAHB 2024 median finished-lot value is $60k nationally: Pacific $152k, West South Central $58k, East South Central $48k (eyeonhousing.org). Taking the BiggerPockets anecdote that raw or stalled land trades at 15-25% of finished value, the full raw-to-finished multiple is only about 4-7x. Most of that gap is the $40-65k per lot of horizontal cost, so the spread created by entitlement alone is about 2-3x at best.

3) The Lincoln Institute 'Combating Zombie Subdivisions' PDF (text extracted locally):
- Vacant entitled lots make up 15% to two-thirds of all lots in the Intermountain West counties studied.
- Teton County, ID had 9,031 platted lots against about 10,170 residents, a stockpile 'adequate to accommodate growth' for years, with three vacant entitled lots for every developed lot.
- In one example, redesigning a project cut its infrastructure cost from $24M to $800k.
So zombie plats sit mostly in oversupplied, low-demand exurbs. In those markets the entitlement is not scarce and does not command a premium. The binding constraints are infrastructure cost and demand, not hidden legal facts.

4) The buyer is real: Forestar, Lennar and land bankers. But they buy finished lots on takedown schedules or option land under return hurdles of about 15%, which prices in entitlement risk. No source shows a capitalised buyer paying a jackpot multiple at the moment a right is proven. Transaction volume is large: Forestar alone delivers about 14k lots a year. But the per-transaction spread is a developer margin, not a step-up.
verifiers.killer: Forestar, the archetypal paper-to-finished lot company, spends about 80% of its land capital on development and only 20% on acquisition. It earns 20-23% gross margins and roughly 8% annualised ROE, and it underwrites to a 15% return on inventory. Raw land at 15-25% of a $60k median finished lot gives only a 4-7x total multiple, and most of it is consumed by $40-65k per lot of horizontal construction. Entitlement alone adds about 2-3x. Lincoln Institute data shows zombie plats cluster in oversupplied exurbs with three vacant entitled lots per developed lot, so the revived right is not scarce. The step-up is far below 30x, and self-development returns are under 2x on capital. C1 and C2 fail.

(1) Zombie status is legible, not hidden. (3) An incumbent data vendor occupies the space. Zonda (formerly Meyers/Metrostudy) says the 'top 100 builders use Zonda'.
