LandTech plays the same land-sourcing AI role in the UK (land.tech), so the model is proven elsewhere and an obvious US entry.

(4) The residual edge is weak. Vesting ambiguity in recorded development agreements and extension ordinances is the only plausibly illegible signal. The outcome turns on council hearings and utility capacity, which Lincoln's cases show are negotiated replats (Mesa County, Teton County, Maricopa), not facts ML can read. Base revival rate is plausibly 30-60% and proving costs $50k-500k+ (per the finalist's own estimate; unverified), so C3 passes only weakly at about 1.1-1.3x.

(5) C2 is weak. Self-development makes the company a Forestar-style lot developer with roughly 20% gross margins (per the finalist's own Forestar source), well under 2x on capital, with no ML-created spread over what Zonda-equipped builders and REO desks already pay.
verifiers.killer: The candidate signal is legible and already commercialised. Vacant-platted-lot ratios come from a plain assessor and plat join, which Lincoln did by hand for 50 counties. Zonda already sells lot-pipeline and future-lot data at the subdivision level to the top 100 builders, and is launching Zonda Land AI for site sourcing. The remaining uncertainty is local politics, utility capacity and demand, and ML cannot read those from documents. So ML has no proprietary edge, the buyers are better informed than the startup would be, and self-development returns are ordinary lot-developer margins under 2x.

verifiers.evidence: Seen this run: (1) Forestar Q3 FY2025 call: of about $372M put into land and land development in the quarter, about 20% went to buying land and about 80% to horizontal development. Gross margin was 20.4% (about 21-23% normalised). Average lot price was $106.6k. So inside the rung that a well-funded buyer actually pays for (finished lots), the physical step is about 80% of the capital. That is the geothermal counter-example again, not Terranox. (2) Lincoln Institute Land Lines, Jan 2014, 'Combating Zombie Subdivisions': one owner, a paper plat and no improvements is the only easy case. Selling even one lot to an individual makes entitlement changes legally harder, needs every owner to agree, and any one of them may sue. Buying land does not by itself create a vested right; vesting usually comes from investing in improvements, so the 'hidden vested rights' thesis rests on the physical step, not on reading documents. In the Canyon Creek Ranch example (Teton County ID), 350 lots needed $24M of infrastructure (about $69k per lot, matching the $40-65k+ estimate), it sat 23 miles from city services, and it was DOWN-platted to 21 lots. The documented stock of zombie subdivisions is mostly remote, low-demand land in the Intermountain West, and the policy trend is to vacate entitlements, not revive them. (3) A Teton-style single owner (bank, fund or developer, often with a lender's consent needed) is a sophisticated seller who knows the plat status. Many-owner antiquated plats mean holdouts and lawsuits, so the right cannot be bought cheaply at scale. Not re-verified here (from the finalist's sources): NAHB median finished-lot value of about $59k, and the anecdotal claim that distressed land trades at 15-25% of finished value. Note: the web search budget was used up (limit reached), so I fetched cited source pages directly instead of running fresh searches.
verifiers.killer: The right can be bought, but not cheaply from owners who can't read the data, and not at scale. Clean single-owner paper plats are held by banks, funds or developers who know their status. Fragmented antiquated plats need every owner to agree and invite holdouts and lawsuits (Lincoln Institute). Vested rights generally come from physical improvement investment, not from hidden documents. Inside the rung a capitalised buyer pays for, horizontal construction takes about 80% of the capital (Forestar: 20% land, 80% development; Canyon Creek: about $69k per lot of infrastructure). The physical step dominates, as with bespoke geothermal plants. Margins are about 21% gross for a lot developer, not 5x on capital. The documented stock of zombie subdivisions is mostly remote, low-demand land being down-platted, not revived. It does not hit a hard exclusion (no drilling, and it owns the asset), but the frame fails.

verified.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
verified.one_line: Buy patents from Chapter 7/11 estates, ABC sales, dead startups (fabless, LiDAR, photonics, quantum, microLED) and lapse-bound owners for $2-50k; ML maps claims against FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, SEM cross-sections, datasheets, driver code and papers to build evidence-of-use charts; sell charted patents to NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools and funders.
verified.old_fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion whose value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation (about $2-5M per case to trial, with roughly 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidating all challenged claims). So buyers pay roughly 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4x, and the market is thin. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a trillion-dollar chain.
verified.frame: The rung is 'buy an orphan patent and turn it into a charted, assertable patent'. Inside that rung, finding the infringing product and mapping claims to it (from FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, datasheets, driver code) is about 80-90% of the work. The physical step, buying a teardown or SEM cross-section, costs a few thousand dollars and is easy. But the rung's output is a contestable opinion, not proof. Real proof (a license, settlement or verdict) sits in the next rung, litigation, and there the work is mostly legal spend and fights over validity, not discovery. Buyers exist (NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools like RPX and Unified Patents, litigation funders), but the market is thin and opaque.
verified.step_up: Unproven: orphan patents from estates, ABC sales and lapse-bound owners go for about $2-50k each (the candidate's figure, consistent with bulk estate sales). Large estate portfolios cleared at about $0.5M per patent (Kodak about $525M for about 1,100; Nortel $4.5B for 6,000+), but those were premium, already-licensed SEP-heavy pools. Proven: a well-charted patent on a high-volume product typically sells for about $100k-$1M to an NPE or funder. Asserting it ourselves, NPE campaigns settle at $0.5-10M+ per defendant (outlier: Samsung's $191M NPE verdict). That is roughly a 10-30x step on the sale route. Asserting ourselves can reach far more, but at about $2-5M per case to trial.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Producing the chart is cheap, about $5-30k per patent with ML plus a teardown, so on that measure proving fails the C3 'expensive' test. The real proving step is litigation or licensing: about $2-5M and 2-4 years per case to trial, with about 98% of district-court cases settling. Rough base rate: maybe 20-40% of assertions give a positive return. About 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidate all challenged claims. ML can plausibly lift the share of bought patents with a real, high-revenue infringer by 1.5-2x, because it filters before purchase. It does little for validity risk, which is the main way cases fail. Net, about 1.2-1.5x on cost per monetised patent. Sources: patent-litigation cost surveys (AIPLA, my estimate from memory), Unified Patents slide (98% settle), PTAB statistics.
verified.data: The signal is public but hard to read: FCC equipment-authorization internal photos and test reports, third-party teardowns, die shots, datasheets, open-source driver code, academic papers. These are scattered, image-heavy and unstructured, and no legible field records 'this patent reads on product X'. That does not hold for validity. Prior art and PTAB outcomes are legible and widely mined. Incumbents (RPX, Unified Patents, aggregators, claim-chart vendors) increasingly run their own AI charting tools, so the edge is real but eroding.
verified.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought, not claimed first-come. Sellers are Chapter 7/11 trustees, ABC assignees, dead startups' investors and owners about to let maintenance fees lapse. They usually cannot chart against products and sell cheaply, often in bulk at section 363 auctions. Lapse dates are legible from USPTO maintenance data, so the cheapest orphans are visible to anyone. The discount comes from the charting work, not from data access.
verified.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: NPEs (for example IP Bridge-type entities), aggregators (Acacia, Dominion Harbor), defensive pools (RPX, Allied Security Trust, Unified Patents) and litigation funders (Burford, Fortress). Under round 6 the company can also operate as its own funded NPE. The market is thin, prices are negotiated privately, and buyers discount heavily for validity risk.
verified.ladder: orphan patent purchase -> ML evidence-of-use chart -> sale to NPE or funder, or own licensing campaign -> funded assertion vehicle / patent fund -> maybe a defensive-pool or licensing platform. It tops out at a few-$B NPE, fund or aggregator: global patent assertion and licensing revenue is roughly $10-20B a year, and political and legal headwinds against NPEs and litigation funding keep growing. There is no physical-industry chain to integrate into, so no trillion-dollar path.
verified.fatal_flaw: Proof is never actually established. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion, and value comes only after years of litigation or licensing (about $2-5M per case, with about 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions killing all challenged claims). ML improves the infringement side but not validity, which is the main way cases fail. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a vertically integrated chain.
verified.one_line_reason: Under the round-6 rubric, operating as our own NPE lifts C2 to a real 2-5x on capital, but charting is cheap, real proof (litigation) is a validity coin-flip ML barely helps with, and the ladder caps at a niche few-$B assertion business.

verifiers.evidence:
STEP-UP FROM PROOF (the key claim): The 2025 Richardson Oliver Patent Market Report (IAM, Sept 2025) says that over five years, packages with evidence-of-use (EOU) materials or claim charts got price premiums of 32% to 108%. That is a 1.3-2.1x step-up, not 10-30x and nowhere near 10^3-10^4x. EOUs also raise the chance of a sale. Only 21% of 2024 packages included an EOU.

PRICES:
- Median asking price per asset: $163k (2024), up from $125k (2023).
- Median asking price of assets that actually sold: $95k (2024), $33k (2023), $63k (2022).
- Closing prices run 0% to 75%+ below asking.
- AST's IP3 2025 no-haggle buy program: 47 deals, $5.1M total, about $92k per patent family. An earlier IP3 round ranged from $10k to $325k per family.

So a charted patent realistically clears at around $50-150k, not $100k-$1M. The candidate's $2-50k purchase price from estates is unverified. Per-patent prices are rarely disclosed in Hilco/363 sales; Brevity's whole IP estate sold for $400k. Any gap between the $2-50k purchase and roughly $95k comes from illiquidity and fire-sale discounts, not from ML proof. Fire sales are well documented: more than 40% of bankrupt Chapter 11 firms sell patents, and they sell their core ones.

MARKET SIZE AND BUYERS:
- The whole brokered and secondary patent market was $158M in 2024, flat against 2022 and 2023.
- Brokers handled 87% of sold packages, and sell-through is about 20-30%. Packages listed in 2019 are only now reaching 30% sold.
- NPEs took 11-50% of packages in 2020-24, but only about 2% of assets in 2024 (the report says this is likely understated).
- Defensive aggregators are moving away from buying patents outright and toward licence-only deals.

So buyers exist, but the market is tiny and illiquid. That works out to roughly 1-2k assets a year at under $100k each, not a market where a capitalised buyer pays a step-up at once.

OWN-NPE ROUTE (C2 under round 6):
- RPX (2014/15): the median NPE defendant paid $407k in combined legal plus settlement costs; the median resolution cost was $480k against a mean of $5.6M; the average settlement was $1.6M. So typical per-defendant recoveries are in the hundreds of thousands, against $2-5M to take a case to trial.
- PTAB FY2024: 312 of 446 final written decisions (about 70%) found all claims unpatentable. FY2025: about 65% (250 of 387). Validity, which ML barely helps with, remains the main way cases fail.

A multi-defendant campaign can plausibly return 2-5x, but the prize is a niche business inside a $158M brokered market and a roughly $10-20B assertion ecosystem that faces growing headwinds.

DATA EDGE IS ERODING: Richardson Oliver itself notes that AI tools such as Patlytics now produce element-by-element claim charts against product specifications at low cost. That turns the charting step into a cheap commodity and removes the illegibility moat.
verifiers.killer: The proof step (an evidence-of-use chart) raises a patent's price by only 32-108%, about 1.3-2x, in the actual brokered market. The step-up claim is therefore false by more than an order of magnitude. Charted assets clear at a median asking price of about $95k in a $158M-a-year market with roughly 20-30% sell-through. The own-NPE route earns about $400-500k per median defendant, and validity (65-70% of PTAB final decisions find all claims unpatentable) is the deciding risk, which ML does not address. Cheap AI claim-charting tools are already standard, so the illegibility edge is gone.

verifiers.evidence:
DATA AND COMPETITION lens.

(1) The space is crowded, and one player already runs this exact thesis. SIM IP, Erich Spangenberg's patent monetization firm, bought Garden Intel for about $150M in Feb 2026 (Bloomberg Law, ipfray). Garden sells AI-generated evidence-of-use (EoU) charts and infringement detection, and is now 'the technology engine behind SIM IP's licensing and royalty business'. That is AI charting combined with owned-patent licensing, done by one of the best-known NPE operators, with 20+ years of transaction data. Other players: Patlytics (a $14M Series A in Feb 2025, $21M total; a $40M Series B reported by one source; customers include Quinn Emanuel, Google and Xerox); XLSCOUT ClaimChart LLM; Lumenci iLumOS; and Amplified, IPRally and Cipher.

(2) The illegible physical-evidence moat is already industrialised. TechInsights has five teardown labs and an archive of 'thousands of reports and over one million images' going back to the 1970s. It sells EoU packages and court-defensible claim charts to licensing entities, and says 37 of the top 50 US patent holders are clients. It also tells licensing entities that 'if infringement is not found in our database, ... ROI is low.' FCC internal photos are already scraped and indexed by third parties such as fccid.io. The die shots and SEM cross-sections the finalist relies on are therefore exactly what incumbents already sell.

(3) The assets are not bought from people who cannot read the data. Brokers and competitive auctions sell estate patents. Ocean Tomo ran a Chapter 7 sale of 68 Li-Fi patents through a section 363 stalking-horse auction. The biggest 2025 buyers were entities linked to Dominion Harbor, Fortress and InterDigital (IAM, H1 2025). Average asking prices were about $150-186k per patent (Ocean Tomo, 2020-2022). So a $2-50k orphan is usually one these informed buyers have already passed on. Lapse dates in USPTO maintenance-fee data are legible to everyone.

(4) The market is thin. The secondary brokered market was about $158M a year in 2022-2024, down from $290-300M in 2019-2020 (Richardson Oliver, IAM). Only about 20-21% of brokered packages sell. That caps the 'sell charted patents' route.

(5) Proof cost cuts both ways. A manual chart takes 8-20 hours (XLSCOUT), so charting is cheap and fails the C3 'expensive' test. The expensive step is litigation. One correction in the finalist's favour: its figure of 65-70% of PTAB decisions invalidating all claims is now stale. Institution fell to 14% in Q4 2025 under Director Squires (RPX), and to 24.6% against NPEs in Q1 2026. PTAB petitions fell 64% year on year (Unified Patents, Q1 2026). This policy tailwind lowers validity risk for owners. But it helps every holder equally, so well-capitalised incumbents such as Fortress and Dominion Harbor are bidding up assets. Meanwhile ex parte reexamination requests rose 157% and district court filings fell 21.6%. ML adds nothing on this axis.

Net: the infringement-evidence signal is not illegible to incumbents, a well-funded player already owns the AI-plus-assertion combination, and the purchase discount mostly reflects patents that informed buyers already rejected.
verifiers.killer: Incumbents already own the edge, and one runs this exact model. TechInsights sells teardown-based EoU charts to licensing entities from more than 1M archived images. Patlytics, XLSCOUT and Lumenci sell AI EoU charting. SIM IP (Spangenberg) paid about $150M for Garden Intel in Feb 2026 to pair AI charting with owned-patent licensing. Brokers auction estate patents competitively to Fortress- and Dominion Harbor-linked buyers in a thin market of about $158M a year with about 20% sell-through. So no illegible-data discount is left to capture, and cheap orphans are cheap because informed buyers already passed on them.

verifiers.evidence: RIGHT (survives the lens). Supply is huge, legal and cheap. Patently-O (Mar 2026): about 60% of US patentees now abandon before full term, and only about 40% pay all maintenance fees, so a large pool of lapse-bound owners exists. Trustees sell at deep discounts for certainty. In re Hansen (Bankr. D.N.H. 2017): a Chapter 7 trustee sold patents to PixArt for $150k while a pending suit on them was claimed at $28M. Demand is thin, which keeps acquisition prices low. The whole brokered secondary market was $158M in 2024 (Richardson Oliver 2025 report, via IAM), with about 20% sell-through, so most patents on offer find no buyer at ask. Asking prices are about $280k per US patent (RO 2019), and closing prices for orphans run far lower. Buying cheaply at scale is credible: a buyer's market with legal title transfer (section 363 sales, assignments). Diligence risks are real but manageable. Under section 365(n) and the Crumbs line of cases, prior licensees can keep their rights after a sale, so estates may already have licensed the obvious infringers. Undisclosed or unassumed licenses (Provider Meds, 5th Cir. 2018) create title noise. No hard exclusion applies: the company owns the asset and sells or asserts the asset, not a service. FRAME (weakened). The physical step (teardown, die shot, SEM) costs a few thousand dollars and is trivial, unlike a bespoke geothermal plant. But the rung's output, a charted patent, sells into a $158M/yr market at about 20% sell-through, so the 'capitalised buyer' leg is thin. On the round-6 operate-it-yourself route, the dominant cost and time is litigation or licensing (about $2-5M and 2-4 years per case). That is the analogue of the bespoke plant, and charting is perhaps 10-20% of total effort. Contingency counsel and funders can abstract that cost (at least 30% of patent litigation was financed by 2020 per Unified Patents/Ray, and RPX shows funded NPE campaigns growing through 2025). That keeps the frame alive rather than killed. One tailwind the finalist missed: PTAB institution collapsed in 2025 under discretionary denial (RPX: 68% in Q1 to 23-35% in Q3, and about 14% in Squires-decided Q4 petitions; denials hit hardest for patents in force more than 6 years). That substantially reduces the 'validity coin-flip' and supports C2 at 3. Data caveat: FCC internal photos are routinely held under short-term (180-day) confidentiality, and long-term confidentiality is available when the internals are not user-accessible. So a key evidence source is partly withheld or delayed, and incumbents (RPX, Unified, chart vendors) already run AI charting. C4 goes from 4 to 3.
verifiers.killer: The right is buyable cheaply and legally at scale, and the teardown step is trivial, so this lens does not refute it. The frame is weak for two reasons. The 'proven' output (a charted patent) has a buyer market of only about $158M a year with about 20% sell-through. And on the operate-it-yourself route, litigation, not discovery, is roughly 80% of the cost and time, which plays the same role as the bespoke geothermal plant, though contingency counsel and funders can carry it. The main residual risks are prior licences that survive the sale under section 365(n) and FCC confidentiality on internal photos.

verified.name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
verified.one_line: Take abandoned-in-place pipelines and easements from operators carrying decommissioning liabilities; ML over easement instruments proves broad 'any substance' assignable scope and continuity; sell to CO2/H2 trunkline and fiber developers.
verified.old_fatal_flaw: The proving step is not where the value or the difficulty is. Corridors that look cheap are often legally void (the easement lapsed on abandonment, or its scope has to be litigated per parcel), every parcel in the chain must pass (one gap kills the corridor), and turning a proven corridor into value still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or hydrogen buyer that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, and owners who can read their own easements alre
verified.frame: The rung is buying an abandoned-in-place line and proving that its easement chain is continuous and broad in scope ('any substance', assignable). Title proving is maybe 40-50% of the work in this rung. The rest is physical and bespoke: in-line inspection, hydrotest, dehydration and crack-propagation analysis (the CO2 repurposing studies flag these), compression, and jurisdictional changes such as Trailblazer's FERC abandonment. Buyers are CO2 and H2 trunkline developers and long-haul fiber. CO2 trunklines are largely stalled (Navigator cancelled, Summit delayed), so the capitalised buyer is thin. This is not an 80%+ discovery frame.
verified.step_up: No clean unproven vs proven price exists. Abandoned lines are liabilities that operators sell at roughly zero or negative value. A requalified corridor's value comes from avoided new-build cost. Repurposing estimates range from about 25% cheaper over the life cycle (PipeChina/CUP study) to about 80% cheaper on pipe cost (Indonesian IPA case study). New-build CO2 pipe costs roughly $1-4M per mile, so a proven corridor is worth perhaps $0.3-3M per mile of avoided cost. But that value is only realised after requalification capex, and only if a CO2 or H2 shipper exists. Trailblazer (392 miles, more than 10 Mtpa) was converted by its own operator, Tallgrass, so the spread went to the incumbent.
verified.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, with no sourced figure: proving one corridor means title work on roughly 1,000-3,000 parcels (about $0.5-2k each), so roughly $1-5M plus legal opinions. Proving is expensive, which satisfies C3. My guessed base rate is 30-60% of corridors that come out clean or curable, because one parcel gap or one narrow-scope instrument breaks continuity. ML over scanned instruments could plausibly triage corridors about 1.3-1.6x better. But the decisive outcomes, whether an easement lapsed on abandonment or what its scope covers, are settled by state law and litigation per parcel (e.g. the Georgia Plantation Pipe Line case found no telecom rights in the easement). That caps the lever.
verified.data: The easement instruments are scanned, unstructured and scattered across county recorders, so the data is genuinely illegible and public. But the outcome (scope and lapse) is a legal question that is often already litigated, not a hidden physical fact. The sellers are pipeline operators with right-of-way and land departments who hold their own ROW files. They are not owners who cannot read the data, and Tallgrass converted Trailblazer itself.
verified.right_bought: Yes, in principle. Operators carrying decommissioning liability would transfer abandoned-in-place segments cheaply, possibly with liability attached. But the purchase discount reflects a liability the seller understands, not an information gap. Where a corridor has real reuse value, the operator keeps it.
verified.buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Tallgrass, Summit; the demand is stalled), hydrogen hub pipelines (early, with DOE hub funding uncertain), and long-haul and dark-fiber builders (real but small value per mile). The capital is thin and policy-dependent, mainly 45Q.
verified.ladder: The ladder is real: corridor title, then a requalified line, then an operated CO2 or H2 transport utility, then sequestration hubs or storage, then a full midstream energy-transition network. The top of the ladder is a large midstream company. The weak point is the bottom rung, not the ladder.
verified.fatal_flaw: The spread is captured by the incumbent operator, not by the ML reader. Operators have land departments that can read their own easements, and they convert valuable lines themselves (Tallgrass and Trailblazer). What sellers will hand over cheaply are mostly the segments that are legally void or too narrow in scope. Even a proven corridor still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or H2 shipper that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode: the hard part is the build and the demand, not the discovery.
verified.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 lifts the hit-rate score modestly, because title proving is expensive and ML can triage corridors. But the sellers can read their own easements, the outcome is set by law rather than hidden in data, and value depends on bespoke requalification and stalled CO2/H2 demand. It stays weak.

verifiers.evidence:
The tooling limited what I could check. The shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so I ran no new searches. WebFetch reached only one source: the IPA (Indonesian Petroleum Association) abstract, which says repurposing 'could potentially reduce around 80% of pipeline cost'. It gives no absolute figures, and the full paper needs a member login. The S&P Global and RBN pages on Trailblazer both returned 403. The verdict below therefore rests on the finalist's own sourced material and this one IPA figure. It is a failure to find support, not a positive disproof.

1) Price of the unproven right. I found no transaction price for an abandoned-in-place pipeline segment sold together with its easement chain. The finalist's own position is that these lines are liabilities sold at roughly zero or negative value. A ratio cannot be computed from a zero or negative base, and no market price exists to anchor one.

2) Price of the proven right. I found no sale of a 'proven, title-clean corridor' as a standalone asset. The only value proxy is avoided new-build cost. New CO2 pipe costs about $1-4M per mile, and repurposing saves about 25% over the life cycle (PipeChina/CUP study) or about 80% of pipe cost (IPA). That makes a proven corridor worth about $0.3-3M per mile in gross avoided cost. That figure is before requalification capex: in-line inspection (ILI), hydrotest, dehydration, crack-propagation analysis and compression, which use up a large share of the saving. It is also realised only by whoever owns the shipper contract, not at the moment title is proven.

3) Buyer. The one real US example, Trailblazer (392 miles, more than 10 Mtpa), was converted by its own operator, Tallgrass, in-house, so no arm's-length buyer paid for a proven corridor. Navigator CO2 was cancelled and Summit is delayed, and hydrogen hub funding is uncertain. Fiber buyers pay small per-mile easement or IRU (indefeasible right of use) fees, not millions of dollars per mile. No capitalised buyer is shown paying 'at once' on title proof.

4) Market size. The transaction count for this rung is effectively zero to a handful per year. Every visible conversion was done by the incumbent.

Even under the relaxed C2, which allows value capture by operating, the company would have to fund requalification and win a scarce 45Q-dependent shipper. The spread is then construction-and-offtake margin, not ML-proof margin. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern. C3 stays modest: proving is expensive (title work on about 1,000-3,000 parcels), but the outcome is decided by state law per parcel. C4 is low: sellers have right-of-way (ROW) departments and keep their valuable lines. C5's ladder (transport, then storage, then midstream) is real, but its bottom rung fails.
verifiers.killer: There is no observable market for the step-up. Unproven abandoned lines trade at about zero or negative value as liabilities. Proven corridors are never sold standalone: their value, about $0.3-3M per mile in avoided new-build cost, appears only after bespoke requalification and only with a scarce CO2 or H2 shipper. The one US precedent, Tallgrass converting Trailblazer, kept that spread in-house with no third-party buyer. That leaves no measurable step-up, no real capitalised buyer of the proven rung, and roughly zero transactions a year.

verifiers.evidence:
Search note: the shared web-search budget (200 calls per turn) was already used up when this verifier ran, so no new searches were possible. Two finalist sources (RBN, S&P Global) returned 403. The evidence below comes from the finalist's own cited sources, the two opinions I could read, and background knowledge, which I label as such.

(1) The outcome is legible, and the sellers can read it. The Fifth Circuit opinion in Angus Chemical v. Glendora Plantation (No. 14-30416, 2015), from the cited ca5.uscourts.gov PDF which I extracted and read, shows the decisive questions are legal, not hidden data. The issues were (a) whether the operator could abandon a 12-inch line in place under the right-of-way instrument, and (b) whether it could install fiber optic cable. Both were resolved by reading the instrument's granting language ("pipeline for the transportation of liquids..." with successors and assigns) under state law. The operator held the instrument, and the landowner litigated it.
- Plantation Pipe Line (257 Ga. App. 709, 2002; vlex excerpt read): a Hart County court found "telecommunication rights were not contained in Plantation's easement", and the appeal was about partial abandonment.
- So scope and lapse are settled by legal construction per parcel, often already litigated. They are not a physical fact that ML can find in illegible data.
- The operators that would sell already hold their own ROW files and land departments.
- Background (not re-verified this round): PHMSA's National Pipeline Mapping System already records line location, operator and status, including abandoned. Commercial courthouse-record vendors (for example Enverus/DrillingInfo courthouse documents, Courthouse Direct) and ROW and title service firms (Contract Land Staff, O.R. Colan and others) already index and abstract recorded easements. So the instrument layer is not untouched.

(2) The space is occupied by incumbents who keep the spread.
- Tallgrass converted its own Trailblazer (392 miles, more than 10 Mtpa CO2, removed from FERC's purview) from inventory it already owned. This is per the finalist's own S&P and RBN sources (fetches returned 403, but the facts are uncontested).
- Background: Level 3 and others historically negotiated directly with pipeline operators, and the railroad/pipeline fiber right-of-way class actions show that landowners, not acquirers, capture any scope gap.

(3) Proving cost and hit rate are unsourced.
- The $1-5M title-proving cost and the 30-60% clean-corridor rate are the finalist's own guesses with no figure behind them.
- ML can help triage clauses, but abstraction is commoditised. The binding result (a court ruling or a landowner settlement) comes after ML and is not predicted by it.

(4) Value capture by operating (C2): owning the line still requires bespoke requalification (ILI, hydrotest, fracture analysis per the CUP/PipeChina and IPA studies). Shippers are thin: Navigator was cancelled and Summit delayed. The purchase discount prices a known decommissioning liability, not an information gap. So the realistic return is under 2x with no informed-buyer spread.
verifiers.killer: The decisive outcome, whether the easement survives abandonment and allows CO2, H2 or fiber, is a legal question. It is resolved per parcel by reading the instrument's granting clause under state law, as in Angus Chemical v. Glendora and Plantation Pipe Line. The sellers hold these instruments and can read them, and they convert the valuable lines themselves (Tallgrass Trailblazer). That leaves no information asymmetry for ML to exploit. Easement abstraction and status are already served by PHMSA NPMS, courthouse-record vendors and ROW title firms. What reaches a buyer cheaply is the adversely selected remainder.

verifiers.evidence:
Search budget: the shared web-search budget was used up before this verifier could run any query, so all evidence comes from fetching the finalist's own primary sources. More searches would need a follow-up run.

(1) Angus Chemical v. Glendora Plantation (5th Cir. No. 14-30416, 2015; text extracted from the court PDF). This instrument is the ideal case the thesis relies on. It conveys a right of way to 'successors and assigns' to 'construct, maintain, inspect, operate... replace and change the size of a pipeline for the transportation of liquids, gases, solids... or any other substances.' Even with that wording, the right to abandon a line in place was found ambiguous. The court vacated summary judgment, and the case had to be litigated against one holdout landowner after all the other landowners had signed. Fiber was allowed only as 'incidental... necessary and convenient' to running the pipeline itself, because it controlled wastewater flow. That gives no support for selling the corridor to a third-party long-haul fiber or H2/CO2 shipper. The operator also offered to pay the landowner for a ratification. So the 'proven' scope came from negotiation and litigation, not from reading documents.

(2) Plantation Pipe Line (Georgia; vLex summary). The trial court found the pipeline had abandoned part of its easement over seven plaintiffs' parcels. In the related Level 3 condemnation, the court found that telecommunication rights were not in Plantation's easement. Level 3 had to rely on eminent domain and pay compensation. So the act that creates a cheap seller, abandonment, is the same act that tends to extinguish the right being bought. And third-party fiber or substance uses fall outside scope, so they need fresh condemnation or new purchases from landowners.

(3) Trailblazer (finalist's S&P and RBN sources; RBN returned 403). Tallgrass, the incumbent operator, converted its own 392-mile line and handled the FERC abandonment itself. Owners of valuable corridors can read their ROW and capture the spread themselves.

(4) The CUP/PipeChina and IPA repurposing studies cited by the finalist (not re-fetched) put the savings at roughly 25-80%. Those savings arrive only after bespoke requalification: in-line inspection, hydrotest, dehydration, fracture-propagation analysis and new compression. This is the physical, bespoke step, comparable in kind to the geothermal plant.

Exclusions: no hard exclusion is hit. This is pipeline transport, not drilling or prospecting, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service. But the rubric's frame test fails.
verifiers.killer:
The right being bought gets weaker at the moment it becomes cheap.

Operators hand over lines that have been abandoned in place. Abandonment is exactly the act that courts treat as extinguishing the easement, as in Plantation Pipe Line, where the court found partial abandonment and no telecom rights. Even model 'any substance, successors and assigns' language leaves abandonment and replacement ambiguous, and third-party fiber falls outside its scope, as in Angus v. Glendora. So the outcome is decided parcel by parcel through holdout litigation, ratification payments or condemnation, not by ML reading scanned deeds.

The sellers are operators with ROW departments who can read their own files. Valuable corridors get converted in-house, as Tallgrass did with Trailblazer.

Even a proven corridor still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or H2 shipper. That shipper demand is stalled.

So the right cannot be bought cheaply and at scale from owners who cannot read the data, and the physical step dominates the work inside the rung. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode.

deep.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
deep.memo:
## Frame of reference
The rung: buy an option on farmland near a substation, then get a utility large-load study or will-serve letter for it, and sell the result to a data-center developer as "powered land". The frame fails C1. A buyer pays for an executed ESA or final interconnection, not for a study. In the Plug Power to Stream deal (Graham TX), $26.5M of the price depended on the load capacity in the final agreement ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). Altus calls committed load "the strongest variable" in data-center land prices, and says power and utility coordination usually takes 30-40 months before a deal is recorded ([Altus](https://www.altusgroup.com/insights/where-value-is-created-in-data-center-land/)). So picking the site is perhaps 30-40% of the work (estimate). Collateral, rezoning and utility negotiation make up the rest. This is the geothermal failure mode: the capital step dominates the discovery step.

## Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** about $10k/acre in low-cost markets with no power path ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). PA farmland averages $9,560/acre ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/02/21/farmer-15-million-dollar-data-center-developers-farmland-prices-preservation-backlash-agriculture-economy)).
- **Proven price:** "six figures" per acre once power is established ([DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). The median in markets with limited committed load is $28k/acre, and Central OH, Phoenix and Atlanta run $100k-460k/acre ([Altus](https://www.altusgroup.com/insights/where-value-is-created-in-data-center-land/)). Plug/Stream paid a $50M base for about 66 acres, roughly $760k/acre (my calculation from [DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). In NoVA, entitled land without power is about $4M/acre and powered land at least $6M/acre, so power alone adds only about 1.5x there.
- **Ratio:** about 3-35x, and it arrives only with committed capacity (estimate drawn from the figures above).
- **Volume:** about $6B in H1 2026, up 79% YoY ([DCK/Avison Young](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)). That is a few hundred deals a year at most (estimate; Cushman puts the average deal at 224 acres).

## Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Cost per attempt:** each study or deposit costs $75k-600k and takes 6-24 months. EKPC charges $75k + $1k/MW ([KY PSC](https://psc.ky.gov/pscecf/2025-00140/jacob.watson@ekpc.coop/07142025083010/2025-00140_Responses_to_Staffs_DR1.pdf)). Xcel CO asks about $600k upfront ([i2i](https://i2i.org/xcel-energy-proposes-large-load-tariff-for-data-centers/)).
- **Texas:** the draft PUCT rule adds $50k/MW of security, with 80% forfeitable, which is about $10M per 200 MW site ([Foley](https://www.foley.com/insights/publications/2026/03/public-utility-commission-of-texas-issues-proposed-rules-for-large-load-interconn/)).
- **Base rate:** about 12% of 1,066 GW of requested load has firm service, and about 28% is expected to be served ([Wood Mackenzie via Capacity](https://capacityglobal.com/news/wood-mackenzie-us-grid-operators-set-to-serve-28pc-of-data/)). Most of the failure comes from commitment and speculation, not from picking the wrong substation.
- **ML lift:** a competitor can simply subscribe to modelled substation offtake data, so ML likely lifts cost per proven site by under 1.2x (estimate). Earlier work found lookup tables match ML on grid siting.

## Data source
Public inputs: FERC Form 715 power-flow cases, ISO queue files, utility hosting-capacity maps, IRP appendices and large-load tariff dockets. Some pieces are scanned or unstructured, such as IRP appendices and substation one-lines. But the outcome is already a legible field you can buy. LandGate sells "offtake capacity data for every substation in the US" with 98% coverage across more than 84k substations, built from DC and AC models ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)). Enverus sells parcel-level MW feasibility ([Enverus](https://www.enverus.com/solutions/site-and-screen/)). Fails C4.

## How the right is bought
A purchase or lease option comes from the farmer. Texas's draft rule accepts an option as site control ([Foley](https://www.foley.com/insights/publications/2026/03/public-utility-commission-of-texas-issues-proposed-rules-for-large-load-interconn/)). But sellers are informed:
- A PA farmer turned down $15M at $60k/acre ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/02/21/farmer-15-million-dollar-data-center-developers-farmland-prices-preservation-backlash-agriculture-economy)).
- NE Wisconsin dairy land doubled in price ([Dairy News](https://dairynews.today/news/ai_data_centers_drive_up_wisconsin_dairy_land_prices_8754400.html)).
- LandGate's PowerLeads marketplace offers "ready to sign deals with landowners" ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).

Share of uplift kept: if the company sells at the study stage, perhaps 10-30% (estimate). If it posts ESA collateral and holds the site, more, but then the return comes from capital, not from information.

## Capitalised buyer
Yes, and well funded: hyperscalers, colocation developers (QTS, Stream, Vantage) and land platforms such as Tract. Plug/Stream shows they will pay about $300k/MW for capacity that is actually established (my calculation from [DCK](https://datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-land-buying-hits-6b-as-power-premiums-rise)).

## Integration ladder above
The rungs run: powered land, then entitled and energised campus, then powered shell or build-to-suit, then data-center operation, then on-site generation and PPAs. Tract shows the land-to-campus path can support a multi-$B company. Strong C5.

## Who else does this
- Tract
- Cloverleaf ($300M raised; abandoned Greenleaf WI; [DCD](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/cloverleaf-backs-out-of-data-center-project-in-greenleaf-wisconsin/))
- Scale/Reload ([Latitude](https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/scale-buys-reload-as-the-hunt-for-powered-land-heats-up/))
- Silver Lake/Commonwealth ($400M powered-land platform)
- Quinbrook's Rowan
- Exowatt's ExoRise
- Data vendors: LandGate, Enverus, Acres

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Run a backtest in one ISO, such as PJM's AEP Ohio zone. Label parcels that sold at data-center prices from county records plus the Altus/DCK comps. Score them three ways: (a) a simple rule (within 0.5 mi of a 230kV+ substation); (b) LandGate's offtake field; (c) an ML model over FERC 715, queue and IRP text.
2. Call 20 owners near the top-ranked substations and record their option asks as a multiple of farm value.
3. Kill criteria: kill the idea if ML beats LandGate by less than 0.03 AUC, or if the median ask is above 3x ag value.

## Verdict (relaxed rubric)
| | Score | Why |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 2 | Buyers pay for committed capacity, which needs collateral, not discovery |
| C2 Value capture | 2 | Holding and developing the site is possible, but sellers already price in the premium; return on capital is likely 1.5-2.5x (estimate) |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 2 | Proving is expensive, but ML adds under 1.2x over vendor offtake data |
| C4 Data + right | 1 | The outcome is sold as a field; owners are informed |
| C5 Ladder | 4 | Tract-style path to campus and operation |
| **Total** | **11/25** | Not excluded, but weak |

The prior verifiers agreed: all 3 refuted it, and their revised totals averaged 12.7. Recommend dropping it.

My web search budget was used up for this turn, so I could only open existing sources directly, not run new searches. I did not independently re-verify the Cloverleaf sale price, the adopted Texas rule text, or the Fortune, Dairy News, Enverus and Latitude pages.

deep.name: Entitlement arbitrage on exurban residential land (ML over planning records)
deep.memo:
## Entitlement arbitrage on exurban residential land: feasibility deep-dive

*Search note: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was already used up, so no new searches ran. Figures come from direct fetches of the finalist's sources, Forestar's investor page and Shovels' blog. A number with no source is marked as an estimate.*

### Frame of reference
The rung is: option a farm parcel on the Sun Belt fringe, take it through annexation, rezoning or a preliminary plat with utility will-serve letters, then sell the entitled acreage to a builder or land banker. The rung is discrete and sellable. But picking the parcel is only about 25-40% of the work (estimate). The rest is a 1-4 year campaign of engineering, traffic, drainage and environmental studies, staff negotiation, neighbour management and offsite utility commitments. acres.com says entitlement "is not passive" and needs coordination with several agencies (https://www.acres.com/blog/what-is-land-investing). That is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: doing the proving step is harder than finding the site.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** $10-30k/acre for raw fringe land (the candidate's estimate; no hard source).
- **Proven price:** entitled land sells for 2-4x equivalent raw land (https://www.acres.com/blog/what-is-land-investing). The candidate's 3-10x is optimistic.
- **The spread is narrowing.** Since 2019, raw land per acre is up 86.5% against 53.3% for build-ready lots. Year over year, raw land fell 2.4% and build-ready fell 1.1% (Realtor.com via https://themortgagepoint.com/?p=22526). Sellers are already pricing in hope value.
- **Transactions/yr:**
  - 426,986 land listings in Q1 2026, median $62,365/acre across all categories (same source).
  - Forestar sold 14,240 lots in FY2025 and controls 91,700 (https://investor.forestar.com/).
  - Millrose manages about 143k homesites with $8.7B invested capital (https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/millrose-mrp-q1-2026-earnings-210651199.html).
  - "$50B+ of US builder land spend a year" is unverified (estimate).
- **Return on total capital:** about 3-5x on cash at risk for winners. After failed entitlements and carry, about 2-3x blended (estimate).

### Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Cost per attempt:** about $150k-$2M and 1-4 years (candidate estimate, consistent with acres.com's "years of regulatory risk"). The expensive-proving leg is met.
- **Base hit rate:** 40-65% from parcel pick to approval (estimate, no hard source). Cases that reach a hearing are mostly approved, because staff negotiate them first.
- **Existing ML evidence:** a Frederick County MD logit study found rezonings largely follow the ordinance and the staff recommendation (https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/159252, returned 403 on fetch, so this is the finalist's summary).
- **With ML:** about 1.2-1.5x better cost per entitled parcel, mostly from dropping doomed options before deposits go hard. 2x would need a signal beyond the future land-use map and sewer service area, which is not shown (estimate).

### Data source
- **Datasets:** Legistar/Granicus agendas, minutes and staff reports; YouTube meeting video; CIP, sewer and water master-plan PDFs; annexation agreements; comp-plan future land-use maps; county GIS parcel, assessor and deed records. All are public and free.
- **Legibility:** partly illegible (scanned PDFs, video). But staff reports carry a legible approve/deny recommendation, and future land-use maps and sewer boundaries are often already GIS layers.
- **Extraction is already commercial.** Shovels bought ReZone in January 2026. Its Decisions API covers 600+ cities and about 200,000 final decisions, and names "home builders and real estate investors tracking rezonings" as a use case. It plans proposed/discussed/approved/postponed status fields (https://www.shovels.ai/blog/decisions-api-launch/; https://www.shovels.ai/blog/shovels-acquires-rezone/). The outcome is fast becoming a legible field.

### How the right is bought
- **From whom:** farm families, estates and local brokers.
- **Mechanics:** a purchase option or contingent contract. Typically 1-5% of price as a deposit, going hard at milestones, with closing at entitlement or simultaneous with resale (estimate).
- **Uplift kept:** the company keeps the spread minus study spend, carry and option fees. That is perhaps 40-60% of gross uplift on winners (estimate).
- **The problem:** fringe sellers are courted by builder land teams and land bankers, so they ask hope-value prices. Sun Belt vacant land per acre more than doubled in the two years to Q2 2022 (WSJ/Land.com, https://www.business.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/documents/running-short-land-housing-wsj-morris-davis-9-26-2022.pdf, per the verifier; the PDF was unreadable on my fetch). Truly uninformed sellers exist only at the margin.

### Capitalised buyer
The buyer is strong and active:
- **Builders:** D.R. Horton (through Forestar), Lennar, Pulte, NVR and Toll.
- **Land bankers:** Millrose earned about $185M of option fees in Q1 2026, has 17 counterparties and a 10.7% yield on non-Lennar agreements (Yahoo source above).
- **Caveats:** builders report 200-500 bps of margin compression and Texas has excess inventory (same source). Demand for entitled land is cyclical right now.

### Integration ladder above
Entitlement leads to horizontal development and finished lots (Forestar's model), then build-for-rent or vertical homebuilding, then master-planned community operator. The chain is very large, but every rung is crowded with capitalised incumbents.

### Who else does this
- Local entitlement developers and land brokers.
- Forestar (D.R. Horton), Millrose and Varde.
- Builder in-house land teams.
- Data vendors: Shovels/ReZone, Zoneomics and Bassett.ai (https://www.zoneomics.com/, per the verifier).

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
**Is the ML signal already priced into land?**
1. Pick one fast-growth Sun Belt county with Legistar coverage, such as one exurban Texas or Carolina county.
2. Pull 5 years of rezoning decisions (the Shovels Decisions API free tier, plus scraped staff reports and CIP/sewer PDFs).
3. Train an approval model on features available at the time of application.
4. Benchmark it against a two-feature baseline: staff recommendation plus consistency with the future land-use map.
5. Join model scores to assessor and deed sale prices per acre for parcels sold before their rezoning.

**Kill criteria:**
- the model's AUC beats the baseline by less than 0.05; or
- high-score parcels did not sell at least 30% below comparable hope-value prices.

### Verdict
The buyer, ladder and prize are real. But the rung is an execution-heavy entitlement campaign in an informed land market. The step-up is about 2-4x, and the rezoning outcome is being commoditised into a legible field by Shovels. ML-led discovery is not 80% of the rung, and the land cannot be bought at a deep discount to its proven value.

| Criterion | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 2 | Sellable rung, but the campaign dominates the work |
| C2 Value capture | 2.5 | About 2-3x blended on total capital, multi-$B prize, thin spread |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 3 | Proving is expensive; ML lever about 1.2-1.5x |
| C4 Data + right | 1.5 | Outcome increasingly legible; sellers informed |
| C5 Ladder | 4 | Long, real ladder, but crowded |

**Total: 13/25. Not a Terranox-shaped frame. Do not pursue unless the 2-week pricing test shows a structural discount.**

deep.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)
deep.memo:
## Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage): feasibility deep-dive

*Method note: the shared web-search budget for this turn ran out before my first query, so I could not run any new searches. The evidence below comes from 7 page fetches (the finalist's and verifiers' sources plus the Data Center Watch homepage). Figures marked "est." are my estimates.*

### Frame of reference
The rung is "entitled land": take an option on agricultural parcels, win a rezoning or special exception, then sell to a data center developer. Picking the parcel and predicting the vote from minutes is about 40-50% of the work (est.). The rest is political and legal work, plus proving power through a utility load study, a will-serve letter and a substation. Power is the bespoke physical step, the same pattern as the geothermal counter-example. Even the best case shows this: Kuhn's Twin Creeks site needed a 13.3-acre substation parcel sold to Dominion for $45M ([NoVA Mag](https://northernvirginiamag.com/news/2025/11/06/chuck-kuhn-sells-leesburg-land-to-data-center-developer-for-615-million/)).

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven:** farmland at about $6k/acre in Kentucky and $10.5-23k/acre in Wisconsin ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/02/21/farmer-15-million-dollar-data-center-developers-farmland-prices-preservation-backlash-agriculture-economy), [Dairy News](https://dairynews.today/news/ai_data_centers_drive_up_wisconsin_dairy_land_prices_8754400.html)). Speculative entitlers already pay about $26k/acre for land with no rezoning and no utility commitment: Arizona Land Consulting paid $25M for 956 acres in Tonopah ([Hoodline](https://hoodline.com/2026/05/tonopah-desert-mega-deal-supercharges-data-center-land-grab/)).
- **Proven:** Google paid $42.5M for 948 acres, about $45k/acre, after a C-1 rezoning in Nov 2024 ([Baxtel](https://baxtel.com/data-center/google-monroe-county)). Developers offered $60k/acre in Lancaster PA ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/02/21/farmer-15-million-dollar-data-center-developers-farmland-prices-preservation-backlash-agriculture-economy)). In Loudoun, JK Land paid $57M (mostly 2021) and sold 97 acres for $615M, about $6M/acre ([NoVA Mag](https://northernvirginiamag.com/news/2025/11/06/chuck-kuhn-sells-leesburg-land-to-data-center-developer-for-615-million/)).
- **Ratio:** about 5-10x in greenfield counties and about 11x in the best powered Northern Virginia case, i.e. 10^0.7 to 10^1.
- **Transactions per year:** dozens of large US deals (est.; no source found).

### Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Cost:** about $100-500k per attempt (est.). Rezoning takes 6-12+ months, and 24-36 months or denial under opposition ([Acres](https://www.acres.com/blog/zoning-trajectory-data-center-land-costs)).
- **Base approval rate:** unsourced. My estimate is 50-80% and falling. At least $152-156B of projects were blocked or delayed in 2025, with hundreds of opposition groups active in 42 states ([DCW](https://www.datacenterwatch.org/q3-q4-2025)). Archbald PA denied one project 5-0 in March 2026 ([DCW](https://www.datacenterwatch.org/)).
- **With ML:** about 1.2-1.5x on cost per entitled parcel (est.). The cap comes from two things:
  - The staff recommendation and the opposition data are already legible.
  - Power, which planning records do not show, is a second gate that passes maybe 30-50% of the time (est.).

### Data source
- **What exists:** planning commission agendas, packets, minutes, hearing videos, comprehensive plans and overlay maps for about 3,000 counties. All public, scattered and unstructured.
- **Is the outcome already written down?** Partly. The staff recommendation in the agenda packet is a legible field that likely predicts most votes (untested; this is the C4 kill risk). Opposition is already compiled and sold: Data Center Watch sells project-level data, Paces sells AI power and permitting screens, and Zoneomics sells zoning data for 23,500+ cities via API ([verifier sources](https://www.paces.com/)). Power signals (IRPs, queues) are semi-legible.

### How the right is bought
- **From whom:** private farmland owners, through purchase options.
- **Price:** option fees of about 1-3% of the strike per year (est.), with a strike near farm value plus a premium.
- **Mechanics:** a recorded option with a rezoning-contingent close, plus owner consent to the land-use application.
- **Problem:** sellers can read the opportunity. Press coverage of $35-60k/acre offers is widespread, a land trust outbid a developer in Lancaster, and hyperscalers such as QTS/Compass contract directly with owners on rezoning-contingent terms, so the owner keeps the premium (Pageland, per verifier).
- **Share kept:** an intermediary keeps maybe 20-50% of the uplift, and only in unwatched counties, which are also where power is usually missing (est.).

### Capitalised buyer
Real and very large: Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, SDC and Compass. They pay most for land that has both power and entitlement.

### Integration ladder above
Option, then entitled land, then powered land (substation and interconnection), then a powered shell, then a leased campus, then operator or REIT, possibly with on-site generation. This runs to a very large company. Each rung above entitlement needs $100M+ of capital and utility access, where ML gives no edge.

### Who else does this
- **Asset owners:** Tract, Arizona Land Consulting, JK Land Holdings, brokers and land trusts.
- **Data/analytics sellers:** Paces, Zoneomics and Data Center Watch (10a Labs).

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
Backtest about 100 data center rezoning or special-use votes from 2024-26 in Virginia, Georgia, Indiana and Pennsylvania:
1. Scrape the pre-vote agenda packets and minutes.
2. Fit two predictors: (a) the staff recommendation plus zoning class only, and (b) an LLM reading the full record plus opposition signals.
3. **Kill test:** if (b) beats (a) by less than about 0.05 AUC, or the staff recommendation alone is at least 85% accurate, the illegibility edge is dead.

In parallel, call 15 owners or brokers in "unwatched" counties that have a substation within 5 miles, to learn the option strikes actually on offer.

### Verdict (relaxed rubric)
| | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | 2 | Discovery is not 80%+ of the work; proving power is physical and bespoke. |
| C2 | 3 | Options give leverage: a Kuhn-style ~11x is possible, but only where power and competition already exist. Risk-adjusted, it is about 2-4x on capital in a multi-$B market. |
| C3 | 3 | Proving is expensive, but ML gives at best about 1.2-1.5x. |
| C4 | 2 | The data is illegible, but the staff recommendation and opposition data are legible or already sold. |
| C5 | 4 | A real ladder to a very large company. |

**Total: 14/25. Not excluded.** This is not a Terranox analogue. The ML proves the wrong thing (zoning), while power sets the premium and sellers already know it. Run the 2-week backtest only if the staff-recommendation baseline turns out weak.
